content: Why It’s Not a Bodhisattva or Patriarch BodhiThe old monkey’s shadow image has already helped us eliminate these possibilities. Some say he is Guanyin Bodhisattva. Some say he is Patriarch Bodhi. Others say he is Sun Wukong himself.
heading: Why It’s Not a Bodhisattva or Patriarch Bodhi
title: Who is the Old Monkey in Black Myth Wukong

content: Why It’s Not Patriarch BodhiThe immobilization technique used by the Black Wind Mountain land god was taught by an immortal, who instructed him to pass it on to the Chosen One. Black Wind Mountain Land God Shadow ImageThe image hints at leaves—long and slender with a faint fragrance. These are the characteristics of Bodhi leaves. Bodhi Leaves
heading: Why It’s Not Patriarch Bodhi
title: Who is the Old Monkey in Black Myth Wukong

content: Why It’s Not GuanyinWhen the Chosen One sets off, he will personally make a willow stick for them. Breaking a willow branch to bid farewell, he feels a sense of reluctance. Many people speculate that the old monkey is Guanyin based on the willow stick. The primary function here is clearly the poetic symbolism of breaking a willow branch to bid farewell. Additionally, this is a willow stick, not a willow branch, and there is no hint of the jade vase. What relates to Guanyin is the item used for brewing (unlocked in the second playthrough)—the jade vase and willow leaf. This is a reference to the jade vase and willow leaf. A single willow stick certainly cannot represent Guanyin. Jade Vase and Willow LeafWhat relates to Guanyin is the BOSS Black Bear Spirit, who, after being defeated, says he will return to the South Sea to apologize. If the old monkey were Guanyin, staying in the Flower-Fruit Mountain all along, who would the Black Bear Spirit go back to apologize to??? Black Bear Spirit Defeat CG Animation
heading: Why It’s Not Guanyin
title: Who is the Old Monkey in Black Myth Wukong

content: Why It’s Not Yuan HongFirst, let’s take a step back and assume that Game Science really defaults to Meishan being the Seven Sages, and even follows the “Investiture of the Gods” setting! The old monkey is Buddhist, while Yuan Hong is Taoist, which directly contradicts. Throughout the journey, the Meishan brothers, as a subplot, each mention their elder brother in their dialogue. Why doesn’t the old monkey mention him? The old monkey’s encyclopedia entry is only unlocked in the second playthrough. As a character from “Investiture of the Gods,” is Yuan Hong worthy of such a grand reveal? White-robed scholar, Yellow-robed official, Green-hatted martial artist, Black-handed Taoist, White-axed warrior. Each name has a color, and white is already taken by the white-robed scholar. If it were the White Ape, it wouldn’t fit the naming pattern. (White and white are both white, but they are deliberately distinguished here. The White Ape’s original name is white, so including it would violate the naming rules.)
heading: Why It’s Not Yuan Hong
title: Who is the Old Monkey in Black Myth Wukong

content: Is the Old Monkey Lying?Many people argue the old monkey is lying, but is he really lying? Look at what the old monkey comments on at the end—the six roots. Chapter 1—Eye: Seeing what one likes and wanting to possess it. Elder Jinchi covets the kasaya, desiring material wealth. Chapter 2—Ear: Listening to one-sided words, where good intentions may lead to evil deeds. Lingji, as a Buddha, and Huangfeng, as a demon, each only see their own perspectives, leading to the destruction of Huangfeng Ridge. The scholar, due to a dream, kills an innocent white fox. The side quest involves killing the kind-hearted Shi Zi family. Chapter 3—Nose: Obsessed with emotions, unable to extricate oneself. Kang Jinlong becomes infatuated and falls into depravity, while Huang Mei becomes obsessed with winning and strays from the path. Chapter 4—Tongue: Treating others as mere tools, harming others for personal gain. The world is a furnace, and the fourth sister becomes a pill. The demons of the mortal world are merely materials for the gods. Chapter 5—Body: Fear of disasters, fearing everything, and thus losing everything. The Bull Demon King faces a midlife crisis, losing his wife and children. The Bull Demon King fears everything, and thus loses everything. The old monkey is commenting on the themes and messages of the first five chapters! The conflict between Buddhism and Taoism turns the world into a furnace. The gods are obsessed with spiritual essence, causing all living beings to struggle in the world. Are these thematic lines really lies? Or are they meant to provoke thought? Are Sun Wukong’s desires seen as wrong by Buddhism and Taoism, but are they truly wrong? Was Sun Wukong born mischievous, or is the world inherently unjust? Thus—Chapter 6—in a place unknown to the old monkey, the Great Sage’s will is born—the will to desire. Will to DesirePlease look again at Jin Chanzi’s attitude—non-interventionist pursuit of truth. If he believes the world is unjust, how can he prove it? If he intervenes, wouldn’t he be like Huang Mei, reversing cause and effect? He appears to criticize Sun Wukong, but in reality, he is anticipating Sun Wukong’s own will. The true will to desire does not require external intervention. Like in “Elden Ring,” only by experiencing the suffering and desires of all beings can one forge their own law. In practice, the old monkey is the one who believes in Sun Wukong the most. That’s why he believes he is not gambling, because he trusts that Sun Wukong’s will to desire will be inherited. This process should not and cannot be interfered with. The traces of the journey to the West cannot be erased. Thus, although the old monkey does not know about the will to desire, he knows that Sun Wukong’s essence will be passed down. Experiencing everything, feeling everything, reflecting on everything—this is the Great Sage’s will to desire. What are the Buddhist will clones, the Golden Headband clones? They are all externally imposed and must be rejected!
heading: Is the Old Monkey Lying?
title: Who is the Old Monkey in Black Myth Wukong

content: Will? Enlightenment!True will emerges from reflecting on what one has seen and done. This is why some interpretations frustrate me. Many answers try to prove their own version of the Great Sage, their own version of Jin Chanzi, over-interpreting the ending dialogue. The official shadow images make it clear, but people refuse to connect or believe them. It seems that interpretations always aim to be grander, more unique. Well, let me say this: all those theories about Buddhist will, Yuan Hong, Guanyin, Taibai Jinxing, Six-Eared Macaque, and Sun Wukong are nonsense! The Jin Chanzi theory is lofty enough. Unity of knowledge and action, unbound by Buddhism, unbound by Taoism, transcending the three realms, existing beyond the five elements. —Only such a will is worthy of the Great Sage and the journey to the West.
heading: Will? Enlightenment!
title: Who is the Old Monkey in Black Myth Wukong

content: A passing thought, still unfinished. If I have gotten something wrong, feel free to correct me. Clever ideas often look especially simple, so simple that people start to think they were obvious all along. But don’t assume those ideas are obvious, because they absolutely are not. Clever ideas seem too simple only because we see the final result. The mess in the middle has been cleaned away. The false starts go unmentioned. The beginning of the problem gets brushed past. All the paths that once seemed possible disappear with it. The irony is that ideas that end up shaping how later generations think are eventually treated by the young as plain and unremarkable. ——3Blue1Brown People often say empirical economics papers are obvious in hindsight: either post hoc, or just confirming what everyone already intuits. In that view, only papers with predictive power or counterintuitive conclusions really count as valuable. Here I want to push back from a few angles and explain why an intuitive result is not necessarily an obvious one.
title: Empirical economics: intuitive does not mean obvious

content: Intuitive conclusions can contradict each otherSome people think social welfare helps fertility. That feels intuitive, because it lowers the cost of raising children. Some people think social welfare hurts fertility. That also feels intuitive, because children can function as old-age support, and social welfare lowers the need for that support. Some people think housing creates a wealth effect. This one needs a bit more explanation. Disposable income obviously affects consumption, but Friedman also argued that a key factor behind consumption is permanent income. Assets such as housing fit into that picture and can encourage spending. Others argue for a house-poor effect instead: housing mortgages squeeze consumption. Beyond rational consumption decisions, behavioral economics is full of contradictions too when it comes to “irrational” consumption. Peer effects suggest that seeing others spend more will push up one’s own spending. Prospect theory suggests that people make decisions relative to reference points, so expected income shapes consumption. Mental accounting, meanwhile, says people experience different kinds of spending differently; for example, people are often more willing to spend on education and healthcare. So what empirical papers need to do is sort out the boundary conditions of intuitive conclusions. Which institution is causing the effect? Which effect is actually operating? Under what social conditions does it hold?
heading: Intuitive conclusions can contradict each other
title: Empirical economics: intuitive does not mean obvious

content: Intuitive conclusions are not easy to arrive atWith the explosion in popularity of Black Myth: Wukong, Chinese gamers have been arguing online about the size of the domestic single-player market. A lot of people directly use Palworld sales as a benchmark. That is obviously not right. At the very least, the structure should look something like this: $$黑神话销量 \times 黑神话价格 = 帕鲁价格 \times 帕鲁销量$$ A more careful estimate would also have to consider income levels, population structure, game quality, marketing, genre, and so on. But let us assume all of those are the same, and let us even assume that the utility from spending x yuan on a game is simply x. Now add one more seemingly obvious proposition - the higher the price, the lower the demand - and something interesting happens. Even within the same single-player market, different prices change the realized market size. The aggregate may look identical in some abstract sense, but the actual market scale still moves with pricing.
heading: Intuitive conclusions are not easy to arrive at
title: Empirical economics: intuitive does not mean obvious

content: Counterintuition hides behind intuitionI want to use one of Feynman’s examples. You ask why someone slipped on the ice. Why did he slip? Because he was on ice. Why is ice slippery? Because under pressure, ice melts into water? Why does ice melt into water under pressure? Because that is how matter behaves under force. And just like that, we arrive at mechanics, then particles, then the place where things stop feeling intuitive. Here is another example. Students in physics, mathematics, and economics are all familiar with the brachistochrone problem. The starting point is simple enough: light refracts. Put a chopstick into water and it looks bent. The high-school explanation is that light travels at different speeds in different media, so the angle of refraction depends on those speeds. But a deeper question follows: why should light - why should nature - pursue this kind of optimization in time? Does saving time matter to light? That is where quantum mechanics later gives us the idea of “action.” Put simply, light tries every path, but the inefficient ones are canceled out by interference, leaving only the most efficient path in the end. Social science and scienceA scientific question: is theoretical science invented, or discovered. At the theoretical level, both natural science and social science seem to begin by recognizing patterns. The key is what pattern we recognize in what phenomenon. I can recognize different patterns in the same phenomenon, and I can also extract the same pattern from different phenomena. Simple questions can also rise into a perspective: Common sense may be widely shared, but the principles behind common sense are not themselves common sense. A paper in China Economic Quarterly titled “Climate change increases household electricity consumption: from the perspective of adaptive behavior” uses air-conditioning data. The argument is that earlier work mostly studied climate improvement itself, whereas air-conditioner consumption is a form of human adaptation to climate change, so AC data can be studied from an adaptation perspective. A Nature sub-journal paper does something similar with food delivery under extreme heat: Urban food delivery services as extreme heat adaptation. The financial crisis had long-lasting effects, and so did the Great Famine. So people began studying how those who lived through particular historical periods make decisions later in life, shaped by those experiences. That is where economics gets cohort effects: people who went through the same historical environment tend to share certain traits. Dragon years tend to bring baby booms, because in China the dragon is a favored zodiac sign. At the same time, research finds that Dragon-year babies often perform better later on. One explanation is that if parents deliberately choose a Dragon year, that signals high expectations, and they also invest more care and effort. The pattern researchers uncover, then, is the self-fulfilling power of a superstition. It is exactly the old idea of believing in belief itself. US data show that transgender people smoke more frequently. At first glance that sounds pretty dull, but the perspective drawn from it is minority status and stress consumption. From primary school onward, we are taught to move from the small to the large. Elegant mathematical models and good analysis of social phenomena work the same way: they generalize from the particular.
heading: Counterintuition hides behind intuition
title: Empirical economics: intuitive does not mean obvious

content: On intuitionA lot of people like to use the term “research taste.” Some even start mixing Chinese and English at this point and say taste in English. I dislike this tendency to mystify research design. Research is not mysterious, and it does not need to be genuinely counterintuitive. Every study moves forward by standing on the shoulders of earlier work. Just because each small innovation fits intuition does not mean it contributes nothing. What matters is summarizing what earlier work has taught us and refining a genuinely fresh perspective.
heading: On intuition
title: Empirical economics: intuitive does not mean obvious

content: Site runtime with multilingual supportAdd the site runtime and total blog word count to the footer, with automatic multilingual switching: The effect looks like this: Chinese and English comparisonA typical multilingual Hugo blog has an i18n file, whose purpose is to read the page language parameter and then replace the corresponding text.
heading: Site runtime with multilingual support
title: Hugo Customization 2

content: Total word countAdding a total blog word countFind <your blog folder>\layouts\partials\footer.html, and add the following code inside it: {{ $articleCount := len .Site.RegularPages }} {{ $totalWordCount := 0 }} {{ range .Site.Pages }} {{ $totalWordCount = add $totalWordCount .WordCount }} {{ end }} {{ i18n "articleCount" (dict "Count" $articleCount) }}，{{ i18n "totalWordCount" (dict "WordCount" $totalWordCount) }}。Then find <your blog folder>\i18n and add the following in zh-CN.toml: # === footer/wordcount === [articleCount] other = "发布了 {{ .Count }} 篇文章" [totalWordCount] other = "共 {{ .WordCount }} 字"and add the following in en.toml: # === footer/wordcount === [articleCount] other = "published {{ .Count }} posts" [totalWordCount] other = "total {{ .WordCount }} words"Multilingual switching is clearly a one-to-one character match. So in the i18n file, each [call name] can only have one other=, and [call names] must not be duplicated, so that characters can be switched one-to-one automatically. A bugIf, like me, you added a music player to every blog post page via aplayer, you’ll hit a bug. Hugo’s built-in word count conflicts with aplayer. A pure-music player will disappear, while a player with lyrics might stick around. The reason is unknown. When rendering locally, updating the blog content and triggering a refresh makes the music player reappear, but after uploading to GitHub for rendering it doesn’t work. Updated February 21, 2026Recently I used Claude Code with the DeepSeek v3.2 model to test this bug. I found the music plugin’s failure is roughly due to this: The LoveIt theme uses Hugo’s Scratch system as a “feature flag” mechanism: The music shortcode sets this when it executes: {{- .Page.Scratch.SetInMap "this" "music" true -}} assets.html checks: {{- if (.Scratch.Get "this").music -}} to load the music assets. wordcount.html introduces a change: {{- $posts := where .Site.RegularPages "Type" "posts" -}} {{- range $posts -}} {{- $totalWords = add $totalWords .WordCount -}} {{- $totalPosts = add $totalPosts 1 -}} {{- end -}}When Hugo executes .Site.RegularPages: To get the WordCount, Hugo needs to compute each post’s content, which resets the page’s Scratch state. In the process, the Scratch state that was maintained within a single rendering pass gets disturbed. My personal observation is that whether a comment plugin is installed also affects this bug, seemingly for the same reason — the Scratch state value appears to be cleared. In the comment section, layouts/partials/comment.html has code like this: {{- dict "comment" $commentConfig | dict "config" | merge (.Scratch.Get "this") | .Scratch.Set "this" -}}Local rendering can reload the this map in scratch by updating the site, but after uploading to GitHub it tends to get mapped to empty. The modified flow: Previous flow: music shortcode → Scratch set → theme conditional check → load assets Modified flow: directly detect the DOM → dynamically load assets → self-initializeLooking back, this bug is quite similar to the one in Chinese blog TOC navigation failure.

content: Site runtimeAdding a custom custom.jsCreate a custom JavaScript file \static\js\custom.js in the site root directory. Write the following code into it: /* Site runtime */ // Get the current language setting function getCurrentLanguage() { // Assume you have a global variable or method to get the current language return document.documentElement.lang || 'zh'; // Defaults to Chinese } // Update the site runtime function runtime() { window.setTimeout(runtime, 1000); let startTime = new Date('02/18/2024 15:00:00'); //Write your own site launch time here let endTime = new Date(); let usedTime = endTime - startTime; let days = Math.floor(usedTime / (24 * 3600 * 1000)); let leavel = usedTime % (24 * 3600 * 1000); let hours = Math.floor(leavel / (3600 * 1000)); let leavel2 = leavel % (3600 * 1000); let minutes = Math.floor(leavel2 / (60 * 1000)); let leavel3 = leavel2 % (60 * 1000); let seconds = Math.floor(leavel3 / (1000)); // Select the corresponding text based on the language setting let language = getCurrentLanguage(); let runtimeText; if (language === 'zh') { runtimeText = '本站已运行 ' + ((days < 10) ? '0' : '') + days + ' 天 ' + ((hours < 10) ? '0' : '') + hours + ' 时 ' + ((minutes < 10) ? '0' : '') + minutes + ' 分 ' + ((seconds < 10) ? '0' : '') + seconds + ' 秒 '; } else if (language === 'en') { runtimeText = 'Running for ' + ((days < 10) ? '0' : '') + days + ' d ' + ((hours < 10) ? '0' : '') + hours + ' h ' + ((minutes < 10) ? '0' : '') + minutes + ' m ' + ((seconds < 10) ? '0' : '') + seconds + ' s '; } else { // Default text (you can choose another language or keep Chinese/English) runtimeText = '本站已运行 ' + ((days < 10) ? '0' : '') + days + ' 天 ' + ((hours < 10) ? '0' : '') + hours + ' 时 ' + ((minutes < 10) ? '0' : '') + minutes + ' 分 ' + ((seconds < 10) ? '0' : '') + seconds + ' 秒 '; } // Update the content on the page document.getElementById('run-time').innerHTML = runtimeText; } runtime();Those who are interested can also check out this site’s complete custom.js. Find <your blog folder>\layouts\partials\assets.html, and add the following code on the line above the {{- partial "plugin/analytics.html" . -}} at the very end: {{- /* custom js file */ -}} This way the blog can call the custom js file. Other js files can be written here too. Modifying i18nFind <your blog folder>\i18n Add the following in zh-CN.toml: [runtime] other = "本站已运行{{ .Days }}天 {{ .Hours }}小时 {{ .Minutes }}分钟 {{ .Seconds }}秒"Add the following in en.toml: [runtime] other = "The site has been running for {{ .Days }} days {{ .Hours }} hours {{ .Minutes }} minutes {{ .Seconds }} seconds"

Write the following code into it: /* Site runtime */ // Get the current language setting function getCurrentLanguage() { // Assume you have a global variable or method to get the current language return document.documentElement.lang || 'zh'; // Defaults to Chinese } // Update the site runtime function runtime() { window.setTimeout(runtime, 1000); let startTime = new Date('02/18/2024 15:00:00'); //Write your own site launch time here let endTime = new Date(); let usedTime = endTime - startTime; let days = Math.floor(usedTime / (24 * 3600 * 1000)); let leavel = usedTime % (24 * 3600 * 1000); let hours = Math.floor(leavel / (3600 * 1000)); let leavel2 = leavel % (3600 * 1000); let minutes = Math.floor(leavel2 / (60 * 1000)); let leavel3 = leavel2 % (60 * 1000); let seconds = Math.floor(leavel3 / (1000)); // Select the corresponding text based on the language setting let language = getCurrentLanguage(); let runtimeText; if (language === 'zh') { runtimeText = '本站已运行 ' + ((days < 10) ? '0' : '') + days + ' 天 ' + ((hours < 10) ? '0' : '') + hours + ' 时 ' + ((minutes < 10) ? '0' : '') + minutes + ' 分 ' + ((seconds < 10) ? '0' : '') + seconds + ' 秒 '; } else if (language === 'en') { runtimeText = 'Running for ' + ((days < 10) ? '0' : '') + days + ' d ' + ((hours < 10) ? '0' : '') + hours + ' h ' + ((minutes < 10) ? '0' : '') + minutes + ' m ' + ((seconds < 10) ? '0' : '') + seconds + ' s '; } else { // Default text (you can choose another language or keep Chinese/English) runtimeText = '本站已运行 ' + ((days < 10) ? '0' : '') + days + ' 天 ' + ((hours < 10) ? '0' : '') + hours + ' 时 ' + ((minutes < 10) ? '0' : '') + minutes + ' 分 ' + ((seconds < 10) ? '0' : '') + seconds + ' 秒 '; } // Update the content on the page document.getElementById('run-time').innerHTML = runtimeText; } runtime();Those who are interested can also check out this site’s complete custom.js. Find <your blog folder>\layouts\partials\assets.html, and add the following code on the line above the {{- partial "plugin/analytics.html" . -}} at the very end: {{- /* custom js file */ -}} This way the blog can call the custom js file. Other js files can be written here too. Modifying i18nFind <your blog folder>\i18n Add the following in zh-CN.toml: [runtime] other = "本站已运行{{ .Days }}天 {{ .Hours }}小时 {{ .Minutes }}分钟 {{ .Seconds }}秒"Add the following in en.toml: [runtime] other = "The site has been running for {{ .Days }} days {{ .Hours }} hours {{ .Minutes }} minutes {{ .Seconds }} seconds"

content: Rendering math formulas in the blogAlthough the LoveIt theme provides math formula support via KaTeX, I personally think the experience is not as good as MathJax. To use MathJax, first create mathjax.html in <your blog>\layouts\partials. mathjax.html: right-click on the site’s formulas to support copying the formula code. As shown{{ if .Params.math }} {{ end }}Then add the call in <your blog>\layouts\partials\header.html: {{ partial "mathjax.html" . }}In each post, to enable math formula rendering, put this at the top: Math = trueSince Hugo, when rendering Markdown documents, generates HTML based on syntax like _/*/>>, and some escaped-character text (like \(/\)/\[/\]/\\) gets escaped automatically, you need extra escape-character expressions in these places to enable automatic rendering: _ -> \_ * -> \* >> -> \>> \( -> \\( \) -> \\) \[ -> \\[ \] -> \\] \\ -> \\\\ For example, if I render the following formula: \[ V(\varepsilon)=\int_{0}^{T}F[t,\underbrace{y^{*}\left(t\right)+\varepsilon p\left(t\right)}_{y(t)},\underbrace{y^{*}\left(t\right)+\varepsilon p^{\prime}\left(t\right)}_{y^{’}\left(t\right)}]dt \]It will actually become: $$ V （\varepsilon）=\int_{0}^{T}F[t,\underbrace{y^{*}\left （t\right）+\varepsilon p\left （t\right）}_{y （t）},\underbrace{y^{*}\left （t\right）+\varepsilon p^{\prime}\left （t\right）}_{y^{’}\left （t\right）}]dt $$ Only by converting to \_ ^\* \\[ \\] is it correct: \\[ V(\varepsilon)=\int\_{0}^{T}F[t,\underbrace{y^{\*}\left(t\right)+\varepsilon p\left(t\right)}\_{y(t)},\underbrace{y^{\*}\left(t\right)+\varepsilon p^{\prime}\left(t\right)}\_{y^{'}\left(t\right)}]dt \\]\[ V （\varepsilon）=\int_{0}^{T}F[t,\underbrace{y^{*}\left （t\right）+\varepsilon p\left （t\right）}_{y （t）},\underbrace{y^{*}\left （t\right）+\varepsilon p^{\prime}\left （t\right）}_{y^{’}\left （t\right）}]dt \] But in my own experience, sometimes converting only half the commands in a formula is enough for it to render — how many commands to convert seems related to rendering complexity. For example, I render $2\_i^\*-2_j^*$ — $2_i^\*-2_j^*$, and since the formula is simple, it renders the same whether or not I convert the commands.

title: Ace Attorney review: the path to a turnabout lies within

content: Philosophy matters more than logicThink about the kind of turnabout philosophy you can find in other games: 《Death Stranding》: ropes meant for protection and sticks meant for attack switch places. 《Red Dead Redemption 2》: instead of showing the glory days of the West, it shows an era and a protagonist already in decline. 《Elden Ring》: it is not that the enemies and levels keep getting harder; it is that the player keeps getting stronger. 《Honkai Impact 3rd》: it is not Fu Hua turning into a Herrscher, but the Herrscher turning into Fu Hua. 《In/Spectre》: the protagonist has to fabricate the truth instead of exposing it. These examples are not meant to say that every design above is “turnabout thinking.” I only want to say— “if you look at a problem through a framework that flips one of its key elements, you can end up with a surprisingly interesting perspective.” In a familiar detective setup where clues are used to catch the criminal, how do you reverse it? You make a game where evidence is used to defend the suspect! Do not think about what evidence can prove the criminal did. Think instead about what consequences must follow once the criminal has done it. Do not ask why the culprit wanted to do it. Ask instead about the reason the culprit had no choice but to do it. To me, the elegance of Ace Attorney lies in the way it brings in a turnabout-like philosophical perspective rather than airtight logical deduction. (If you want to pick apart the cases, you definitely can.)
heading: Philosophy matters more than logic
title: Ace Attorney review: the path to a turnabout lies within

content: Rhythmic expressionUsing courtroom debate as its core mechanic, Ace Attorney attacks by finding holes in testimony and presenting evidence. Paired with the “Hold it! Objection! Take that!” voice clips, the trials give you the thrill of trading moves in a turn-based battle. The unbeatable speech bubbleEvery character has a distinct animation set, and the controller rumbles a lot, too. As for the way each case builds, the way the characters perform, and the way the BGM rises at exactly the right time, there is not much more I need to add. The one weak point is that when several pieces of evidence relate to several statements, the game often expects a strict one-to-one match, and that can be misleading. The story works more as suspense than deduction. In other words, the pleasure comes from seeing earlier setup pay off, not from predicting the big reversal in advance. When the ending suddenly runs through everything that came before it, that is the moment when even the toughest player starts tearing up. The true ending is always written for the people who stay with the whole story. That is where Shu Takumi is strongest. What I like even more is the rhythm of thematic escalation across the cases in games 1 through 3. First layer: the lawyer’s stance, the pursuit of innocence. At this stage, the core idea is to let the evidence speak, fight to the very end, and never give up on the defense. Second layer: the prosecution enters, and the focus shifts to truth and trust After the first game lays the groundwork, the defense attorney feels almost heroic. But then what about the prosecution, the side responsible for securing a conviction? The defense pursues innocence, and the prosecution pursues guilt. When the same piece of evidence is pulled back and forth by both sides, it becomes possible to see it from a more objective angle. Truth is born from that struggle between guilt and innocence. What matters in a courtroom system is that both sides can trust it. If each side fully carries through its own convictions, truth has a chance to emerge from the collision. Third layer: the player’s own sense of ethics The setting may be fictional, but ethical philosophy always shines in thought experiments. In the game, innocence is the result the player chases, and it usually lines up with a happy ending. But what if innocence leads to the bad ending instead? That is the contradiction the defense has to face. An innocent verdict that hurts people, and a guilty verdict that comforts them: the game throws out the question and refuses to hand over an answer. (Still, when the friendship-and-bonds energy kicks in, it absolutely works.)
heading: Rhythmic expression
title: Ace Attorney review: the path to a turnabout lies within

content: Visual novels never really endEven though Ace Attorney is not a galgame, its pixel look and looping BGM always remind me of 16bit Sensation. Even rough technology can still produce a great story. Even if the story has already drawn to a close, a brief moment of persistence might still spark a miracle. A lawyer should smile more when things get dangerous. Maybe that is the final turnabout spirit. Trust in your client, trust in your opponent, digging into contradictions, pursuing the truth, the will to never give up…… It can all begin with a single line— “異議あり!” Objection!
heading: Visual novels never really end
title: Ace Attorney review: the path to a turnabout lies within

content: The essentialsThe paper Pensions and Fertility: Microeconomic Evidence uses Brazilian microdata to study the relationship between pension provision and fertility. Conclusion: Viewed through economic circulation and factor substitution, one traditional role of raising children is old-age support. Naturally, the provision of pensions eases that worry, so fertility falls. Contribution: Historical experience shows that fertility fell around the time many high- and middle-income countries introduced or expanded their social security systems1🤯. On the mechanism side of how fiscal public policy affects fertility, there’s relatively little research, and most of it uses OLG macro models; this paper uses micro analysis. Econometric design: I quite like this paper’s econometric design. It studies how a pension reform affects women’s fertility decisions, and since women in different states should react differently, it adds event-study analysis across different women’s groups to strengthen the argument.
heading: The essentials
title: Pensions and Fertility

content: Theoretical and real-world background
heading: Theoretical and real-world background
title: Pensions and Fertility

content: TheoryPeople say Chinese papers love to coin terms, but doesn’t this AER paper coin a bunch of its own terms in its theoretical explanations? It even goes out of its way to phrase things convolutedly to highlight a made-up effect. But correspondingly, the interesting part of this paper is how it decomposes fertility decisions and summarizes them into quantifiable constraints. Women’s ageSurvival effect: Before and after the pension reform, there are both new and old women; old women already have two children and face lower fertility risk. Information effect: older women are more familiar with childrearing and so won’t hoard children. Saturation effect: mothers who have already reached their desired number of children, or are in the late stage of childbearing, will reduce their likelihood of having children. Pension wealth effect: mothers near retirement and young mothers get different discounted pension streams from the reform, so their decisions react differently. Salience effect: the more obvious the pension reform’s outcome, the more salient people’s reaction2. Consider a woman’s decision to have a child. Her decision basis includes her own physical suitability for pregnancy and the number and gender composition of children she already has. Young mothers will react more readily to the pension reform, while older mothers react less; comparing the two groups’ data makes the paper’s analysis more credible. Number and structure of childrenThe more children before the reform, the less likely to add another birth. The more sons a family has before the reform3, the less likely to add another birth.
heading: Theory
title: Pensions and Fertility

content: RealitySince the mid-twentieth century, under the influence of urbanization, medical care, education, and other expansions, Brazil’s fertility fell sharply. Against this backdrop, Brazil carried out a comprehensive pension reform. Before the 1970s, only urban workers with formal jobs were entitled to scattered, occupation-specific pensions, but the reform in the October 1988 constitution of the Federative Republic of Brazil significantly expanded pension coverage, giving rural workers pension benefits for the first time in Brazilian history. The pension reform took effect after being legally approved in July 1991. For urban workers, the pension rules and benefits barely changed. But for rural workers, regardless of whether they had formal employment or paid any social security contributions, women (men) became eligible for a pension from age 55 (60). It is precisely against this historical background that, in the paper’s event study, 1988 became the event check contrasting with 1991.
heading: Reality
title: Pensions and Fertility

content: Data and methods
heading: Data and methods
title: Pensions and Fertility

content: APC panelThe paper uses multiple cross-sections from the Brazilian National Household Sample Survey (PNAD), covering the years 1981-1990, 1992-1993, 1995-1999, 2001-2009, and 2011-2014. On APC panels — see my earlier note: HLT: Lifecycle and Wage Decomposition, section one. Although the paper uses an APC panel, it doesn’t actually decompose the relevant effects; instead it restricts the age cohorts and then uses event-study analysis to compare how differently people react to the policy. A supplement on APC panels and the three effectsPanel data tracking the same individuals is always hard to obtain, so people turned to long cross-sections, matching multiple cross-sections together. This kind of panel data is common in epidemiological and demographic statistics and is called APC (age-period-cohort) data. Obviously, an APC panel contains three data dimensions. Age: age, i.e. the influence of biological characteristics. For example, age’s biological characteristics can divide fertility suitability, labor-force quality…… Period: the time when the cross-section was collected, e.g. the technology level and infrastructure level at the time of each year’s census…… Cohort: the birth year/month of each cross-section, generally seen as a group that jointly experienced certain social environments or historical events, and hence is similar. Since age+cohort=period, these variables are often confounded, and collinearity arises in practice. In econometrics, one often first estimates one of the effects through some means (a clever difference based on the object’s characteristics) and then regresses the remainder; or imposes additional linear constraints on the regression; or uses high-order differences (like individual-effect estimation) to estimate the three effects separately. Demography often uses APC panels to draw Lexis diagrams: The horizontal and vertical axes are period time and age time, and the lines in between are grouped by cohort; analysis and prediction unfold by comparing the trends and differences of the lines. content: Variables and the econometric specificationDependent variablesShort-run effect: equals 1 if the woman gave birth within one year of the data-collection year, and 0 otherwise (based on the household roster and birth data). The sample includes female respondents of childbearing age (15 to 44) from 1981 to 1999. Long-run effect: the total number of children of a woman at age 45 (including surviving and deceased children). The sample includes female respondents born between 1930 and 1969, who were aged 45 to 69 in the given survey year. The authors trace the total births of respondents older than 45 in the survey year (1984-2014) back to their fertility at age 45 (1975-2014). The treated group is urban workers; the control group is rural workers. The econometric regressionDifference-in-differences$$ \begin{aligned}y \_{igtr}^{SR}&= \alpha^{SR}+\beta\big(RURAL \_{g}^{SR}\times POST \_{t}^{SR}\big)\\\\&+ \gamma RURAL \_{g}^{SR}+\lambda_{t}^{SR}+\phi \_{r}^{SR}+\psi^{\prime}\mathbf{X} \_{igtr}^{SR}+\epsilon_{igtr}^{SR} \end{aligned} $$ Subscripts: r region, g rural-urban group, i individual, t year, r state. $y_{igtr}^{SR}$: the short-run effect. Gave birth within one year of the survey year. $RURAL_{g}^{SR}$: dummy for rural-worker women. $POST_{t}^{SR}$: dummy for the July 1991 rural pension policy reform. $\mathbf{X}\_{igtr}^{SR}$: controls for individual, job, family, and region-level characteristics. Effects: time effects $\lambda_{t}^{SR}$, individual effects $\phi_{r}^{SR}$, robust clustering at the federal-state level. The pension reform lowered fertility in the short run; In the group regression, the young group (15-29) is insignificant, while the older group (30-44) shows a significant fertility decline; the more children there are, and the higher the proportion of sons, the lower the desire for more children. Instrumental variablesTreat the DID (differences in the pension-reform policy implementation) as an instrument for pensions ($\ln(pensionwealth)_{igtr}$). First stage: $$ \begin{aligned}\ln(pensionwealth)\_{igtr}&= \sigma^{SR}+\theta\big(RURAL\_{g}^{SR}\times POST\_{t}^{SR}\big)\\\\&+\eta RURAL\_{g}^{SR}+\delta\_{t}^{SR}+\tau\_{r}^{SR}+\kappa^{\prime}\mathbf{X}\_{igtr}^{SR}+\mu\_{igtr}^{SR}\end{aligned} $$ Second stage: $$ \begin{aligned}y\_{igtr}^{SR}&=\alpha^{SR}+\beta\ln\left(\widehat{pensionwealth}\right)\_{igrt}\\\\&+\gamma RURAL\_g^{SR}+\lambda\_t^{SR}+\phi\_r^{SR}+\psi^{\prime}\mathbf{X}\_{igtr}^{SR}+\epsilon\_{igtr}^{SR}\end{aligned} $$ Event studyOn event studies, see Econometrics: Event Studies 1. In short, an event study can be viewed as the dynamic treatment effect of difference-in-differences. In terms of the equation, this means time-slicing the policy variable $POST_{t}^{SR}$ and expanding it into $\sum YEAR_T^{LR}$. $$ \begin{aligned}y\_{igtr}^{LR}&=\alpha^{LR}+\sum_{t=-16}^{23}\beta_t\big(RURAL\_g^{LR}\times YEAR_t^{LR}\big)\\\\&+\gamma RURAL_g^{LR}+\lambda\_t^{LR}+\phi\_r^{LR}+\psi^{\prime}\mathbf{X}\_{iglr}^{LR}+\epsilon\_{iglr}^{LR},\end{aligned} $$ Subscripts: r region, g rural-urban group, i individual, t year, r state. $y_{igtr}^{LR}$: the long-run effect. Total number of children at age 45. $RURAL_{g}^{LR}$: dummy for rural-worker women. $YEAR_{t}^{LR}$: policy-time dummy. $\mathbf{X}\_{igtr}^{SR}$: controls for years of education, marriage dummy, and lifetime labor supply. Effects: cohort effects $\lambda_{t}^{LR}$, individual effects $\phi_{r}^{LR}$, robust clustering at the federal-state level. In the difference-in-differences part, $\lambda_{t}$ is the survey-year time dummy, a time effect representing the technology level, medical level, and infrastructure at the time the data were collected; In the event-study part, $\lambda_{t}$ is the birth-year time dummy, used to flag that a particular group experienced a particular historical social environment. In the difference-in-differences part, $\lambda_{t}$ is the survey-year time dummy, a time effect representing the technology level, medical level, and infrastructure at the time the data were collected; In the event-study part, $\lambda_{t}$ is the birth-year time dummy, used to flag that a particular group experienced a particular historical social environment. heading: Confounders
title: Pensions and Fertility

content: RobustnessAlternative age-band group regressions for comparison: use new age bands to compare the fertility responses of different cohorts of women to the pension policy. Alternative econometric specifications: add education level as a control; linear time trends, linear time-region; distinguish whether the respondent lives with a pension recipient. Sample selection: (1) three types of sample draws: the non-self-representative municipality sample frame; self-representative areas; metropolitan areas. (2) Tighten the definition and scope of the treated and control groups based on individual occupation, home address, and parents’ occupation. (3) Add rural-urban samples where husband and wife work in different occupational fields. (4) Exclude women under 15 and over 44. (5) Exclude women who gave birth past 45. Standard errors: in addition to state-level clustering, add clustering at the settlement level. To address autocorrelation, subtract the pre- and post-treatment result means respectively.
heading: Robustness
title: Pensions and Fertility

content: ConclusionI want to summarize this paper’s conclusion from the angles of elevation and detail. It verifies the historical experience — pension expansion may lower fertility. Elevation: public welfare spending may carry a certain policy cost; there is a mechanism linking social welfare and population change. Detail: as mentioned above. This paper’s highlight is combining the context of Brazil’s 1981 and 1991 reforms, and strengthening the rural-urban and women’s-age-group comparisons, so the event study is also used well. Some personal doubts. Why don’t most people think to link pension services to fertility? Because everyone assumes pension recipients have already lost the ability to become pregnant. So this is an expectations problem: women expect future pension income, so their fertility decisions change. The paper never proves this logic chain with econometric data; it’s mainly argued through social and historical background analysis. Framed this way, the question instantly becomes interesting. ↩︎ My understanding here is to emphasize that people did form expectations about the pension reform, thereby changing their fertility decisions. ↩︎ The paper uses Brazilian land-inheritance data as evidence of son preference; most Brazilian land is inherited by men. ↩︎ The paper adds event-study analysis based on historical background; I think the fit is perfect. ↩︎
heading: Conclusion
title: Pensions and Fertility

content: Appendix B: Parameter restrictions for Timing-basedWhen estimating event effects in DID, you generally don’t add a time trend, but you do add individual fixed effects and time fixed effects, whose role is to decompose the intercept. The usual ways to handle collinearity are to default $t_{-1}$ to 0, merge or drop some variables, impose other constraints, or make it nonlinear…… For the Timing-based data form, since there is no control group, we can only compare within the treated group. More parameter restrictions are needed. The variation in event timing is itself part of the information. The larger the minimum difference in event timing across treated groups, the more information is lost. The more individuals there are, the more information there is. So what Appendix B’s code studies is — When studying a Timing-based data structure, for different timing and individual distributions, how many additional parameters are needed to solve the problem? My understanding: this may be a matter of building a system of equations through a series of regressions, forming a matrix from the system, and then judging via the matrix’s rank how many more parameter constraints are needed before it can be solved. Appendix B code output: a figure the authors say is very strangeLet me explain what Appendix B’s output figure means. First, take a dataset where everyone receives the event shock, but the event timing differs. In the initially generated dataset, the event shock times are 4 and 16. At this point the additional constraint parameters needed to solve are 12 (which can be understood as how many degrees of freedom are still missing). Here’s what the figure means: First look at the first column of blue dots. When you add other samples whose event shock time is 4 (the x-axis), no extra information is added. The whole dataset is still two types of samples — event shock time 4 or 16 — so the additional parameters needed to solve are still 12 (the y-axis). Similarly, the second column of blue dots means that when you add a third group of samples with shock time 5, the difference in event timing shrinks and information increases, so the additional parameters needed drop to 1. The red triangles mean: on top of the dots in each column, what happens to the parameters needed when you add the samples the triangles represent. I originally expected that, given a fixed timing difference, the more individual groups there are, the fewer additional parameters would be needed. It turns out only the fifth column behaves that way, which is why the paper says this is strange and worth studying — though the author doesn’t know why either. The following code has comments added via GPT: #delimit ; cap log close ; set trace off ; set more off ; clear all ; set seed 101 ; cap prog drop runme ; prog def runme ; args list ctrl trends ; qui gendata "`list'" `ctrl' `trends' ; qui forvalues i = 0/20 { ; gen D_p`i' = (etime == `i') ; // generate the positive treated-group dummy gen D_m`i' = (etime == -1 * `i') ; // generate the negative treated-group dummy summ D_p`i' ; // summarize the positive treated-group dummy local dropme = (r(mean) == 0) ; if `dropme' == 1 { ; drop D_p`i' ; // if the mean is 0, drop the positive treated-group dummy } ; summ D_m`i' ; // summarize the negative treated-group dummy local dropme = (r(mean) == 0) ; if `dropme' == 1 { ; drop D_m`i' ; // if the mean is 0, drop the negative treated-group dummy } ; } ; drop D_m0 ; // drop the baseline case of the negative treated-group dummy egen unittype = group(E_i) , miss ; // generate a unit-type variable from E_i, handling missing values qui tab unittype , gen(udum) ; // summarize the unit-type variable and generate the corresponding dummies qui tab t , gen(tdum) ; // summarize the time variable and generate the corresponding dummies unab vars : D_* udum* tdum* ; // generate the variable list for everything related to D_*, udum*, and tdum* mata: count() ;

content: Appendix C: Choosing the estimatorThere are currently two kinds of estimator choices: Constrain the coefficient of the pre-event period variable to 0 Constrain the sum of the pre-event dummy variable coefficients to 0 Estimation under different constraints; both estimators use individual fixed effects summing to 0The code in this part is a simulation experiment. First, generate the treatment effect according to the conditions, with the treatment effect fixed at 1 (the red line in the figure is the actually generated treatment effect). Then add a random noise term, and finally run the regression. The constraint on the left normalizes the pre-event period; the constraint on the right constrains the pre-event dummies. You can see the right one is closer to the actual treatment effect (the red line). The following code has comments by GPT, with some corrections by me. content: Appendix D: Approaching the raw dataDID gets deified again and again 🤣（ Appendix D can essentially be understood as a decomposition that adds a time trend (a slope comparison). The code structure is the same as before; what’s added this time is predicting the counterfactual group, and using it to strengthen the causal argument through another comparison. /* create the counterfactual prediction cf_ES2 */ gen cf_ES2 = y ; // initialize cf_ES2 as the observed variable y /* loop over the time range */ qui summ etime ; // get summary statistics of etime local mymin = r(min) ; // get the minimum local mymax = r(max) ; // get the maximum forvalues i = `mymin'/`mymax' { // loop over the time range if `i' < 0 { // if time is less than 0 local j = abs(`i') ; // take the absolute value replace cf_ES2 = cf_ES2 - _b[D_m`j'] * D_m`j' ; // subtract the treatment-effect coefficient times the corresponding dummy } else { // if time is greater than or equal to 0 replace cf_ES2 = cf_ES2 - _b[D_p`i'] * D_p`i' ; // subtract the treatment-effect coefficient times the corresponding dummy } } /* compute the counterfactual prediction mean by unit type and time */ egen meancf_ES2 = mean(cf_ES2), by(t unittype) ; // compute the mean of cf_ES2 by t and unittypeTaking the difference of the coefficients before and after use again to get the result

content: Appendix E: Repeated event shocksThe problem this part solves is: if an event occurs repeatedly at different times, how should you choose? Here the generated true treatment effect is a continuously decaying curve. Approach 1 constrains the coefficients of the event dummies to be equal ($\gamma_1=\gamma_2$): The constraints below are segmentations into two-period, three-period, and four-period groups. Here’s an example of the constraint code: #delimit; /*two periods per group*/ constraint define 9 D_m10=D_m9; constraint define 10 D_m8=D_m7; constraint define 11 D_m6=D_m5; constraint define 12 D_m4=D_m3; constraint define 13 D_m2=D_m1; constraint define 14 D_p0=D_p1; constraint define 15 D_p2=D_p3; constraint define 16 D_p4=D_p5; constraint define 17 D_p6=D_p7; constraint define 18 D_p8=D_p9; /*three periods per group */ #delimit; constraint define 21 D_m1=D_m2; constraint define 22 D_m1=D_m3; constraint define 23 D_m4=D_m5; constraint define 24 D_m4=D_m6; constraint define 25 D_m7=D_m8; constraint define 26 D_m7=D_m9; constraint define 27 D_p0=D_p1; constraint define 28 D_p2=D_p1; constraint define 29 D_p3=D_p4; constraint define 30 D_p3=D_p5; constraint define 31 D_p6=D_p7; constraint define 32 D_p6=D_p8;Approach one: constrain the event-time dummy values to be equalApproach 2 constrains the slopes between coefficients to be equal ($\gamma_1-\gamma_0=\gamma_2-\gamma_1$) Here’s an example of the constraint code: constraint define 9 D_m10=D_m9; constraint define 10 D_m8=D_m7; constraint define 11 D_m6=D_m5; constraint define 12 D_m4=D_m3;Constraining the slopes between coefficients to be equalTop-left is the ordinary case. Top-right is the grouping with equal two-period slopes. Bottom-left is the grouping with equal three-period slopes. Bottom-right is the grouping where the two periods before and after are each constrained to be equal.

content: DID: one unit, two timesTwo kinds of constraints. One adds a trend control — adding trend_group2 to the controls: //trend control variable gen byte group2 = E_i == 11 gen trend_group2 = t * group2 same constraint //other constraint types are the same as before, ensuring event-time dummies have equal coefficients or equal slopesThe constraints applied include the trend control and the event-time dummy constraints

title: Econometrics: Event Studies 2

content: Time-based: one unit, two timesNext, verify the Time-based data form. The DID form has a control group to help generate counterfactual predictions, but time-based lacks a control group. The usual options are: The event-time dummy coefficients for the earliest and latest periods are equal, making the plot smoother The slopes between the earliest and latest event-time dummy coefficients are equal, better showing the trend The sum of the pre-trend coefficients is constrained to 0 The trend-weighted constraints across multiple event times sum to 0 You can see that in the experiment below, the fourth plot actually produced a strange result. The constraints applied were: Individual fixed effects sum to 0 Pre-event effects sum to 0 The slopes at the end of the post-event period are equal The weighted pre-trend is 0 \\I don't understand where the 5.5 base period in this constraint comes from? constraint define 8 (10-5.5)*D_m10 + (9-5.5)*D_m9 + (8-5.5)*D_m8 + (7-5.5)*D_m7 + (6-5.5)*D_m6 + (5-5.5)*D_m5 + (4-5.5)*D_m4 + (3-5.5)*D_m3 + (2-5.5)*D_m2 + (1-5.5)*D_m1 = 0 ; time-based simulationSo should we choose the constraint that the coefficients’ slopes are equal or that the coefficient values are equal? The answer depends on the situation. If a policy’s true effect doesn’t change over time, choose the equal coefficient values constraint; if the policy effect changes over time, choose the equal coefficient slopes constraint. Simulation of a jump shock whose effect doesn’t change over time, where the equal-coefficient-values estimator is more efficientI think this conclusion has become circular reasoning. The whole point of event studies is to estimate the treatment effect (whether it is dynamic or static is precisely what we need to find out), and now it’s turned into choosing the method based on the result. Still, the takeaway is simply to analyze the policy background, form an assumption, and then choose the constraint.

content: DID: many units, many timesFor multi-period DID, adding multiple event-time trend-weighted constraints that sum to 0 makes the estimation more efficient. As shown: The first column is the ordinary estimate, with no restrictions beyond two-way individual and time fixed effects. The second column adds, on top of the first, the constraint that the pre-event trends sum to 0: //event dates are still 10 and 5; I don't understand where the 5.5 base period comes from constraint define 3 -4.5*D_m10 - 3.5*D_m9 - 2.5* D_m8 - 1.5* D_m7 - 0.5*D_m6 + 0.5 * D_m5 + 1.5 * D_m4 + 2.5 *D_m3 + 3.5 *D_m2 + 4.5 *D_m1 = 0 ;The third column adds a type control: gen treated_time = treated * t DID estimation: the orange part is the counterfactual group predicted from residuals

content: Time-based: many units, many timestime-based; orange is also the counterfactual groupAbove is a Time-based structure where everything is the treated group, but this time there are individual differences. The second column adds, on top of the first, individual grouping and a time-weighted trend of 0: //individual grouping Egen unittype = group (E_i) ; Egen meany = mean (y) , by (t unittype) //time-trend weighting; I still don't understand where the 3.5 base period comes from constraint define 103 (6-3.5) * D_m6 + (5-3.5) * D_m5 + (4-3.5) * D_m4 + (3-3.5) * D_m3 + (2-3.5) * D_m2 + (1-3.5) * D_m1 = 0 ; The third column adds coefficient constraints on top of the second: constraint define 8 D_m7 = D_m6 ; constraint define 9 D_m6 = D_m5 ;

title: Econometrics: Event Studies 2

content: SummaryEvent study analysis is a generalization of DID. My understanding is that event studies further slice DID over time. Because there are more time dummies, solving requires more constraints, so we have to add time-trend controls based on the research context. DID and event studies complement each other; event studies can further show the dynamic effects of the DID estimate (increasing, decreasing, or reverting to the normal value after variation over time). If the two estimates point in opposite directions, it may be because the wrong constraints were chosen, or there is a collinearity issue. Different data structures call for different numbers and types of additional constraints in event studies. From the appendix-code experiments — Solving a Time-based dataset requires adding constraints, and how many depends on the number of event times and individuals. In event studies, standardizing the pre-trend generally tends to be more accurate. A dataset with only one unit but shocks at different times needs constraints added carefully, or you may get the opposite result. Data with many individuals, whether time-based or did, should add a group-type control.
heading: Summary
title: Econometrics: Event Studies 2

content: Econometrics: Event Studies 1 Econometrics: Event Studies 2 Econometrics: Event Studies 3 Anyone who has done DID is no stranger to parallel-trends tests. And a parallel-trends test is one special application of the event study method. Recently my advisor had me read and study the paper An Introductory Guide to Event Study Models. The authors also published a YouTube video series. This post records my own reflections based on that paper’s framework. I haven’t looked closely at the code yet, so for now I’ll put down my understanding of the statistical theory.
title: Econometrics: Event Studies 1

content: How does economics study event shocks?Event studies study whether a specific event affected the object of study. This method was first applied in finance — for example, analyzing the impact of company renamings, corporate scandals, and information disclosures on stock price movements.1 Of course, this method calls for more rigorous statistical analysis — Zhihu, for instance, is constantly full of questions like this: After a policy was implemented or a product launched, Apple’s or Nvidia’s stock evaporated or surged by tens of billions the next day — what’s the reason? That kind of analysis is the starting point of event studies, but the statistical test still needs to be more rigorous. Introduced into econometrics, event studies are mainly used to study dynamic treatment effects. By slicing the treatment effect into time groups, we can further discuss the impact of an event. For example, in the figure below studying the effect of unemployment on income,2 dynamic time dummies are built from each person’s unemployment timing: one year before unemployment (t-1), one year after (t+1), two years after (t+2). These include anticipatory trends and post-event trends. Earnings losses of displaced workersPre-event trends: For example, if everyone expects a wave of unemployment to come, you can see a slow decline before the event arrives, but the shock is still clearly visible right around the moment the event hits (where the x-axis is 0). Post-event trends: After the shock passes, the effect starts to rebound. That is, compare whether the effect strengthens or weakens year by year after the shock. Model assumptions: The parallel-trends test in DID is also an event study. It verifies that the policy satisfies the model assumption — an exogenous shock. So before the policy starts, the treatment effect should be insignificant with a coefficient close to 0, and after it starts, the coefficient should be significantly different from 0. Take the paper on English listening exams and educational inequality3 as an example. The time dummy it sets is when the English listening section was added to the gaokao. Dependent variables: English scores, math and Chinese scores, and admission rates. Heterogeneity groups: urban and rural samples. The figure also shows that before English listening was introduced, the urban-rural gap was small, and after its introduction the gap kept widening. English listening exams and educational inequality
heading: How does economics study event shocks?
title: Econometrics: Event Studies 1

heading: The “countless” little details of event studies
title: Econometrics: Event Studies 1

content: The regression specificationIn econometrics, an event study estimates dynamic treatment effects — it slices the regression over time. Taking panel data as an example, the distinctive feature is adding event-time dummies $D_{i, t-j}$ . $$ y_{ii}=\underbrace{\left(\sum\_{j\in\{-m,\ldots,0,\ldots,n\}}\gamma_{j}\cdot D_{i,t-j}\right)}\_{\text{事件时间虚拟变量}}+\underbrace{\alpha_{i}+\delta_{i}}\_{\text{面板固定效应}}+\underbrace{\beta\cdot X_{ii}}\_{\text{ 控制变量}}+\epsilon_{ii}. $$
heading: The regression specification
title: Econometrics: Event Studies 1

content: Data structure classificationAn introductory guide to event study models4 gives two classification criteria: Is there a sample group that “never received treatment”? Do different sample groups have substantially different event dates for treatment? GroupingNo “never-treated” sampleHas a “never-treated” sampleSame event dateN/ADID-typeDifferent event datesTiming-basedHybridTL;DR — N/A: no control group, so the treatment effect can’t be estimated at all. DiD-type: a perfect controlled experiment — the traditional DID. Timing-based: everyone is in the treated group, but the event shocks differ across units, so a comparison can still be made. Take a panel-data study on relocation for poverty alleviation as an example.5 Renmin University’s relocation database has long run surveys at relocation resettlement sites, so their study is actually an ITT — all samples are treated units that went through the relocation policy. But! Relocation was carried out in batches — some people moved out earlier, some later. So in the same year, there is both a treated group that already moved and a control group that hasn’t, which means the study can still be done. By the way, the paper’s conclusion is that once living conditions improve, migrant workers no longer want to leave home. Hence the paper’s title, Home Sweet Home. Hybrid: has both a comparison between treated and control groups and a comparison within the treated group in the same year.
heading: Data structure classification
title: Econometrics: Event Studies 1

content: Choosing the event timeThe overall logic of the event study method is: Choose the event and when it occurs, choose the base period for the event, choose the window (the range of dynamic treatment effects), choose the treated and control groups, and compute and decompose the average treatment effect. Choosing the event dateEven if a policy is rolled out nationwide at a specific time, markets may react in advance; moreover, most of the time the shock is uneven, spreading out gradually by group, by carrier, by time, and by space. But in applied statistics you just work with what you have and pick the best option available. Take the study of Facebook’s effect on college students’ mental health as an example.6 When each person started using Facebook is obviously hard data to get, so the study matches individual mental-health questionnaires to the timing of when Facebook rolled out on each campus, and runs the regression with that. By the way, the finding: social media use worsened college students’ mental health. A channel test shows it was driven by comparison anxiety. Handling the base periodA quick refresher on dummy variables in econometrics: To avoid collinearity, use n-1 dummy variables to estimate the relative gaps among n variables. For example, compare air-pollution levels across the spring-summer-autumn-winter cycle. Estimating such treatment effects requires a base period for comparison. We can default to spring as the base period, so the estimated coefficients for summer, autumn, and winter are all results compared against spring’s data. The time dummies in event studies also need a base period, hence the following choices or treatments: Absolute base period: usually choose the period right before the event (the contrast works better and highlights the jump): it reflects long-run gaps, used when there are many pre-event periods. Relative base period: use the previous period as the base: used when focusing on anticipatory effects, or when there are few pre-event periods. Merging periods: to handle collinearity. For example, merge t-6 and earlier into one period, and t+5 and later into one period, or drop a certain period. Base-period treatment: normalize it, set it to 0…… Time trends: whether to add time trends, individual fixed effects, and time fixed effects. Event endpoints: the endpoints may be shifted and look ugly, or may reflect the event’s trend. An introductory guide to event study models notes that since the choice of event dummies can affect the results, one should strengthen the description of how the dummies are set and restricted. But in the top-5 papers I’ve read recently, event studies seem mainly used to visually display heterogeneity and the model’s exogenous-shock assumption. So this part is usually glossed over — they just say how the dummies were set, without stressing why. Choosing the windowChoosing the window is essentially a balance between prettier results and statistical bias. Too short, and the statistics are biased; too long, and the counterfactual estimate isn’t efficient enough. From a pragmatic standpoint 🤪 — it’s best to let the regression show a clear trend. A symmetric pre- and post-event window is best. You can go further with fitting — for example, first estimate the dynamics by month, then weight by season to bring out a trend. Weighted fitting across multiple events works the same way. A quadratic weighted fit, better at showing a trendChoosing the treated and control groupsExclude special samples. With Chinese city data, for instance, we usually drop municipalities directly under the central government because they’re too special! And in the heterogeneity section, we usually look at the difference between provincial capitals and non-capital cities. Pay attention to the parallel-trends test. That is, before the shock, the treated and control groups should look as similar as possible. Add control variable

content: Future directionsMeasuring event effects with varying intensity Interact the time dummies with the size of the event. I feel this is similar to the shift-share instrumental variable (shift-IV). It uses the group trend net of the individual, multiplied by the individual’s size, as the instrument. Multiple events per unit Weight them, or restrict to a single one — count only the largest event or the first occurrence. Handling heterogeneity Interactions, or grouping by time — for example, earlier-affected and later-affected groups. Estimate further through the counterfactual. Because event studies can be biased when fixed effects and trends aren’t estimated, the paper uses an estimation technique to make it more accurate (I didn’t understand this part). Because event studies can be biased when fixed effects and trends aren’t estimated, the paper uses an estimation technique to make it more accurate (I didn’t understand this part).Considering non-year event time For example, cohort effects. This is really just custom grouping of time dummies. State transitions An Introductory Guide to Event Study Models doesn’t mention this, but I think there’s one more direction worth exploring — decomposing the extensive and intensive margins. See Is the Log(y+1) Transformation Reliable?

content: TL;DREvent studies fundamentally estimate dynamic treatment effects. For accurate estimation, here are some suggestions: Standardize the coefficients Choose an appropriate base period and event window Account for individual effects, time effects, and time trends Account for confounders arising from sample characteristics (use the estimator provided in the paper).

content: Beijing’s popular tourist spots are often located in the east and south—head east to Qinhuangdao or travel south to the Tianjin seaside. The southeast, near the sea, is a favorite among visitors. In the northwest, it’s a paradise for hiking and mountain adventures. For example, heading north to Miyun Research Note 2: Miyun Wild Great Wall. This time, the destination for our field research is the Mentougou District on the western side of Beijing.

content: Beijing Three PeaksThis field research takes us to Jianjian Village in Mentougou District, situated at the foot of Miaofeng Mountain. The main peak of Miaofeng Mountain stands at an elevation of 1291 meters, making it the closest peak over a thousand meters to Beijing’s urban area1. Along the way, almost every 20 minutes, a backpacker can be seen jogging down the mountain, waving trekking poles. Upon inquiry, we learned that this is the famous “Beijing Three Peaks” hiking route. The Three Peaks Traverse: from Dajue Temple in Haidian District to Yangtai Mountain and finally to Miaofeng Mountain.In Beijing, this kind of hiking business model is quite common, and many friends in my social circle have participated. If you explore the mountains in the suburbs of Beijing, you’ll often see red ribbons with writing fluttering from the trees—these are usually route markers and advertisements from hiking groups.
heading: Beijing Three Peaks
title: Research Note 3: Mountains and Red Roses

content: Miaofeng MountainDue to time constraints, I only managed to climb the main peak of Miaofeng Mountain. A brief map is provided below: Miaofeng Mountain
