title: Research Note 3: Mountains and Red Roses

content: Pingxi Intelligence StationDuring the War of Resistance against Japan, Jianjian Village served as a liaison station for joint intelligence with the Northeast Anti-Japanese forces. The Pingxi Intelligence Station is a red education-themed museum dedicated to this history. You can bike up Miaofeng Mountain along the road, and at the foot of the mountain, there’s a cycling station with a café.
heading: Pingxi Intelligence Station
title: Research Note 3: Mountains and Red Roses

content: Dayun TempleIf you choose to take the mountain path (hiking route), the trail up the mountain is hidden among the streets and alleys. Pay attention to the signs and the backpackers coming down the mountain. The starting point of the climb is hidden among the residential streets at the foot of the mountain.It takes about 40 minutes from the foot of the mountain to the top. On the mountainside is the Lingguan Temple (free). Lingguan Temple on the mountainsideThe summit is Dayun Temple (admission fee required). These temples are all privately managed. Dayun Temple is nominally open from 8:30 to 17:00. The entrance fee is 40 ￥ per person. Because the ticket seller arrived late and left early, I started climbing at 7:20 am and reached the summit gate at 7:55 am. The ticket seller had not arrived yet, but the gate was open2, so I went in directly. gatesave pointInside, there are four halls: the Lower Niangniang Temple, the Temple of the God of Wealth, and one temple that is currently under renovation. The Chinese characters “招财进宝” mean to attract wealth and treasure. Here, the Chinese character “宝” is missing a part “、”, and they promote it as “少了一点你,” implying that the part that is missing is you. attract wealth and treasureJust up another long flight of stairs is the summit, where you’ll find Yuhuang Temple. When I entered Yuhuang Temple, the temple gate had just opened. The caretaker who opened the gate expressed surprise that someone had come so early. On June 16, 2024, I was the first person to enter Yuhuang Temple on Miaofeng Mountain. It was me! From the top of Yuhuang Temple, the view is quite stunning. The early bird 😤 gets to enjoy the scenery from up high for free! Standing on the top of the mountain overlooking the first floorStanding on the top of the mountain overlooking the first floor
heading: Dayun Temple
title: Research Note 3: Mountains and Red Roses

content: Mountains and Red RosesNot far from Yingtao Gou, there is another local specialty in red — the red rose. Only this place can grow it, also known as Alpine Rose or Miaofeng Mountain Rose. Jianjian Village faces north and south, forming a basin shape, with good conditions for heat drainage. During the summer solstice, it receives no fewer than 13 hours of sunlight. The flowering period has little rain, abundant sunshine, which is conducive to the formation and accumulation of aromatic oil. The soil has a thick humus layer, slightly acidic, with high content of trace elements such as iron, manganese, copper, and zinc. The unique natural conditions produce roses with distinctive fragrance and quality. Reference from Specialty China. The restaurant owner said that since her grandmother’s generation, red roses have been a specialty here. They offer rose cakes, rose wine, rose sauce, and rose perfume. Rose scrambled eggs are indeed delicious 😍, while rose cakes lack distinctive flavor, primarily aromatic. Hawthorn and red fruit 3 are also local specialty produce, and both are red What determines my ranking is the attributive! ↩︎ The gates of the scenic area are opened because the staff on the mountain came down to repair the mountain road. ↩︎ It tastes no different from hawthorn. ↩︎
heading: Mountains and Red Roses
title: Research Note 3: Mountains and Red Roses

content: Beijing WTownDue to a shortage in the research team, I was roped in by my professor to join the weekend’s door-to-door survey. The destination was Chao Guan Village in Beijing WTown, Miyun District, Beijing. This place is quite remarkable, embodying the robust spirit of the north while cloaked in the delicate facade of the south. Miyun District is renowned for its reservoirs, and Gubei Water Town stands proudly along the river. Despite being in the north, it exudes the charm of a southern waterscape. White walls and black tiles, interwoven alleys, rivers running through, and reeds swaying gently in the breeze. Miyun is very rich in water resources.However, looking far along the river, one can see the northern foothills of the Yan Mountains. Steep mountain ranges border the village’s edge, obscuring much of the sky. In this rugged landscape, the Great Wall of the Ming Dynasty winds and twists, like a dragon turning over in its sleep. Majestic and ancient, grand and serpentine, this Great Wall now stands as the boundary, separating Beijing from Hebei. The Great Wall of the Ming Dynasty, followed by the Simatai Great Wall, a stop in front of Shanhaiguan
heading: Beijing WTown
title: Research Note 2: Miyun Wild Great Wall

content: Wo Hu Mountain Great WallHaving been in Beijing for so long, I had yet to climb a wild section of the Great Wall. The Wo Hu Mountain Great Wall, part of the Ming Dynasty’s construction, is unique for its circular beacon towers1. The owner of the guesthouse2 gave directions to my classmates on how to reach the Wall, and I decided to join them for the sunrise. We set off at 3 a. m., walking along the national highway beside the guesthouse. After spotting a tourism signpost, we found Yang Qilang’s tomb and temple nearby. Passing through the temple, we reached a dirt path leading into the mountains. The stone-brick road of the Great Wall was mostly in ruins, with only the bricks near the beacon towers remaining relatively intact. Starting from this point was particularly memorable because of the presence of a train tunnel. The first relatively complete beacon tower we arrived at. Around 4 o’clock, the sky was already glowing red.Because we needed time for the door-to-door survey, we ended our climb at the third-to-last beacon tower. It was around four o’clock then. Climbing all the way up would take about an hour and a half, while descending would be much faster, less than an hour. I haven’t climbed many mountains, and before this, I had only watched the sunrise once on Mount Emei. Watching the sunrise on Mount Emei feels like forging iron3. The sea of clouds at the peak rolls like icy rivers, and suddenly, a spark of the sun pierces through the shroud, creating a hole in the canvas. In an instant, the sea of clouds boils, and the flowing mist splashes around, much like the steaming heat during iron forging. Paired with the golden, gleaming Buddha at the summit, it feels like a celestial realm. Watching the sunrise from the mountainside of Wo Hu Mountain, the sun is initially blocked by the distant peaks, making the process slower and more nurturing. As the red foam slowly rises in the distance, the ink-wash painting ambiance gradually ascends from near to far. The layers of verdant mountains, the dissipating mist, and the distant lights flickering on one by one—this is the mortal world. sunrise viewTaking photos at this time has the feeling of silhouette - other students’ photography skills are so good. In my hand is a wooden stick that I picked up casuallyAt 4:46, the sun officially crested the mountain peak4. At that moment, I kept thinking of Shi Tiesheng’s words— But the sun, it is always both a setting sun and a rising sun. As it extinguishes itself, descending and gathering up the desolate remnants of light, it is simultaneously blazing and climbing the peak on the other side, spreading its radiant dawn. One day, I too will quietly descend the mountain, supported by my crutch. One day, in some mountain hollow, a joyous child will surely run up, clutching his toy. Of course, that child won’t be me. But is it not me? —Shi Tiesheng, I and the Temple of Earth sunrise view
heading: Wo Hu Mountain Great Wall
title: Research Note 2: Miyun Wild Great Wall

content: Research SummaryThis survey was conducted at the village level, which made the social interactions significantly easier compared to the previous county-level research I had participated in—finally, no more socializing over alcohol. Personal Reflections: Addressing climate change is indeed urgent. Gubei Water Town is blessed with ample water resources, with most of its land being irrigated fields, including many paddy fields. However, villagers reported that since 2018, the water levels have been declining annually, leading to many irrigated fields being converted into forested areas due to the decreasing water levels. The suburbs of Beijing aren’t much different from my hometown. It is often assumed that poorer areas tend to favor sons over daughters, but here, due to men’s jobs being insufficient to support a family and the bride price system, people actually feel it’s better to have daughters. The attitude of the residents reflects the quality of governance. In areas with rampant corruption, villagers clearly distrusted us, feeling that despite all the surveys, nothing changes: “We common folks, no matter how much we talk, it doesn’t help.” In well-governed areas with good welfare, every response was filled with gratitude towards the state, with villagers willing to comply with any government directives. I realized I am indeed quite careless! My fellow classmates, especially the female students, were much more meticulous than I was. Their questionnaire filling and reviewing were more rigorous, and I should learn from them. Survey Methods: Elderly party members and enthusiastic grandmothers make the best interviewees—they are attentive, sincere, and willing to actively cooperate with door-to-door surveys. When it comes to income-related surveys, respondents often understate their wealth. In such cases, it is important to observe the room (decoration, presence of a car, size, quality of furniture, etc.) and learn to ask disaggregated questions. For example, break down farming into the yield per mu, the number of mu farmed, and the price per jin. Similarly, use cross-verification by asking unexpected questions. For instance, when calculating income and expenses separately, ensure they balance. For household expenses, consider the number of family members and their consumption. When respondents are uncertain, set ranges—do you have 100 yuan? 200 yuan? The answers to questions can easily be manipulated. For example, asking if villagers come together to discuss solutions when faced with difficulties will invariably get a positive response. However, asking specific questions reveals more. After a recent storm in Beijing knocked down trees in many parks and schools, asking about the storm’s impact on their fields and if they sought collective solutions will likely reveal that everyone managed their own fields independently. Village-household integration. When implementing subsidy programs at the village level, the approach is often straightforward and crude. For example, the distinction between reforestation and ecological public welfare forests is blurred for villagers, who view both as tree planting for money. Subsidies are divided into planting subsidies and other types, but in the village, they are distributed together, making farmers think they get money just for planting. To address this, policies need to be broken down and explained in conjunction with villagers’ responses. Praise should be moderate. Each questionnaire typically takes about an hour5. To ensure cooperation, we often praise the respondents during the interview. However, if the praise is excessive, some attitudinal questions may receive overly positive responses, distorting the results. Moreover, for questions about marital harmony or neighborly relations, unless asked about neighbors, personal responses tend to be uniformly positive. The owner of the B&B said that the circular beacon tower here is one of only two in Beijing.&#
heading: Research Summary
title: Research Note 2: Miyun Wild Great Wall

content: I only started using Obsidian recently, so this post is a quick record of my workflow. I mainly use Obsidian to write and manage blog posts and literature-reading notes.
title: Using Obsidian for Literature Reading and Blog Writing

content: Obsidian and plugin usageForum: https://forum-zh.obsidian.md/ Recommended tutorial: An Incomplete Beginner Guide to Obsidian Obsidian represents the idea of bidirectional linking: notes can connect to each other and gradually form a network of knowledge. For me, the real reason to use Obsidian is its absurdly good plugin ecosystem. It makes writing and organizing notes genuinely enjoyable. A quick note: the minimum entry requirement is knowing basic Markdown syntax.
heading: Obsidian and plugin usage

content: Downloading the softwareDownload the app from the official website: https://obsidian.md/ After installing it, the startup screen looks like this. A vault is simply the folder where your notes are stored. In my case, I keep separate vaults for blog writing and literature notes. Startup screenAfter you choose a vault location, an extra .obsidian folder appears inside it. That folder stores the app settings, including plugins, interface style, and so on. My own layout looks like this: My interface layoutThe rich have a second monitor. The rest of us make do with split view 😤 Obsidian settings: Just replace the .obsidian folder in the vault. You can download my .obsidian config from my GitHub repository. After downloading it, remember to unzip themes.zip. Each vault has its own settings. That means every vault can use a completely different theme and plugin setup. I really like this, because writing blog posts and managing notes often call for different tools, so independent vault settings feel necessary.

content: About bidirectional linksDocument properties: if the first line is blank, type --- three times to add document properties. If the first line is not blank, --- creates a horizontal rule instead. Adding tags: #tag1, #tag2 Links: Link to a note: [[文件名]] Link to a heading in a note: [[ # ]] Link to a paragraph (block) in a note: [[ # ^ ]] Create an alias for a link (keyword): [[ | 关键词]] Link to an external file such as Evernote: [关键词](链接) Add an image: ![[]] or ![图片标题](图片引用路径)

title: Using Obsidian for Literature Reading and Blog Writing

content: Plugin usageAfter replacing the .obsidian folder, open the vault, click Trust author, and turn off safe mode. Settings page: you can change themes under Appearance, and install or enable community plugins hereClick the gear icon labeled Settings in the lower-left corner to open all installed plugins. You can also check for plugin updates and browse the community plugin marketplace (you need a VPN/proxy for that).
heading: Plugin usage
title: Using Obsidian for Literature Reading and Blog Writing

content: CommandMost plugins are easy enough to use once they show up in the interface. The rest are mainly driven by keyboard commands. Click the >_ icon in the far-left sidebar (shortcut: ctrl+p), type the command you want in the pop-up, and run the plugin from there. Some plugins need to be called through commandsThe Command plugin can also help you add quick-access buttons for commands. Where you add a command buttonOpen the right-click menu, or click the three-dot icon at the top right of the note pane, then choose Add command. After going through choose command -> choose icon -> choose name, the shortcut button is added.

title: Using Obsidian for Literature Reading and Blog Writing

content: PandocIt is not enough to install only the plugin. Obsidian notes use Markdown syntax and can export to PDF. Pandoc lets you export to more formats too, such as LaTeX, epub, and HTML. There are two steps: Go to the official site and download the Pandoc application itself. Then install and enable the Pandoc plugin and the Enhancing export plugin. In the settings for both plugins, fill in the Pandoc file path and set the export directory. After that, an Export as... option will appear under the three-dot menu in the top-right corner of the note pane.
heading: Pandoc
title: Using Obsidian for Literature Reading and Blog Writing

content: Easy typingThis is one of the main plugins that sold me on Obsidian. When you write documents that mix Chinese and English, there are lots of little conventions to keep track of. For example: Put spaces between Chinese text and numbers or English words; Switching input methods is annoying; English sentences should start with a capital letter. With easy typing enabled, numbers and English words are automatically spaced in Chinese text; typing a Chinese punctuation mark twice turns it into the English version; and the first letter of an English sentence is capitalized automatically…
heading: Easy typing
title: Using Obsidian for Literature Reading and Blog Writing

content: AnnotatorObsidian itself cannot read PDF files directly, so people usually use the annotator plugin. In a new note, type --- on the first line to add document properties, then add annotation-target, click the field that appears, and choose the PDF you want to read. Close and reopen the note, and it turns into a PDF reading interface that also supports annotations. Example of document properties
heading: Annotator
title: Using Obsidian for Literature Reading and Blog Writing

content: Copilot chatThere are roughly three ways people integrate AI into Obsidian. One is direct embedding, where you continue writing notes from context through commands. Another focuses on built-in file search and note-style management. The third keeps the conversation in a sidebar. Personally, I recommend that third route, and Copilot chat is the plugin I would pick. After installation, open the settings page. For Default model, I recommend choosing OPEENROUTER. AI. It is basically a broker that lets you access different models through one service. Scroll down to the model settings and choose the model you want. I recommend OPEENROUTER. AIScroll down a bit further and you will find the place to enter the OPEENROUTER API. Scroll down to find the model settings and choose the one you wantOpenrouter. Ai API key can be generated here The model list is here: You are not limited to GPT-3.5 either. Just search for the keyword free, and the listed AI models can all be used for free. Choose the free model name you wantFor example, copy one of the following model names into openrouter model: openchat/openchat-7b:free meta-llama/llama-3-8b-instruct:free google/gemma-7b-it:free gryphe/mythomist-7b:freeClick Copilot chat in the left sidebar, and an AI chat panel will appear on the right. It can read your notes too.

content: Hugo and ObsidianRecommended reading: Best practices for writing with Hugo One-click blog publishing with Obsidian Obsidian + Hugo + Cloudflare: making blog publishing ridiculously simple I would also recommend the hugo preview plugin. It basically loads an online blog preview page inside Obsidian. Once the plugin is enabled, click the blue square in the lower-right corner to open it. In practice, it is just importing a specific webpage into Obsidian for preview. Best of both worlds!Another plugin worth mentioning is mermaid. The LoveIt Hugo theme supports flowchart rendering, and I can never remember every last detail of the syntax, so this plugin helps a lot. I still use local image references for now (I just like managing files locally 😀), imge converter can automatically compress, rename, and convert image formats; the clear unsed images plugin can help clean up local images that are no longer referenced. As for changing image reference paths (copying post/img to static/img) and pushing the blog to Git, I do not use Obsidian’s Git plugin. I let .bat scripts handle both jobs instead (honestly, just letting GPT write them is enough), and it is simple. That way I can focus on writing. As for creating new blog templates, there is no need to set up a quick plugin. Obsidian already has built-in template support: just create a template folder, put your Markdown template files in it, and when you create a new post, click the corresponding template-import icon in the left sidebar.

content: The note-taking app debateA lot of people online compare Notion, Obsidian, and other note-taking apps. I picked Obsidian mainly for its rich open-source plugin ecosystem and the peace of mind that comes with local storage. That said, the usual complaint about Obsidian is easy enough to understand: there are too many plugins, the features can get flashy, and the learning curve is not exactly low, so the priorities sometimes feel blurred. Even so, I still have not used Obsidian to build a proper knowledge graph. Just using it as a writing tool already feels great. Beyond that, Obsidian was originally meant to help people build a knowledge system. What inspires me in other people’s setups is not how pretty their notes look, but how they use Obsidian to carry out their own way of organizing information🦾. Using plugins to rotate periodic notes for review; building keyword-based note blocks and expanding them over time; connecting Obsidian with other tools to refine a workflow; combining note structure with design…

content: Brief Review of Streaming SolutionsHuawei: I flashed a Huawei PC Manager onto the Tianxuan; in its settings you can enable remote control, and on Huawei phones and tablets you can find remote control under Smart Connection. Includes a privacy screen, decent speed, no gaming mouse support, lower image quality — basically a ToDesk with an extra privacy screen. ASUS: requires a personal Microsoft account; mine is a family account, so it does not work. Parsec: high image quality, low latency, game support, no privacy screen, easy to set up (you just need a VPN when logging into the software on the device). It should be the best solution in general — but it is not compatible with the Huawei tablet, where the mouse wheel and audio playback fail. Moonlight + Sunshine: a drop-in replacement for Parsec, and optimized for Steam — the ultimate solution for streaming from anywhere. Another drawback — occasionally the audio still stutters, and the mouse optimization is poor too. Changing to a remote-friendly mouse in moonlight works, but then it no longer suits games2. content: Is the log(y+1) transformation reliable?
heading: Is the log(y+1) transformation reliable?
title: Econometrics: Is the log(y+1) transformation reliable?

content: AbstractTitle: Logs with Zeros? Some Problems and SolutionsAuthors: Jiafeng Chen; Jonathan RothJournal: The Quarterly Journal of Economics (2024/3/30)DOI: 10.1093/qje/qjad054Translated abstract: When studying an outcome variable $Y$ that can equal 0 (for example, earnings), many researchers estimate the average treatment effect (ATE) after applying a transformation that behaves like $\log(Y)$ when $Y$ is large and is defined at zero by using $\log(1+Y)$. Our paper shows that the average treatment effect under this kind of log-like transformation should not be interpreted as a percentage effect, because the estimate depends on the units in which the outcome is measured. In fact, we show that one can obtain treatment effects of arbitrary magnitude simply by changing the units of $Y$ before applying the transformation. This happens because, for observations whose outcome moves from zero to nonzero, the individual-level percentage effect is not well defined, and the units of the outcome implicitly determine how much weight the transformed ATE places on the extensive margin. More generally, we uncover an “impossibility triangle”: when the outcome variable can equal zero, one cannot simultaneously have an estimand that is an average treatment effect, is invariant to the units of $Y$, and is point identified. We discuss several alternative approaches that may be reasonable in settings with both intensive and extensive margins, including (1) estimating average treatment effects in levels and then expressing them in percentage terms afterward (for example, with Poisson regression), (2) explicitly calibrating the weight placed on the intensive and extensive margins, and (3) estimating intensive-margin and extensive-margin treatment effects separately (for example, with Lee bounds). We illustrate these methods in three empirical applications.
heading: Abstract
title: Econometrics: Is the log(y+1) transformation reliable?

content: The short versionThis post asks whether log transformations with zeros, such as $log(1+y)$ and $arcsinh(y)=\sqrt{1+y^2}+y$, are actually reliable.
heading: The short version
title: Econometrics: Is the log(y+1) transformation reliable?

content: A code exampleThe output below shows that when the data contain zeros, changing the units of $y$ before taking logs can change the statistical significance of the regression. sysuse nlsw88, clear replace wage = 0 if _n<=400 //前400个观测值的工资改为0值 gen lnwage1 = ln(1 + .128683 * wage) gen lnwage2 = ln(1 + .7744329 * wage) gen lnwage3 = ln(1 + 84.02252 * wage) gen lnwage4 = ln(1 + 4.68e+08 * wage) gen lnwage5 = ln(1 + 3.77e+25 * wage) reg lnwage1 tenure grade eststo m1 reg lnwage2 tenure grade eststo m2 reg lnwage3 tenure grade eststo m3 reg lnwage4 tenure grade eststo m4 reg lnwage5 tenure grade eststo m5 esttab m1 m2 m3 m4 m5, keep(tenure) b(3) se compress /*------------------------------------------------------------------------- (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) lnwage1 lnwage2 lnwage3 lnwage4 lnwage5 --------------------------------------------------------------------------- tenure 0.010*** 0.020*** 0.030** 0.050 0.100 (0.001) (0.003) (0.010) (0.032) (0.090) --------------------------------------------------------------------------- N 2229 2229 2229 2229 2229 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------*/
heading: A code example
title: Econometrics: Is the log(y+1) transformation reliable?

content: ExplanationHow we usually interpret log transformationsThe standard view is that, once you take logs, the coefficient has a percentage interpretation. What a log coefficient meansAfter taking logs, we usually read the coefficient as a percentage change. For example, with lnGDP, the coefficient in a regression is often read as the percentage change in GDP. If the model is reg lny lnx, then the coefficient is an elasticity. See What taking logs means. For the regression below, $$ \ln y_n=\alpha+\beta x_n +\varepsilon $$ the coefficient has the following economic meaning: $$ \begin{align} \beta & = \frac{\ln Y\_{n+1}-\ln Y\_{n}}{X\_{n+1}-X\_{n}}\\ &=\frac{\ln \frac{Y\_{n+1}}{Y\_{n}}}{X\_{n+1}-X\_{n}}= \frac{\ln (1+\frac{Y\_{n+1}-Y\_{n}}{Y\_{n}})}{\Delta X}\\ &= \frac{\ln (1+\Delta Y \\\% )}{\Delta X} \approx\frac{\Delta Y \\\% }{\Delta X} \end{align} $$ Sometimes researchers also take logs because the data are long-tailed, and logging them makes the distribution more compact. The limits of log transformationsThe paper’s main point is this: when the data contain zeros and the unit of measurement changes (for example, hourly wages, monthly wages, and weekly wages in labor economics), the estimated effect from the log transformation changes too, which makes the result hard to trust. We usually think the treatment effect after logging is a kind of percentage effect and should not depend on the scaling parameter $\alpha$. $$ \small ATE=E[\log(1+aY(1))-\log(1+aY(0))]=E\left[\log\left(\frac{1+aY(1)}{1+aY(0)}\right)\right] $$ But once we look more carefully at the structure of the data, things change: $$ \begin{aligned} \lim_{a\to\infty}\log\left(\frac{1+aY(1)}{1+aY(0)}\right)=\begin{cases}\log\left(\frac{Y(1)}{Y(0)}\right)&\text{if }Y(1)>0,Y(0)>0\\ 0&\text{if }Y(1)=0,Y(0)=0\\ \infty&\text{if }Y(1)>0,Y(0)=0\\ -\infty&\text{if }Y(1)=0,Y(0)>0 \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$ The last three cases show exactly where the treatment-effect estimate can be distorted. The paper’s discussion of this bias is somewhat similar to Local Average Treatment Effects (LATE). Suppose the policy being studied is an employment policyTake an employment policy as the example. The policy shock makes the treated group respond in different ways. 0 means unemployed, and 1 means employed. Originally, the treated group contains both unemployed people (0) and employed people (1). After the policy shock, everyone ends up employed (1). If someone is already employed (1) and remains employed (1) after the shock, but income still rises, then the change in the variable comes directly from the policy shock. This is the intensive margin. If someone starts at 0 and moves to 1 after the shock, then the change in the variable comes not only from the policy shock but also from the change in status itself. This is the extensive margin. content: ExplanationHow we usually interpret log transformationsThe standard view is that, once you take logs, the coefficient has a percentage interpretation. What a log coefficient meansAfter taking logs, we usually read the coefficient as a percentage change. For example, with lnGDP, the coefficient in a regression is often read as the percentage change in GDP. If the model is reg lny lnx, then the coefficient is an elasticity. See What taking logs means. For the regression below, $$ \ln y_n=\alpha+\beta x_n +\varepsilon $$ the coefficient has the following economic meaning: $$ \begin{align} \beta & = \frac{\ln Y\_{n+1}-\ln Y\_{n}}{X\_{n+1}-X\_{n}}\\ &=\frac{\ln \frac{Y\_{n+1}}{Y\_{n}}}{X\_{n+1}-X\_{n}}= \frac{\ln (1+\frac{Y\_{n+1}-Y\_{n}}{Y\_{n}})}{\Delta X}\\ &= \frac{\ln (1+\Delta Y \\\% )}{\Delta X} \approx\frac{\Delta Y \\\% }{\Delta X} \end{align} $$ Sometimes researchers also take logs because the data are long-tailed, and logging them makes the distribution more compact. The limits of log transformationsThe paper’s main point is this: when the data contain zeros and the unit of measurement changes (for example, hourly wages, monthly wages, and weekly wages in labor economics), the estimated effect from the log transformation changes too, which makes the result hard to trust. We usually think the treatment effect after logging is a kind of percentage effect and should not depend on the scaling parameter $\alpha$. $$ \small ATE=E[\log(1+aY(1))-\log(1+aY(0))]=E\left[\log\left(\frac{1+aY(1)}{1+aY(0)}\right)\right] $$ But once we look more carefully at the structure of the data, things change: $$ \begin{aligned} \lim_{a\to\infty}\log\left(\frac{1+aY(1)}{1+aY(0)}\right)=\begin{cases}\log\left(\frac{Y(1)}{Y(0)}\right)&\text{if }Y(1)>0,Y(0)>0\\ 0&\text{if }Y(1)=0,Y(0)=0\\ \infty&\text{if }Y(1)>0,Y(0)=0\\ -\infty&\text{if }Y(1)=0,Y(0)>0 \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$ The last three cases show exactly where the treatment-effect estimate can be distorted. The paper’s discussion of this bias is somewhat similar to Local Average Treatment Effects (LATE). Suppose the policy being studied is an employment policyTake an employment policy as the example. The policy shock makes the treated group respond in different ways. 0 means unemployed, and 1 means employed. Originally, the treated group contains both unemployed people (0) and employed people (1). After the policy shock, everyone ends up employed (1). If someone is already employed (1) and remains employed (1) after the shock, but income still rises, then the change in the variable comes directly from the policy shock. This is the intensive margin. If someone starts at 0 and moves to 1 after the shock, then the change in the variable comes not only from the policy shock but also from the change in status itself. This is the extensive margin. So the treatment effect can be thought of like this: DiagramCodegraph LR A(Exogenous policy shock: binary variable Z)--treated group-->C{How the individual responds} C--extensive margin-->D(From 0 to 1) C--intensive margin-->E(From 1 to 1) D-->F{Outcome variable} E-->F{Outcome variable}graph LR A(Exogenous policy shock: binary variable Z)--treated group-->C{How the individual responds} C--extensive margin-->D(From 0 to 1) C--intensive margin-->E(From 1 to 1) D-->F{Outcome variable} E-->F{Outcome variable}graph LR A(Exogenous policy shock: binary variable Z)--treated group-->C{How the individual responds} C--extensive margin-->D(From 0 to 1) C--intensive margin-->E(From 1 to 1) D-->F{Outcome variable} E-->F{Outcome variable}graph LR A(Exogenous policy shock: binary variable Z)--treated group-->C{How the individual responds} C--extensive margin-->D(From 0 to 1) C--intensive margin-->E(From 1 to 1) D-->F{Outcome variable} E-->F{Outcome variable}So the average treatment effect is the sum of the expected values of those two margin effec

content: Main takeawayWhen you’re dealing with a sample where the variable being transformed contains zeros: A lot of social-media summaries overstate what this paper says. content: Possible fixesEach method below amounts to making a trade-off within that impossibility triangle. Use standard normalization or standardization to remove unit effects. Use Poisson regression with maximum likelihood. Drop the zero-value observations. Work out the sample distribution more carefully and separate the intensive and extensive margins. Use other approaches such as Lee bounds (I still haven’t figured out exactly how to do this one).

title: Notes on Learning Calculus of Variations

content: FunctionalLet’s start with the study of functions. In elementary school, we began to encounter unknowns like $x$. In middle school, we started to learn about specific functions like $f(x) = ax + bx^2 + c$. In high school, we began to understand abstract functions like $f(x) = f(-x)$ and $f'(x) = f(x)$. In university, we started to learn about implicit functions like $y' = y + y''$, which solve a class of functions. As our study of functions moves from concrete to abstract, we begin to develop the ability to infer the form of a function based on its properties. Nonlinear functionals in functional analysis are functions of functions. Given specific functional characteristics, we can narrow down the range of functional forms and then select the optimal function based on constraints. For example, a firm choosing the optimal production process, or an architect selecting the best curve for a building… Previously, given a specific type of function, we sought extremum points; Now, given functional characteristics, we seek the best specific function. Generally, the characteristic constraints of a function can be expressed as $f(t, y(t), y'(t))$, which can be understood as $f(\text{time}, \text{state}, \text{direction})$. As shown in the figure below, there are three functions from $a$ to $b$ that satisfy the functional characteristics. Which one is the optimal? This introduces the use of calculus to find the extremum of the functional path. Functions satisfying constraints$$ V(t) = \int_0^T f(t, y, y') dt $$ As the functional form $y$ changes, $V(t)$ also changes. This is the starting point of functional analysis. We aim to find the optimal path $y^*$ from a set of functional forms $y$ by seeking the extremum of $V(t)$ and other constraints.
heading: Functional
title: Notes on Learning Calculus of Variations

content: Calculus of VariationsWhen learning about derivatives, we used the concept of approximation to find limits: $$ \lim_{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x} $$ Here, we use a similar approach. Assume the optimal function is $y^\*$, and represent a class of functions near it as $y^* + \varepsilon P(t)$. Note that $P(0) = P(T) = 0$ Functional representationThus, we obtain the following expression in terms of $\varepsilon$: $$ V(\varepsilon) = \int\_0^T F\left[t, \underbrace{y^\*(t) + \varepsilon p(t)}\_{y(t)}, \underbrace{y^\*(t) + \varepsilon p'(t)}_{y'(t)}\right] dt $$ The first-order condition for the extremum is $\frac{dV}{d\varepsilon} = 0$. Derivative formula in calculus$$ \frac{d}{dt} \int_{g(t)}^{h(t)} F(x, t) dx = F(h, t) \frac{dh}{dt} - F(g, t) \frac{dg}{dt} + \int_{g(t)}^{h(t)} \frac{\partial F}{\partial t} dx $$$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dV}{d\varepsilon} &= \int_0^T \frac{\partial F}{\partial \varepsilon} dt = \int_0^T \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial y} \frac{dy}{d\varepsilon} + \frac{\partial F}{\partial y'} \frac{dy'}{d\varepsilon} \right) dt \\\\ &= \int_0^T \left[ F_y p(t) + F_{y'} p'(t) \right] dt \\\\ &= \int_0^T F_y p(t) dt + \color{red}{\int_0^T F_{y'} p'(t) dt} = 0 \end{aligned} $$ Local transformation$$ \frac{dy}{d\varepsilon} = \frac{d(y^*(t) + \varepsilon p)}{d\varepsilon} = P(t) $$ Similarly, $\frac{dy'}{d\varepsilon} = P'(t)$ Next, we transform the $\color{red}{\text{red part}}$ using integration by parts $\int\_{t=a}^{t=b} v du = vu \big|\_{t=a}^{t=b} - \int\_{t=a}^{t=b} u dv$ (where $u = u(t)$, $v = v(t)$): $$ \begin{align} & \color{red}{\int_0^T F\_{y'} p'(t) dt} \\\\ &= \left[ F\_{y'} p(t) \right]_0^T - \int\_0^T p(t) \frac{d}{dt} F\_{y'} dt \\\\ &= -\int\_0^T p(t) \frac{d}{dt} F\_{y'} dt \\\\ & (\text{Because } P(0) = P(T) = 0\\\\ & \text{ see the image of the perturbation function } P(t)) \end{align} $$ Substituting the $\color{red}{\text{red part}}$ back, we get: $$ \int_0^T p(t) \left[ F_y - \frac{d}{dt} F_{y'} \right] dt = 0 $$ Considering that the perturbation function $P(t)$ can be any function, the only way for the above equation to be zero is if $F_y - \frac{d}{dt} F_{y'} = 0$. Thus, we obtain the Euler equation: $$ F_y - \frac{d}{dt} F_{y'} = 0, \quad t \in [0, T] $$ When the equation constraint only involves three variables, i.e., $F(t, y, y')$, it can be expanded as: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dF_{y'}}{dt} &= \frac{\partial F_{y'}}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial F_{y'}}{\partial y} \frac{dy}{dt} + \frac{\partial F_{y'}}{\partial y'} \frac{dy'}{dt} \\\\ &= F_{ty'} + F_{yy'} y'(t) + F_{y'y'} y''(t) \end{aligned} $$ Expanding, we get: $$ F_{y'y'} y''(t) + F_{yy'} y'(t) + F_{ty'} - F_y = 0, \quad t \in [0, T] $$A problemGiven the functional $V(y) = \int_0^2 (12ty + y'^2) dt$ The general solution to the Euler equation is $y^*(t) = t^3 + c_1 t + c_2$ Extensions of the Euler equationHere, we only mention the extensions without further elaboration. When the functional $F$ contains only some variables, such as $F(t, y')$, $F(y, y')$, or $F(t, y)$, there are shortcut methods for each case. The core of the Euler equation is $F_y - \frac{d}{dt} F_{y'} = 0, \quad t \in [0, T]$ When the functional $F$ contains multiple variables or higher-order variables, the core remains the same, but further expansion is needed.
heading: Calculus of Variations
title: Notes on Learning Calculus of Variations

content: The Catenary ProblemImagine a red string hanging between two poles for drying clothes. Establish a coordinate system and rotate this string around the x-axis. What curvature should the string have to minimize the surface area of the resulting solid? Even a humble clothesline has profound principlesConsider the Pythagorean theorem for a differential element: $$ (ds)^2 = (dx)^2 + (dy)^2 $$ We can obtain the differential of the curve: $$ \frac{ds}{dt} = \sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{dy}{dt} \right)^2} = (1 + y'^2)^{1/2} $$ By differentiating along the curve, the integral of the circumference of each differential circle ($2\pi r$) gives the surface area after rotation. Thus, we obtain the following functional: $$ V(t) = \int_0^T 2\pi y ds = 2\pi \int_0^T y (1 + y'^2)^{1/2} dt $$ Simplifying the expression: $$ V(t) = \int_0^T y (1 + y'^2)^{1/2} dt $$ Using the Euler equation, we get: $$ y (1 + y'^2)^{1/2} - y y'^2 (1 + y'^2)^{-1/2} = c $$ Simplifying (by rationalizing the denominator and squaring to eliminate the square root in the denominator), we obtain: $$ y' \left( \equiv \frac{dy}{dt} \right) = \frac{1}{c} \sqrt{y^2 - c^2} $$ Which is: $$ \frac{c dy}{\sqrt{y^2 - c^2}} = dt $$ Integrating, we get: $$ \int \frac{c dy}{\sqrt{y^2 - c^2}} = c \ln \left( \frac{y + \sqrt{y^2 - c^2}}{c} \right) + c_1 = \int dt = t + c_2 $$ Rearranging the above expression and combining the two arbitrary constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ into $k$, we obtain the general solution: $$ y^*(t) = \frac{c}{2} \left[ e^{(t + k)/c} + e^{-(t + k)/c} \right] $$ And the catenary curve is of the form: $$ y = \frac{1}{2} (e^t + e^{-t}) $$ Catenary curve, image from WikipediaA uniformly dense string (e.g., a clothesline) hanging under uniform gravitational force will also form this curve. Suspension bridges, hyperbolic arch bridges, and overhead cables all utilize the principles of the catenary curve. In architectural design, the following form is generally used: $$ > y = c + a \cosh \frac{x}{a} > $$ Nature and society are always under optimal control!
heading: The Catenary Problem
title: Notes on Learning Calculus of Variations

content: The Brachistochrone ProblemImagine a marble race with three different slides. A contestant has only one chance to choose. Which slide should they choose for the marble to reach the finish line the fastest? Yes, even slides hide profound principlesSource: Beijing Science and Technology Museum. Imagine ancient architecture; which building curve would facilitate easier drainage? The logic is the same.Using the conservation of energy, we get: $$ \begin{align} \frac{1}{2} m v^2 &= m g y \\ v &= \sqrt{2 g y} \end{align} $$ In the catenary problem, we introduced the differential of the curve as $ds = (1 + y'^2)^{1/2} dt$. Thus, considering velocity as the derivative of distance with respect to time: $$ v = \frac{ds}{dt} = \sqrt{1 + y'^2} \frac{dx}{dt} $$ Combining the above equations: $$ \begin{cases} v = \sqrt{2 g y} \\ v = \sqrt{1 + y'^2} \frac{dx}{dt} \end{cases} $$ We obtain: $$ dt = \frac{\sqrt{1 + y'^2}}{\sqrt{2 g y}} dx $$ The target functional seeks the minimum total time: $$ T = \int dt = \int \frac{\sqrt{1 + y'^2}}{\sqrt{2 g y}} dx $$ Using the Euler equation, we get: $$ 2 y'' y + y'^2 + 1 = 0 $$ For the complete solution, refer to A Brief Discussion on the Calculus of Variations, which also mentions other mathematicians’ solutions to this problem. In any case, one form of the solution is (where $a$ and $c$ are arbitrary constants): $$ \begin{cases} x = a (\theta - \sin \theta) + c \\ y = a (1 - \cos \theta) \end{cases} $$ This form is related to the cycloid. Source: Wikipedia
heading: The Brachistochrone Problem
title: Notes on Learning Calculus of Variations

content: Monopoly Economics ProblemConsider a monopoly firm with a profit function written as $F(P, P')$. The economic meaning is that the monopoly firm has the power to set prices. The functional is then: $$ V = \int F(P, P') dt $$ Substituting into the Euler equation, we get: $$ F_{P'P'} P'' + F_{PP'} P' - F_P = 0 $$ Solving this implicit function requires some clever manipulation. Multiply both sides by $P'$ and then rearrange: $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{d}{dt} (P' F_{P'} - F) \\\\ & = \frac{d}{dt} (P' F_{P'}) - \frac{d}{dt} F(P, P') \\\\ & = F_{P'} P'' + P' \left( F_{PP'} P' + F_{P'P'} P'' \right) - \left( F_P P' + F_{P'} P'' \right) \\\\ & = P' \color{red}{\left( F_{P'P'} P'' + F_{PP'} P' - F_P \right)} \end{aligned} $$ The red part is the original equation. Thus, we obtain: $$ F - P' F_{P'} = c $$ Where $c$ is a constant. Writing $F$ as the common profit function $\pi$, we get: $$ \pi - P' \frac{\partial \pi}{\partial P'} = c $$ Considering static monopoly, the monopoly firm makes only one pricing decision (more detailed static game theory also considers product differentiation, information asymmetry, game sequence, and firm entry/exit states). In this case, the profit function only depends on $P$ and not on $P'$ (since there is only one pricing decision, no price change occurs). Clearly, $P' \frac{\partial \pi}{\partial P'} = 0$, so $\pi_s = c$. Now, consider dynamic game theory on top of static game theory. After the first pricing decision, monopoly firms begin to make multiple pricing decisions. The profit function is now: $$ \pi - P' \frac{\partial \pi}{\partial P'} = \pi_s $$ Here, the profit function $\pi$ must depend on both $P$ and $P'$. Thus, consider the elasticity of $\pi$ with respect to $P'$, denoted as: $$ \frac{\partial \pi}{\partial P'} \frac{P'}{\pi} = \varepsilon_{\pi P'} $$ Substituting into the dynamic monopoly game formula, we get: $$ \varepsilon_{\pi P'} = 1 - \frac{\pi_\varepsilon}{\pi} $$ In other words, in dynamic monopoly, firms should continuously adjust their profit functions based on this relationship.
heading: Monopoly Economics Problem
title: Notes on Learning Calculus of Variations

content: 4. Economics at Home and AbroadFinally, some thoughts from reading papers recently. Right now, domestic economists have a terrible reputation, and everyone says you have to go abroad to study economics (poor me, with my bad English, naturally chose to hunker down domestically). I agree, since the mainstream economics framework comes from the West. But this is not a question of comparing totals; it is a question of catching up. A huge number of domestic universities cannot even scrape together quality teaching resources for the “three highs” (advanced micro, macro, and econometrics)3, yet research progress is advancing by leaps and bounds — you could say the new generation has competed the difficulty way up ( Ten years ago, a complete regression workflow in Economic Research Journal was enough. Five years ago, econometrics had already become widespread. Even your thesis would get pushed to include econometrics if it did not have any. Nowadays, look at the recent issues of China Industrial Economics, Management World, and The Journal of World Economy: a large chunk of good papers are already mathematical-model qualitative analysis + social reality analysis + econometric argumentation, three-in-one. At least in format they have fully aligned with international standards. The increasing number of papers I read recently — heterogeneity and mechanism tests — feel like they are mixing testing with economic-meaning analysis. I get the feeling the big shots are at the stage of “a formless move beats a formed move.” Considering only purely domestically-trained scholars: research rigor has caught up, and what remains is original thought. Catching up on that will take at least another 20 years, right? Even if someone proposes a genius innovation theory this year, it still needs 20 years for the theory to pass the test of history and society.
heading: 4. Economics at Home and Abroad

content: Renaming VariablesThe simplest method — select Note! We want to rename the column 年份 to year, i.e., the assignment is year = 年份! If the file contains special symbols, wrap them with `` symbols library(dplyr) names(中国城市数据库) data<-rename(中国城市数据库,year = 年份 ,GDP = `地区生产总值(万元)` ,one = `第一产业增加值(万元)`)By the way, here’s a more complicated way to rename (basic R syntax): # Rename the first column to bb setwd("F:/桌面/R") 中国城市数据库 <- readxl::read_excel("中国城市数据库.xlsx") colnames(中国城市数据库)[1] <- 'bb' # Similarly, row names are changed with rownamesUsing dataset$column_name is how you specify a column variable; many of RStudio’s features are quite handyIf a variable name is too long and we don’t know which column the variable to rename is in, use names(中国城市数据库); the result will show the variable names and their corresponding column numbers.

content: Creating New VariablesI recommend Method 1. Method 1d3 <- mutate(中国城市数据库, year = 年份/2 )Method 2# Mainly use transform() # The first argument is the name of the data frame to operate on # The following arguments are the operation formulas # The left side of the formula is the new variable name # The right side of the formula is the specific operation mydata <- transform( mydata, sum = x1 + x2, mean = (x1 + x2)/2 )Method 3mydata$mean <- (mydata$x1 + mydata$x2)/2 # Create a new variable named mean, obtained by averaging the two original variables (x1 and x2) mydata$empty_variable <- NULL # Create an empty variableExtracting and Appending CharactersCreate a new variable x by extracting a string of length 4 from variable var starting at position 1. 中国城市数据库 <- 中国城市数据库 %>% mutate(x = substr(var, 1, 4)) # Append at the end 中国城市数据库2 <- 中国城市数据库2 %>% mutate(x = paste0(var, "_suffix")) # Add at the front 中国城市数据库2 <- 中国城市数据库2 %>% mutate(x = paste(var, "_suffix"))

content: Matching and MergingAlthough R has a built-in merge similar to Stata’s, it’s weaker and can only do one-to-one matching, so I recommend the dplyr package here. HorizontalVerticallibrary(dplyr) # Horizontal dplyr::left_join(a,b,by="x1") dplyr::right_join(a,b,by="x1") dplyr::inner_join(a,b,by="x1") dplyr::outer_join(a,b,by="x1") dplyr::semi_join(a,b,by="x1") dplyr::anti_join(a,b,by="x1") # Vertical dplyr::intersect(a,b) dplyr::union(a,b) dplyr::setdiff(a,b) dplyr::bind_rows(a,b) # Example # Match city data and pilot policy by id and year # For partial matching, slice by index [m,n:l] merged_data <- dplyr::left_join(中国城市数据库, 智慧城市,by = c("year", "id")) merged_data2 <- merge(中国城市数据库[,3:5], 智慧城市, by = "year", all = TRUE)

content: Handling OutliersRemoving Duplicatesunique_data <- 中国城市数据库 %>% distinct(id, year, .keep_all = TRUE)Data Imputationna.rm = TRUE is a parameter usually used to specify whether to remove missing values when performing calculations on data. When the na.rm parameter is set to TRUE, the function removes missing values from the data before computing; when it is set to FALSE or omitted, the function includes the missing values and returns NA as the result. Cross-Sectional Interpolation # Replace missing values in the gdp column of 中国城市数据库 with the column mean 中国城市数据库[is.na(中国城市数据库$gdp), ]$gdp <- mean(中国城市数据库$gdp, na.rm = TRUE) # Replace outliers less than 0 in the score column of 中国城市数据库 with missing values 中国城市数据库[which(中国城市数据库$score < 0), ]$score <- NA # Replace missing values in the score column of 中国城市数据库 with the column mean 中国城市数据库[is.na(中国城市数据库$score), ]$score <- mean(中国城市数据库$score, na.rm = TRUE)Panel Interpolation Referring to Stata’s interpolation command, I found a similar interpolation method in R. library(dplyr) library(zoo) # Treat the data frame as panel data, group by id and year, and interpolate "地区生产总值.万元." 中国城市数据库_new <- 中国城市数据库 %>% arrange(id, year) %>% group_by(id) # Interpolation 中国城市数据库_new <- 中国城市数据库_new %>% mutate(地区生产总值.万元. = na.approx(地区生产总值.万元.)) # Extrapolation 中国城市数据库_new <- 中国城市数据库_new %>% mutate(地区生产总值.万元. = na.approx(地区生产总值.万元., method = "constant"))WinsorizingReferring to Equivalent Commands in R and Stata - statar, using the statar package. Values beyond a specific range are replaced with the value at the boundary of that range. library(statar) statar::winsorize(v, probs = c(0.01, 0.99)) # R can also first compute the data distribution and then delete based on it # Compute the percentiles quantiles <- quantile(中国城市数据库2$R.D内部经费支出.万元., probs = c(0.01, 0.99)) # Replace the extreme values 中国城市数据库2$R.D内部经费支出.万元.[中国城市数据库2$R.D内部经费支出.万元. < quantiles[1]] <- quantiles[1] 中国城市数据库2$R.D内部经费支出.万元.[中国城市数据库2$R.D内部经费支出.万元. > quantiles[2]] <- quantiles[2]Deleting DataDelete blank values and values that don’t apply to the questionnaire. Since Stata can only operate on one table at a time, you add and remove everything on a single table; but R supports working with multiple tables, so in practice filtering is achieved by extracting the appropriate data to form a new table. # Delete the rows with year 2020, and drop columns 5 and 10 中国城市数据库_new <- 中国城市数据库[中国城市数据库$year != "2020", -c(5, 10)] # Use a loop function # Create a character vector containing the variable names to be imputed var <- c("var0", "var1", "var2", "var3", "genshin") # Loop through each variable name for (i in var) { # Delete specific values in the variable data <- subset(data, !(data[, i] == -88 | data[, i] == -99 | is.na(data[, i]) | data[, i] <= 0)) }

content: PlottingThis section refers to the electronic lecture notes Statistical Software R by Teacher Li Dongfeng. My data source ggplot2 is about divide-and-conquer plotting, so its syntax consists of $$ Step 1 (specify the dataset, specify the axes) + Step 2 (specify the plot type) + Plot 3 (decoration) + Combination 4 (......) $$ The general steps for plotting with ggplot2 are: Prepare the data, usually a data frame, and generally in long format, i.e., each observation time takes one row and each observed variable takes one column. Input the data into the ggplot() function, and specify which graphical attributes each variable in the plot maps to, such as the x coordinate, y coordinate, color, shape, etc. These mappings are called aesthetic mappings, or aesthetics. Choose a suitable plot type; the function name starts with geom_, such as geom_point() for a scatter plot. The plot type is called a geom for short. Connect the ggplot() part and the geom_xxx() part with a plus sign. You can already make a plot at this point; the following steps are further refinements. Set an appropriate coordinate system, such as coord_cartesian(), scale_x_log10(), etc. Again connect with a plus sign. Set the title, legend position, and so on, such as labs(). Again connect with a plus sign. A rough template for this workflow is: library(ggplot2) p <- ggplot(data=, mapping=aes(=, =, <...>)) p + geom_(<...>) + scale__(<...>) + coord_(<...>) + labs(<...>)
heading: Plotting
title: R Notes 2: Data Cleaning, Plotting, and Econometrics

content: Scatter Plots and Line PlotsThe syntax really doesn’t feel as clean and convenient as Stata’s ( geom_point(): scatter points; similarly, add a line plot with geom_line() geom_smooth(): fitted line scale_x_log10: log-transform the x-axis with base 10 color = quality: fill colors by group according to the quality variable facet_wrap(~ quality): slice into groups by the quality variable; it can also be (a~b), which is two-dimensional grouping. You can also use facet_grid(row variable ~ column variable). setwd("F:/桌面/R") testdata <- readr::read_csv("wineQualityReds.csv") names(testdata) library(ggplot2) # qplot for quick plotting qplot(x=chlorides , y=chlorides , data=testdata, geom = "point") # Plot with ggplot p <- ggplot(data = testdata, mapping = aes( x = residual.sugar, y = chlorides, color = quality, fill = quality)) p1 <- p + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "loess") + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar) + labs( x = "横坐标", y = "纵坐标", title = "test标题", subtitle = "随便找的数据", caption = "数据来源: github" )+ facet_wrap(~ quality) print(p1) ggsave(filename="文件名.png")Scatter plot with a fitted lineAfter faceting

content: Bar Charts# Count using the dataset 数据集 <- 原始数据集 |> select(分类变量) |> count(分类变量) |> mutate(比例值 = n / sum(n)) p<-ggplot(数据集, aes( x = 分类变量 y = n, # Can also change to the ratio value fill =religion # Different categories in different colors )) p+geom_col() +labs(y = "纵坐标名字") +guides(fill = "none") # Whether to remove the legend + coord_flip() # Swap the x and y axes + geom_col(position = "stack") # Stack +facet_grid(A ~ B) # Facet into groups A bar chart grouped internally df3 <- gss_sm |> select(bigregion, religion) |> group_by(bigregion, religion) |> summarise(n = n(), .groups="drop_last") |> mutate(ratio = n / sum(n)) p <- ggplot(df3, aes( x = bigregion, y = n, fill = religion)) p + geom_col()A histogram grouped internally

content: Correlation HeatmapReference: Drawing Correlation Heatmaps in R # Load the package library(ggcorrplot) cormtcars <- round(cor(mtcars), 3) # round() sets the number of decimal places ggcorrplot(cor(cormtcars)) # The default is squares; change to circles and add the correlation coefficients ggcorrplot(cormtcars,method = "circle",lab=T) # Use the cor_pmat() function from the ggcorrplot package to compute p-values: pmtcars <- cor_pmat(mtcars) ggcorrplot(cormtcars,hc.order = T, # Hierarchical clustering to reorder the matrix ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_void(base_size = 15), # Theme changes colors = c("CornflowerBlue","white","Salmon"), # Custom colors; choose what you like, or refer to the figure styles in well-designed papers. lab = T,lab_size = 5, # Font size of the correlation coefficient text tl.cex = 15, # Axis label font size p.mat = pmtcars, # Add significance information sig.level = 0.01, # Significance level pch = 4, # Mark the cells that aren't significant enough; pch selects the marking style, and you can try other numbers to see what style each gives pch.cex = 10) # Size of the non-significant marks; use insig = "blank" to blank out the non-significant cellsCorrelation coefficient heatmap

content: Bubble Plots# Set the working environment setwd("F:/桌面/R") 中国城市数据库 <- readxl::read_excel("中国城市数据库.xlsx") # Load the packages library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # Rename the dataset columns names(中国城市数据库) str(中国城市数据库) data<-rename(中国城市数据库,year = 年份 ,GDP = `地区生产总值(万元)` ,one = `第一产业增加值(万元)` ,id=`行政区划代码`) data <- mutate(data, pro = substr(id, 1, 2), # Extract characters; the first two digits of cityid represent the province lgone=log(one,base=10) # Log-transform ) # Plot p<-ggplot(data[1:400,], mapping =aes( x=year, y=GDP, size=lgone, # Bubble size weight color = pro,# Line color grouping, by province fill = pro))# Fill color grouping, by province p+ geom_point(shape=21,colour="black",alpha = .5)+geom_smooth(method = "loess", aes(group = pro))Bubble plot

content: Combining PlotsRecommended reading: The most comprehensive guide to combining and stitching plots in R Loading Packages and Plotting# Load the plotting packages library(ggplot2) library(ggprism) library(reshape) library(ggpubr) # Data df <- data.frame(A = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 13), B = c(1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 10,5,6,8), C = c(1, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13), D = c(1, 2, 5, 8, 10, 13,5,8,6)) df1=melt(df) colnames(df1)=c("group","value") # I often read this expert’s articles on regression, and in their view, economic regression is just a special variant of general/generalized/multilevel linear models. Since R is mainly used in biomedical statistics, the mainstream R package three-line tables and the three-line tables required in economics are not the same.

content: Regression and Word OutputRegressionrobust="HC1": robust mode setting; HC1 is reg y x,r in Stata cluster="stratum": same as Stata; cluster is hierarchical clustering to handle autocorrelation family=binomial: whether to use binomial regression regress(Temp ~ Month + Day + Wind + Solar.R, data=airquality, robust=TRUE) regress(case ~ age + parity + education + spontaneous + induced, data=infert, family=binomial, robust="HC1", cluster="stratum")Regression OutputThe bruceR package merges the three-line table output of reg into generalized multilevel regression, The following two regression code snippets are equivalent: # Code 1: lm2 = lm(Temp ~ Month + Day + Wind + Solar.R, data=airquality) model_summary(lm2, robust="HC1") # Code 2: regress(Temp ~ Month + Day + Wind + Solar.R, data=airquality, robust=TRUE)So use the lm model to output the regression results: library(bruceR) head(airquality) # Built-in dataset names(airquality) lm1 = lm(Temp ~ Month + Day, data=airquality) lm2 = lm(Temp ~ Month + Day + Wind + Solar.R, data=airquality) model_summary(lm1) model_summary(lm2, robust="HC1") model_summary(list(lm1, lm2), file="OLS Models.doc")Regression results

content: R Notes 1: Interface Introduction and Syntax Structure R Notes 2: Data Cleaning, Plotting, and Econometrics Notes on my R learning journey. Personally, as an economics learner who only runs regressions, Stata is more than enough1. Whatever it lacks I usually fill with Python wheels, and even for DSGE I use MATLAB’s Dynare add-on. For econometrics, R’s regression table formatting and export are not very friendly, which is a bit of a turn-off. Although it’s not of much use to me right now, there are three reasons I’m learning it: I support open source2, so I wanted to get my feet wet with R; I’m currently using RStudio to write my blog files; I’ve looked at analyst-type internship postings at big companies like Kuaishou, ByteDance, Tencent, and Baidu, and they generally require using R to handle SQL databases.

content: Interface IntroductionMenu path for page settings: tools - global option - Pane Layout PageAt this point, The source panel in the top-left (after creating a new R script project) is where you write code. The console in the bottom-left shows the results. The top and bottom sections on the right are customizable panels. For example, history shows your code run history; environment is the variable environment, where you can use import Dataset to load Stata, Excel, and other data; file shows the computer directories of your working environment. content: Managing and Downloading PackagesManual InstallationUsing R over the long term is tough on your computer’s storage, because you keep downloading packages. On Windows, R is generally managed with Rtools. Recent versions of R should come with this toolkit; if not, just install it from the official site — just install the .exe. In the file panel, there’s a Packages section; click install there to install packages. Installing packagesInstalling and Loading via CommandsR is a language for statisticians. I personally find its base syntax not very elegant, but since it’s open source, once you load the right packages it becomes a real joy. For example, to install the car package, you can use the following commands: # Installing a package install.packages("car") # This is a comment # Loading a package library(caret) # Load a single function from a package # car::vif() # Update packages update.packages() # Remove a package remove.packages() # Get help ?help help("library") # Help on a keyword help.search("library") # Help on a package help(packages = "ggplot2")Since different packages may have functions with the same name, when loading two packages causes a conflict, the same-named function from the later package will override the earlier one. Setting the Working Directory# View the current directory getwd() # Set the working directory; note that forward slashes are used setwd("F:/桌面") # Get a file path; this opens a file browser to find the file manually, and clicking it returns the file path file.choose() # Save R files (.RData) save() save.image() # Load an R file load("F:/文档1") load(file.choose() ) # Load a package's dataset data()Loading DataIn Stata, one window can only load one dataset, but R can load multiple. The environment panel can be loaded manually# Show all data objects in the current environment panel, listed by dataset name ls() # Remove an object rm(list = ls())

content: Managing and Downloading PackagesManual InstallationUsing R over the long term is tough on your computer’s storage, because you keep downloading packages. On Windows, R is generally managed with Rtools. Recent versions of R should come with this toolkit; if not, just install it from the official site — just install the .exe. content: Data StructuresAssignment and VectorsThe usual order of introduction: assignment, indexing, slicing. # Assignment # object_name <- object_value # Shortcut: Alt - v1 <- 1:5 # Generate the vector v1 corresponding to 1 through 5 v2 <- c(v1,3,2,44,6) # Link/connect, nested v3 <- rep(v2,times = 2)# repeat: repeat the whole sequence twice v4 <- rep(v2,each = 2)# repeat: repeat each element twice v5 <- rep(v2,times=2 , each = 2)# each is applied first, then times v6 <- seq(from = 2, to = 9, by = 3) # Start from 2, add 3 each time, until it exceeds 9 v7 <- seq(from = 2, to = 12, length.out = 3) # Constrain the vector length, so the extra values are averaged out v8 <- c('JOJO' ,'下一个就是你了') v9 <- c('JOJO' ,T , 123) # There is coercion here; character > logical > numeric # Vector names names(v2)<- v9 # Change the names of v2 to v9 # At this point v2 looks like this JOJO TRUE 123 1 2 3 4 5 3 2 3 6 # Vector length length(v9) length(v9)<- 9 # Vector indexing # Unlike Python, whose default index starts from 0, R's index starts from 1 by default # Unlike Python, where a negative sign means the reverse direction, in R a negative index means dropping that index value v7[3] v7[c(1,3,5)] v2[c(1,4)] v2[-c(1,4)] # Drop the values at indices 1 and 4 v2[c('JOJO' ,'TRUE')] v1[v1%%2==1] # Conditional indexing: odd numbers with remainder 1 when divided by 2 # Constants pi # Pi letters # Lowercase letters LETTERS # Uppercase letters month.abb # Month abbreviations, "Jan" month.name # Full month names, "January" MatricesMatrices are just vector commands stacked together. # Matrix m1 <- matrix( 1:6, nrow = 2, # Two rows # ncol = 3, # Columns byrow = F, # Fill column-wise, so there's no need to specify ncol dimnames = list(c('r1','r2'), c('c1','c2','c3')) ) # Like vectors, matrices accept only one data type # Create an empty 3*3 matrix m0 <- matrix(NA,nclo = 3,nrow=3) m2 <- matrix( c(1:6, letters[1:6]), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(c('r1', 'r2', 'r3'), c('c1', 'c2', 'c3', 'c4')) ) # Row and column names colnames(m1) # Columns rownames(m1) # Rows dimnames(m2)<-list(c) # Row and column names # Dimension info, i.e., the shape command in Python dim(m1) ncol(m1) nrow(m1) # Matrix indexing m2[1,2] # Return the value at row 1, column 2 m2[1,] # Return the vector of the first row m2[c(1,3),c(2,4)] # Slicing by index name works the same way m2['r1',] # Convert to a vector as.vector(m1) # Extract column-wise in order #arrayListsUnlike vectors and matrices, lists can combine different data types and structures. v1 <- 1:5 m1 <- matrix( 1:6, nrow = 2, byrow = F, dimnames = list(c('r1','r2'), c('c1','c2','c3')) ) # Unlike vectors and matrices, lists can hold different data types and structures l1<- list(com1 = v1, com2 = m1) # List names names(l1) # List indexing. A video said these commands are different, i.e., they differ in returning a list, matrix, or vector, but I tried them and there doesn't seem to be a difference. l1$com1 l1[['com2']] l1['com2'] l1[20] # Create a new component l1$com3<- 3:6 l1 # Flatten the list unlist(l1) # Reduce the list to a vector; indices become which list and which valueData FramesA special kind of list — the panel data and time series we often work with are built using data frames. # Create a data frame df1 <- data.frame( C1 = 2:5, C2 = letters[2:5] ) df1 # Dimension info dim(df1) ncol(df1) nrow(df1) # Row and column names dimnames(df1) # Column and row names names(df1) # Row names colnames(df1) rownames(df1) # Data frame indexing df1[1:2 ,2] df1[,2] df1[,"c1"] df1['1',] df1[[2]] df1$c1 df1[2] df1['c1'] # Create a new column df1$c3 <- 1:4 # Generate a grid-search data frame expand.grid(mtry = 2:5, ntree=c(200,500))

returns a vector min(v2) cummin(v2) sum(v2) # Sum cumsum(v2) # Cumulative sum prod(v2) # Product cumprod(v2) # Cumulative product mean(v2) # Mean median(v2) # Median sd(v2) # Standard deviation, computed using the sample formula var(v2) # Variance, computed using the sample formula rev(v2) # Reverse the vector, i.e., reverse the order sort(v2) # Sort v2 <- rep(v2,times=2) table(v5) # Frequency count unique(v5) # Value levels, arranged in the order the numbers first appear # Index functions which(v5==7) # Return the indices that satisfy the condition which.max(v5) # Return the index of the first occurrence when the maximum is repeated which.min(v5) # Intersection intersect(1:5,4:7) # Set difference setdiff(1:5,4:7) # Union; keeps only the element's position value, and keeps one even if there are duplicates union(1:5,4:7)Data Frame and Matrix OperationsData Framedfs <- data.frame( a = 1:5, b = 3:7, d = letters[1:5] ) # Row and column merging df1 <- dfs[1:3, ] df1 df2 <- dfs[3:5, ] df2 # Row merging rbind(df1, df2) # Rows increase, columns stay the same cbind(df1, df2) # Columns increase, rows stay the same # Row and column operations colMeans(dfs[,1:2]) # Column means colSums(dfs[,1:2]) # Column sums rowMeans(dfs[,1:2]) # Row means rowSums(dfs[,1:2]) # Row sums # apply(data frame, 1 for rows or 2 for columns, function) apply(dfs[,1:2],2,sd) # Compute the standard deviation by column apply( dfs[,1:2], 2, function(x){sum(is.na(x))} ) # Data structure info str(dfs) # Data types summary(dfs) # Minimum and maximum values View(dfs) # Display the data frame head(dfs,n=2) # Show the first two rows (n=2) tail(dfs,n=2) # Show the last two rows (n=2)Matrixm3 <- matrix( c(5,7,3,4), ncol = 2, byrow = T, ) m3 m4 <- matrix( c(5,7,3,4,8,9), ncol = 3, byrow = T, ) m4 t(m3) # Transpose det(m3) # Determinant m3 %*% m4 # Matrix multiplication solve(m3) # m3 %*% x = E, solve for x solve(m3,m4) # m3 %*% x = m4, solve for xCharacter Functions# Concatenate characters paste(1:5,collapse = "+") paste(letters[1:5],collapse = "-") paste(1:5,letters[1:8],collapse = "~") paste(1:5,letters[1:8]) # Character length nchar(month.name) # Convert letters to uppercase toupper(month.name) # Convert letters to lowercase tolower(month.name) # Index of elements containing a certain character grep("JU",month.name) # Replace characters gsub("e","000",month.name) # Replace the parts of month.name containing "e" with "000"Distribution Functionsset.seed(24) # Random seed sample(1:2,12,replace = T) # Draw 12 samples with replacement (T) from 1 and 2. You've probably seen random sampling in Stata placebo tests rnorm(10,mean=1,sd=2) # r random number + distribution (norm) pnorm(1,mean=1,sd=2) # p cumulative probability qnorm(0.5,mean=1,sd=2) # q quantile dnorm(1,mean=1,sd=2) # d probability density plot(x = seq(-5, 7, length = 1000), y = dnorm(seq(-5, 7, length = 1000), mean = 1, sd = 2), type = "l", ylim = c(0, 0.25)) abline(h = 0, v = 1) # Take 1000 numbers between -5 and 7, following a normal distribution with mean 1 and standard deviation 2 # Add a horizontal line at value 0 and a vertical line at value 1The corresponding distribution function plot

content: Basic SyntaxLoopsStata simplifies this to local, global, and foreach for looping over variables; the downside is that it’s not convenient for adding and subtracting across rows. # For loop for (x in c(-2,3,0,4)){ print(x) y= abs(x) z=y^3 print(z) print("____") } # Using a macro variable to define the loop for (variable in vector){ } # While loop v1 <- 1:5 i<-1 while(i<=length(v1)){ print(i) print(sum(v1[1:i])) i=i+1 print(i) print("####") } df <- data.frame(c1 = 2:5, c2 = 4:7, c3 = -19:-16) # Loop over each row of the data frame for (i in 1:nrow(df)) { # Compute the sum of each row and print it print(sum(df[i, ])) } #next: skip #break: stop for (i in 1:nrow(df)) { # Compute the sum of each row and print it if(i==3){break} print(sum(df[i, ])) }ConditionalsIf-else is old hat, so I won’t give too many examples here. a <- 7 if (a > 6) { print("a > 6") } else { print("a <= 6") } s = 45 if (s %% 2 ==0) { print("偶数") } else { print("奇数") } ifelse(55 %% 2 ==0,"偶数" "奇数")Writing FunctionsAfter defining a function, it also shows up in the variable panelname <- function(parameters){ the actual operation } # Define a function: factorial f1 <- function(aug1){ res1<-1:aug1 res2<-prod(res1) return(res2) } # Use the function f1(10) # Define a function: addition f2<-function(aug1,aug2=4){ res <- aug1+aug2 return(res) } f2(2333) f2(2333,6666) # This overrides the default value aug2=4

content: Import and ExportTable source: R in Data Science FormatCommand.txtread.table().csvread.csv() and readr::read_csv().xls and .xlsxreadxl::read_excel() and openxlsx::read.xlsx().sav （SPSS files）haven::read_sav() and foreign::read.spss().Rdata or rdaload().rdsreadRDS() and readr::read_rds().dtahaven::read_dta() and haven::read_stata().sas 7 bdat （SAS files）haven::read_sas()Internetdownload.file()# Import CSV data # Custom data list d.small <- read_csv("John, 33, 95 Kim, 21, 64 Sandy, 49, 100 ", col_names=c("name", "x", "y") ) # Read a file 1 data <- read_csv("testcsv.csv") # Read a file 2 rawdata<- read.table(file.choose(),head=T,sep=",") # head: treat the first row as variable names; sep: CSV delimiter head(rawdata,n=4) # Output the first 4 rows of the data tail(rawdata,n=10) # Output the last 10 rows of the data rawdata[95:105] # Output rows 95-105 str(rawdata) # Check the data types # read.csv(file.choose()) # data.table::fread(file.choose()) # Export CSV data write.table(rawdata, # Object to export "test.csv", # Export path sep=",", # Export delimiter row.names=F) # Row names # Read an Excel sheet library(readxl) data1<- read_excel(file.choose()) # Get csv files in bulk library(readr) library(dplyr) # Set the folder path folder_path <- "F:/桌面/房地产PB/" # Get the paths of all csv files in the folder csv_files <- list.files(folder_path, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE) # Create an empty list to store the read csv data data_list <- list() # Loop through and read each csv file, storing it in data_list for (file in csv_files) { data <- read_csv(file) data_list[[file]] <- data } # Combine all the data into one data frame combined_data <- bind_rows(data_list) # View the combined data print(combined_data)At least the vast majority of journal master files are do-files. As for plotting, Stata’s schemepack package is already powerful enough to be adjusted to R’s default style. ↩︎ Using Zotero for reference management was the start of my love for the open-source philosophy. ↩︎ Selling courses in China really is second to none. ↩︎
