content: (This article was compiled from an oral account given by Xiaokai Yang to our reporters Xiao Rui and Li Liming in 2003, and was reviewed and revised by him; some parts were cut during editing.) Source: The Economic Observer Xiaokai Yang was a self-taught genius whose path of hardship is deeply moving. Lately I keep complaining that the environment is no good, but after going over Xiaokai Yang’s path of growth again, I feel deeply ashamed. In studying theory, one must be able to enter it and step out of it, to leap out of the knowledge and analyze the current situation; losing oneself in a vacuum world for one’s own pleasure is surely a failure. Accumulation should be persistent; one should actively use mathematics to describe reality, and through that grasp the thought behind it and cultivate intuition. For a partial introduction to Xiaokai Yang’s theory, see Development Economics: Marginal Analysis and Inframarginal Analysis (Introduction) As Heaven’s movement is ever vigorous, so must a gentleman ceaselessly strive along. Salute! My original name was Yang Xiguang; Xiaokai Yang was my childhood name, which I took up again after 1978. I was born in Jilin in 1948 and grew up in Changsha, Hunan. My grandfather was a landlord who ran a school in the countryside. He had received a strict Confucian education, and during the late-Qing movement to promote Western learning he also attended a Western-style school. Our parents’ generation likewise received a Confucian education from childhood; I remember that when I was in elementary school, my father asked an uncle to teach me the Analects at home. Both my parents joined the revolution in 1938. My father was originally a senior cadre of the Hunan Provincial Party Committee. In 1959, because he supported Peng Dehuai’s views and opposed the Great Leap Forward and the public mess halls, he was branded a rightist opportunist. That was in the autumn of 1959. I was still very small then. One day my father carried me to the window and said to me kindly: “Cadres who stay too long in the higher organs don’t understand conditions at the grass roots, so they should go down to learn about conditions.” I looked at the red leaves of a big maple outside the window, a little puzzled why my father’s manner was so unexpectedly gentle that day. My father was in low spirits those days and often argued with my mother. Only three years later did I learn that my father had been branded a rightist opportunist in 1959. My father told me that in 1962 he was rehabilitated, and that they admitted his 1959 views had been correct.
title: Repost: Xiaokai Yang, "My Life"

content: Where Is China Going?The Cultural Revolution broke out in 1966. Because my parents were both sympathetic to the views of Liu Shaoqi and Peng Dehuai, they were again branded counterrevolutionary revisionists, and during the Cultural Revolution we became a family of “black monsters,” deeply discriminated against. At the time I was a first-year senior high student at Changsha No. 1 Middle School. Because I was discriminated against and could not join the Red Guards, I joined a rebel faction that opposed the Red Guards. The organization I joined was called the “Seize Military Power Combat Team,” which belonged to the “Provincial Proletarian Revolutionary Alliance” (“Sheng Wu Lian”). At school the difference between the Red Guards and the rebels was that the Red Guards were all of good class background, while the rebels were mostly of bad background. So during the Cultural Revolution we supported the rebels and opposed the Red Guards; the rebels in senior high mainly opposed the “theory of blood lineage.” In the early Cultural Revolution, the masses could form their own organizations and join different ones according to their own views. By 1967, the military had banned mass organizations and forbidden the masses from forming political organizations. On February 4, 1967, the Central Cultural Revolution Group suddenly ordered the Hunan Provincial Military District to send troops to suppress Hunan’s largest rebel organization, “Xiangjiang Fenglei,” arresting over ten thousand people. So the rebels came into conflict with the authorities. Our rebel organization, the “Seize Military Power Combat Team,” was also drawn into this conflict, and I was arrested and held in the Changsha Public Security Bureau detention center for more than two months. After I was released that time, I wrote many big-character posters one after another, including “An Investigation Report on Urban Educated Youth Going Up to the Mountains and Down to the Villages” and “Political Power Grows Out of the Barrel of a Gun,” and so on. In 1968 I wrote a big-character poster titled “Where Is China Going?,” advocating that China adopt a Paris Commune-style democracy. This article had a great impact at the time. After the second-in-command of the Hunan Provincial Revolutionary Committee preparatory group read “Where Is China Going?,” he hurriedly passed the word to the provincial cadres of the time to characterize it. Soon my article was sent up to the Central Cultural Revolution Group. At nine o’clock on the evening of January 24, 1968, some leaders received members of the Hunan Provincial Revolutionary Committee preparatory group and representatives of some Hunan rebel organizations in the Hunan Hall of the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, and announced the suppression of a Hunan rebel organization called “Sheng Wu Lian,” making some very stern, weighty speeches and instructions. During the meeting, Kang Sheng several times singled out “Yang Xiguang of No. 1 Middle School” and the article “Where Is China Going?,” calling it “the counterrevolutionary ’lament of the warhorse.’” Kang also asserted: “I have a feeling that his theory is by no means something a middle school student, or even a university student, could write; there is a counterrevolutionary black hand behind him!” Jiang Qing put it more bluntly: “That ‘Seize Military Power Combat Team’ — let it go to hell!” A few days later I was “personally named” and thrown into prison, held at the Zuojiatang detention center of the Changsha Public Security Bureau. I was held in the detention center for over a year. In the autumn of 1969, in October, I was transferred from detention to formal arrest. Soon after, on a clear winter day in November, I was sentenced to ten ye
heading: Where Is China Going?
title: Repost: Xiaokai Yang, "My Life"

content: Ten Years Behind Bars“Where Is China Going?” not only landed me in prison but also brought great disaster to my family. In Kang Sheng’s instructions of January 24, 1968, he said that “Where Is China Going?,” “Our Program,” and “Resolutions on the Current Situation” by Sheng Wu Lian were not something middle school students could have written, nor university students; there must be a black hand pulling strings behind them, and they must ferret out “Teacher Chen,” who waved the goose-feather fan behind these students. My mother happened to be surnamed Chen, and after Kang Sheng’s instructions reached Changsha she was denounced many times; her hands were blackened with ink and she was forced to kneel in public as a warning. The blackened hands symbolized the “black hand.” After enduring endless humiliation, unable to bear the disgrace, she hanged herself. After my mother was driven to suicide, my two younger sisters lost their home. My father was locked up in a “Mao Zedong Thought Study Class,” one sister was sent down to the mountains of western Hunan, the other fled to Shanxi to seek refuge with relatives, and my elder brother was also expelled from his work unit and driven to the countryside. During the year and a half I was held at the Zuojiatang detention center, I found a teacher to study English, an electrical engineer to study electrical machinery, and a mechanical engineer to study mechanical drafting. I also read A General History of the World, Marx’s Capital, and a book called Long Live Mao Zedong Thought. I borrowed Capital from a fellow prisoner, Teacher Chen, and so at Zuojiatang I finished the thick three volumes of Capital. My first impression of Capital was quite good; it had far more of an academic flavor. But after I finished the first two volumes, I found that the labor theory of value ignored another important factor determining value — use value. It was many years later that I learned that what Marx called use value is called utility in modern economics. But I quite liked Marx’s elaboration on Adam Smith’s theory of the division of labor. After finishing Capital, for some reason my heart came to expect that I would become an economist in the future. I had three ideas: first, to clarify the importance of use value in the theory of value; second, to weave the problem of the division of labor into the theory of value; and third, to mathematize the theory of value. Later, in the labor reform team, I wrote an economics notebook along this line of thought. It was many years before I realized that these ideas had long ago become far more sophisticated theories in modern economics. The idea of mathematizing economic theory I first saw on a big-character poster at Peking University. Another big-character poster that stimulated me was about how a privileged stratum had already formed in China, and how Marx’s method of economic analysis should be used to reanalyze Chinese society. That stimulus was the intellectual starting point of my later writing of “Where Is China Going?” After I went to prison, my political philosophy was already very different from when I wrote “Where Is China Going?” When I wrote that article, I had a pursuit of idealism; I believed a democratic polity should be elected by the people. By the time I was in prison I had completely lost that idealism. I believed that the standards by which people judge the values they pursue change with history, so how history will develop is far more important than any ideal goal. Before, the question I cared about was “what is good and what is bad, and how should this world be?” In prison I asked instead: “how will this world develop?” The worst things might well happen within our own lifetime, so subjective judgments of good and bad, right and wrong have no meaning; how to adapt to circumstances
heading: Ten Years Behind Bars
title: Repost: Xiaokai Yang, "My Life"

content: A First TrialAfter my release at the end of my term in April 1978, I returned to Changsha. Because no work unit dared accept me, the author of “Where Is China Going?,” I stayed at my father’s home for a year. That year I audited a year of mathematics courses in the mathematics department of Hunan University; these audits were arranged by some rightist professors who had just been reinstated. At this time I began to use my childhood name, Xiaokai Yang, again. Later I worked for half a year as a proofreader at the Hunan Xinhua No. 2 Printing Plant in Shaoyang. In 1979 I applied for the master’s program at the Institute of Economics of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, but because of my “counterrevolutionary history” I was refused permission to take the exam. In 1980 I applied again, and with the help of Yu Guangyuan, then vice president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, I finally got the chance to take the quantitative economics exam. After passing the exam I was admitted as a research assistant and worked for nearly two years at the Institute of Quantitative and Technical Economics of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. From 1979 to 1982 I studied neoclassical economics quite systematically, often auditing courses at various universities, borrowing books from the Beijing Library, and attending econometrics training classes. I studied systems theory, information theory, control theory, and operations research, did some econometric research, computed some shadow prices, translated a textbook on economic cybernetics, and published Preliminary Economic Cybernetics and Foundations of Mathematical Economics, roughly at the level of intermediate microeconomics, which was still quite new at the time. Later I met many people who went abroad to study, and they all said that their main understanding of Western economics in China had come from reading my two books. By 1982 I was hired as a lecturer at Wuhan University, where I worked for a year and a half, teaching mathematical economics and economic cybernetics. During this period I also published Economic Control Theory and Foundations of Mathematical Economics, and I began preparing to study abroad. Because some of the econometric models in my books attracted the attention of Professor Gregory Chow of Princeton University, who was then visiting Wuhan University, I was admitted to the PhD program in the economics department of Princeton University in 1983 with Professor Chow’s help. When I was going abroad, since I had not yet been rehabilitated, I could not pass the political screening for going abroad. At this point it was again thanks to Professor Chow (Zou Zhizhuang), who wrote a letter to the leaders asking for help. Later this letter was forwarded to Liu Daoyu, then president of Wuhan University, asking him to handle it. In the end President Liu Daoyu approved the procedures for me to go abroad, and in 1983 I arrived at Princeton University. At the same time, under the instruction from the relevant leaders that “the Yang Xiguang problem should be handled by the court according to law,” the Supreme Court instructed the Hunan Provincial High Court to re-examine my “counterrevolutionary” case. In 1983 the trial committee of the Hunan Provincial High Court unanimously held that “Where Is China Going?” “belongs to a matter of ideological understanding, had no counterrevolutionary purpose, and did not constitute a crime. Accordingly, the original first-instance and second-instance determinations and sentences were improper and should both be revoked, and Yang Xiguang is declared not guilty.”
heading: A First Trial
title: Repost: Xiaokai Yang, "My Life"

content: A Hidden Dragon Rises from the DeepMy theory of the division of labor took initial shape while I was in prison, but it truly matured during my doctoral studies at Princeton. In the doctoral program there were two years of coursework, and during those two years I gradually compared the ideas of the mainstream school with my own. In the two years in Beijing I basically set aside my own thinking and systematically studied neoclassical economics; much of what I know of neoclassical economics was learned in those two years. After arriving at Princeton, some of the courses I took I had already taught in China, so I compared neoclassical ideas with my own, to see whether there was any difference, to see which of the things I had thought about were valuable and which were not. For example, I had derived Gossen’s Second Law myself using mathematics in prison, and at the time I thought it was a discovery, but the moment I left prison I found people had known about it a hundred years earlier. I had also thought about hierarchy theory and the Nash bargaining model in prison, and I wrote these theories into my Preliminary Economic Cybernetics. I found that on many problems my thinking was not as good as others’; for example, I later found that the bargaining model Nash built was far better than mine, so I gave it up. But this also encouraged me: many of the things others thought of, I could think of too. This is what is meant by “great minds think alike.” The more I read, the more I realized how hard it is to innovate. People are all very similar; what you can think of, others can think of too. This was how I felt when I first went to America. I am a person with many new ideas, but after seeing more, I found that many so-called new ideas had actually been thought of centuries ago. Having slowly read their work, I found my own ideas were not new at all. Still, my luck was not bad; after reading a great deal, in the end I found that some of the things I had thought about had not yet been thought of by others — namely the equilibrium model of the theory of the division of labor, which later became my doctoral dissertation. In 1987 my dissertation was approved at my defense, after which I went to the Economic Growth Center at Yale University for a year of postdoctoral research. A year later I went to teach in the economics department of Monash University in Australia. In 1989 I was promoted to senior lecturer, in 1992 I became a full professor, in 1993 I was elected a Fellow of the Academy of Social Sciences in Australia, and in 2000 I was promoted to chair professor. Over these years, although I have always taught at Monash University, I have spent about a third of each year as a visiting professor in the United States, Hong Kong, and Taiwan. Since 1998 I have also returned to China more often, serving as a visiting professor at Peking University and Fudan University.
heading: A Hidden Dragon Rises from the Deep
title: Repost: Xiaokai Yang, "My Life"

content: In “Development Economics: Marginal Analysis and Inframarginal Analysis,” Yang Xiaokai reshapes the theoretical history of development economics according to his own understanding. This article summarizes the introduction part and adds some points worth discussing.
title: Development Economics: Marginal Analysis and Inframarginal Analysis (Introduction)

content: 1. Intellectual Origins: Marx vs. Adam SmithYang Xiaokai defines the core of mainstream classical development economics as—division of labor is the source of economic growth, and economic growth is the core concept of development economics. Adam Smith’s logical chain: $$ \text{Transport conditions} \Rightarrow \text{Market size} \Rightarrow \text{Division of labor} \Rightarrow \text{Economic growth} $$ With this logical line as the main axis, division of labor occupies the absolute core—the emergence of money and specialized division of labor are inseparable, and investment is a tool to optimize division of labor. William Petty’s logical chain: $$ \text{Reduction in transaction costs} \Rightarrow \text{Promotion of division of labor} $$ Scholars like North and Max Weber link division of labor with capitalist expansion, forming what Yang Xiaokai sees as modern classical development economics: $$ \text{Capitalist system} \Rightarrow \text{Transaction conditions} \Rightarrow \text{Division of labor} $$The Contradiction Between Marx and Adam SmithIn the courses I took on Marx’s “Capital,” the professor argued that Marx’s view is that division of labor determines the market, which is completely opposite to Adam Smith’s view. For example, according to Marx, the division between the propertied and the propertyless is a form of division of labor, which also brings class nature! Based on the labor theory of value, private property is undesirable, and this division of labor ultimately stems from property ownership. Adam Smith uses the “invisible hand” to avoid the part about “the bloody primitive accumulation of capitalism.” If we want to refute Marx’s view, we need to argue that division of labor indeed brings wealth growth. Yang Xiaokai’s inframarginal analysis should be able to address this point, and this contradiction will be mentioned later.
heading: 1. Intellectual Origins: Marx vs. Adam Smith
title: Development Economics: Marginal Analysis and Inframarginal Analysis (Introduction)

content: 2. Classical Development EconomicsYang Xiaokai advocates analyzing economic development from four aspects. This is the historical background of classical development economics—the rapid development of Britain in the 17th-19th centuries and the liberal reforms in 19th-century Europe. Geopolitical landscape Europe: Fragmented, low trade and defense costs, free cities developed before nation-states. China was the opposite. Ideology, moral standards, legal norms Europe: The pursuit of wealth legitimized commerce (e.g., the Glorious Revolution in Britain), and the Industrial Revolution accumulated substantial commercial wealth. The Reformation led to competition among churches, weakening unity. China did not face external challenges to its nation-state. Industrial and commercial institutions and practices Market institutions, patent law, property law Division of labor and economic structure International trade system and colonial movements Total productivity and economic welfare
heading: 2. Classical Development Economics
title: Development Economics: Marginal Analysis and Inframarginal Analysis (Introduction)

content: 3. Refuting KeynesianismEconomic crises and World Wars I and II led to excessive concentration of political power. But does the occurrence of an economic crisis mean the failure of the free market? No, because highly specialized division of labor always comes with contradictions that are difficult to coordinate and couple. In Yang Xiaokai’s view, economic crises are like the risk of accidents on a highway. Choosing to involve the government is like giving up the highway after a single crash, which is an overreaction. Using division of labor to explain economic crises: the cobweb model and the general equilibrium model from the perspective of division of labor. This is also the core contradiction in the debate between Lin Yifu and Zhang Weiying on industrial policy—government intervention can have adverse effects because it disrupts normal industrial division of labor, which is more severe than an economic crisis. However, please note that all this logic is based on the premise that division of labor determines economic growth. The disadvantage of backwardness is the same; imitation can only optimize short-term division of labor, which does not align with long-term natural market trends and will inevitably lead to problems. The Soviet Union’s planned economy made more people admire “social experiments”—attempting government intervention. But the Soviet Union eventually collapsed, so Yang Xiaokai believes the Soviet model also proves Keynes wrong. In my personal view, Yang Xiaokai’s argument ignores the injustice of colonial movements and skips over the economic causes of World Wars I and II, which might have been caused by the excessive laissez-faire market leading to unequal resource distribution. Perhaps the market brings efficiency but neglects fairness, leading to revolutions. Incorporating freedom into development is a historic moment in development economics. Exploring what is just and fair is also a historic moment in development economics. Hayek’s prophecy succeeded, but the correct answer does not mean the process was correct.
heading: 3. Refuting Keynesianism
title: Development Economics: Marginal Analysis and Inframarginal Analysis (Introduction)

content: 4. What is Inframarginal Analysis?Marginal analysis considers the allocation of resources, addressing the question of how much to allocate. But inframarginal analysis is about making choices, dealing with either-or contradictions. In life, people often face many choices between “yes” and “no.” For example: When you graduate from high school and need to choose a major for university, if you choose economics among economics, chemistry, and physics, it means you won’t attend chemistry and physics classes during university, but you will attend microeconomics, macroeconomics, econometrics, and other economics electives. This means that before we perform marginal analysis on the time allocation for major courses, we first consider which major to choose—this preliminary decision-making process is the exploration of the national market’s division of labor. This additional process of choosing a major is inframarginal. From a mathematical perspective, we perform a two-step optimization analysis: Inframarginal analysis part: Find global multiple corner solutions, interior solutions, and compare total costs and benefits. For example, which has better market prospects—studying economics, management, or physics? At this stage, we cannot perform marginal analysis; we can only compare total costs and total benefits. After confirming a major, we then use marginal analysis to determine the time allocation for our studies, which is the marginal analysis of grades and time. For example, the Lewis Turning Point and public choice theory have not been mathematized in mainstream economics because of conflicting interests. The government does not seek to maximize social welfare but rather a game of interests among various parties. The urban-rural dichotomy is also a problem of conflicting interests brought by division of labor. Most importantly—whether it is equilibrium and Pareto optimality analysis or Marx’s economics, none can answer one question: Why can productivity improve through the improvement of division of labor when the production function and resource endowment remain unchanged??? So let’s return to classical operations research and control theory, and Yang Xiaokai also wrote a preliminary control theory. A very dated book. Yang Xiaokai’s books seem quite collectible, and second-hand ones are expensive. I chose to borrow from the library. If anyone has one at home, please keep it well; it seems to hold its value.
heading: 4. What is Inframarginal Analysis?
title: Development Economics: Marginal Analysis and Inframarginal Analysis (Introduction)

content: 5. General Equilibrium and Network AnalysisYang Xiaokai believes that Marshall’s supply and demand analysis is limited to the relationship between two goods, making many things appear exogenous. The Difference Between Exogenous and EndogenousGenerally, exogenous variables are used as fixed parameters, with unchanged values, usually referring to variables outside the model. For example, in the short term, technology and institutions remain unchanged, so they can be understood as exogenous parameters. Correspondingly, variables within the model are endogenous. In the long run, everything can change, so everything tends to become endogenous. Adam Smith did not elaborate on the “invisible hand,” and this process, like machine learning, is a black box. From the perspective of general equilibrium, due to the large number of commodity exchanges forming a trade circle, a huge trading network is formed, where many transactions influence each other, eventually reaching equilibrium, which is the embodiment of the concept of general. Therefore, Yang Xiaokai emphasizes the need for network analysis. Yang Xiaokai’s model endogenizes division of labor through network analysis, thereby demonstrating the spontaneous development of the market.
heading: 5. General Equilibrium and Network Analysis
title: Development Economics: Marginal Analysis and Inframarginal Analysis (Introduction)

content: International Trade and Economic ParadigmsHere, let’s additionally discuss the paradigm of the economics discipline. Many people criticize economics as a pseudo-science wrapped in mathematics, but here we mainly want to explain the reason for the formation of this paradigm. Economics strives to imitate physics, following the process of phenomenon-mathematical model-experimental verification. However, since social sciences do not have the powerful experimental verification of natural sciences, statistical verification is used as a substitute. Whether it is Yang Xiaokai’s neoclassical development economics or Lin Yifu’s new structural economics, both derive conclusions from international trade. Similarly, when a theory encounters phenomena it cannot explain—in the field of international trade, it is the Leontief Paradox—patches or revisions are needed. Many people use human irrationality to refute economics, but In practice, there are many theoretical patches in this area. DiagramCodegraph LR; A(Self-sufficiency)--Introduction of absolute and comparative advantage-->B(International trade)--Introduction of game theory-->C(Tariffs and subsidies);graph LR; A(Self-sufficiency)--Introduction of absolute and comparative advantage-->B(International trade)--Introduction of game theory-->C(Tariffs and subsidies);graph LR; A(Self-sufficiency)--Introduction of absolute and comparative advantage-->B(International trade)--Introduction of game theory-->C(Tariffs and subsidies);graph LR; A(Self-sufficiency)--Introduction of absolute and comparative advantage-->B(International trade)--Introduction of game theory-->C(Tariffs and subsidies);If one wants to establish a new framework, it must also be compatible with the phenomena described in the above flowchart. For example, later, Paul Krugman found that even without comparative advantage, increasing returns to scale can increase trade. (However, some people criticize Nobel laureate Krugman for being more of an economic writer.) Marc Melitz explains the emergence of international trade at the firm level, and many believe this theory will eventually win a Nobel Prize. Yang Xiaokai extended the consumer-producer trade model based on Ricardo’s trade theory. Each individual (unlike countries and firms) is both a consumer and a producer, allowing us to understand international trade from an individual perspective. Domestic trade is a necessity, and international trade is caused by exogenous comparative advantage, with transaction costs affecting individual choices in both domestic and international trade. Endogenizing and mathematizing transaction costs.
heading: International Trade and Economic Paradigms
title: Development Economics: Marginal Analysis and Inframarginal Analysis (Introduction)

content: 6. Successors of Classical Development TheoryCoase and Buchanan: Property rights economics, transaction costs, institutional economics. North’s new economic history. For example, externalities are essentially a property rights issue rather than a public goods issue; principal-agent problems are also an inframarginal manifestation of conflicting interests in division of labor. Policy practice. Believes that government intervention harms the economy. For example, Buchanan’s new political economy. The contribution of entrepreneurs and enterprise systems to economic development For example, Zhang Weiying’s entrepreneurial spirit (believing that entrepreneurs have the ability to create something from nothing, and using this to refute Lin Yifu’s new structural economics). Romer’s economic growth model. High Macro Notes has just updated the Romer model.
heading: 6. Successors of Classical Development Theory
title: Development Economics: Marginal Analysis and Inframarginal Analysis (Introduction)

content: Reflecting on myself, what constitutes enthusiasm for studying economics is essentially a form of showing off, typically preceded by achievements before love. That being said, after the ebbing tide, don’t some seaweeds also leave behind seeds that sprout on the land? This is also what I ponder—Truth becomes fiction when the fiction’s true; Real becomes not-real where the unreal’s real.Enthusiasm for a subject does not require pure reasons or pure motives; by persevering, it becomes genuine. A classmate I know once thought economics wasn’t for them and wanted to switch majors. However, after achieving good grades, they started praising economics. When I see this classmate throwing out various economic terms, it’s like seeing myself from the past. Thus, from the similarities between him and me, it is evident that the starting point of my enthusiasm for economics should be impure—I simply enjoyed the feeling of intellectual superiority. However, upon delving deeper into the subject, I discovered both my own insignificance and the wonders of economics. As for my own learning mentality, I have traversed the following path: Moreover, based on my experience of surfing the internet and interacting with classmates, it seems that almost everyone follows a similar path of upgrading in the hierarchy of disdain.
title: Self-questioning: Econ-Learning mentality within the hierarchy of disdain

content: Theoretical Framework:During High School: Filled with a mysterious fascination for “Das Kapital”. Choosing a Major: Personally, my initiation into economics came from Wu Xiaobo’s " 历代经济变革得失 (The Rise and Fall of Economic Revolutions)"1. Although I no longer agree with the book’s cyclic theory of China’s progress and regress, I am grateful for how it prompted me to actively explore the related theories of “The Joseph Needham Puzzle” during my university years. Some around me, however, had impressions mixed with pure economics, political science, aspirations for civil service, and Wall Street. Study of Economics: Started with mainstream economic theories. First, the clash of the two major internet trends—the Cambridge Capital Controversy, the intellectual battle between Hayek and Keynes (in China represented by Lin Yifu and Yang Xiaokai). Then, a gradual progression through the history of ideas—from Greece… Emphasis on agriculture, emphasis on commerce… Classical, neoclassical, synthesis of neoclassical… Gradually refined theoretical cognition: overlaying macro and micro, dividing into labor economics, industrial economics, sustainable resources, economic growth, quantitative history… And then becoming increasingly detailed, dividing by object, method, and field. Adding Modern Patches: Transformation of value, game theory, complexity economics, non-equilibrium, behavioral economics, interdisciplinary approaches (evolutionary economics, neuroeconomics…). Here, no longer fixated on grandstand positions, but rather focusing on theoretical paradigms and application scenarios, while paying more attention to theory-guided practices.
heading: Theoretical Framework:
title: Self-questioning: Econ-Learning mentality within the hierarchy of disdain

content: Methodology in Papers:Encountering macro and micro structures without self-awareness, at this time unaware of the debate between structure and simplicity. Started with econometrics, delved into causality, and then began to self-proclaim as a “reg monkey” (although in reality, I didn’t even fully understand regression). Through understanding the causal revolution, completed my comprehension of the debate between structural form and reduced form. By this time, many of my classmates had already begun to mix Chinese and English in speech and typing, but I personally detested this kind of mixing, even for default professional terms, so I chose Chinese with English parentheses! When I first began to understand econometrics and causal inference, I was ensnared by the mystique of statistics. After dispelling the allure of DID\RDD\PSM\Bunching\OLS…, came the enchantment with machine learning and Bayesian estimation. R, Python, Matlab, SAS… So much to learn! When I became aware of the existence of structural forms, I began to idolize mathematics. DSGE, engage! Ambition surpassing ability—yearning to master real analysis, measure theory, and functional analysis . And then there’s the endless learning of mathematics, the never-ending array of statistical software, the countless classic books yet to be read, and the me who has yet to take action.
heading: Methodology in Papers:
title: Self-questioning: Econ-Learning mentality within the hierarchy of disdain

content: Cognitive Perspectives in Papers:Empirical papers initially seem daunting, pursuing flashy methods. Feeling sorrowful about lacking originality in my own thoughts, while feeling lost about where to find originality. Choosing a research topic for a paper is essentially driven by methods, data, and questions, often simply permutations and combinations of variables. Started realizing that keeping up with economics requires reading cutting-edge English literature, began advocating that Chinese journals are all rubbish, only reading the top 5 in English. This sentiment is widely supported on the internet, but isn’t it a bit extreme? Started understanding the importance of packaging a story, always saying that a paper tells a good story. Yes, we’ve become storytellers now (image of Zhang Wuchang.jpg)
heading: Cognitive Perspectives in Papers:
title: Self-questioning: Econ-Learning mentality within the hierarchy of disdain

content: ConclusionLooking back, it all seems to be driven by interest, but each step forward is indeed built on the disdain of the previous step. I cannot answer the debate on theoretical paradigms because it’s too vast, and I can’t see clearly. All I hear is the opening line from my history of economic thought professor—“Economics is a chaos.” Ultimately, the economists I admire the most in my eyes possess two modes of thinking. One is the sociological analysis that establishes comparative analysis, familiar with the histories of various countries, effortlessly comparing economies, the gods of institutional economics whose intuition and knowledge reservoirs are astonishing. The other is the mathematical analysis, dealing with various functions and equilibrium analyses, which can make one’s scalp tingle. Recently, while browsing the library, seeing the densely packed borrowing records on those monochrome old books, I can’t help but lament that I’ve read too few classic works. Personally, I feel that the biggest illusion I face is the tool illusion—thinking that learning a bit of coding satisfies me, when in fact my economic thinking hasn’t grown at all. Thanks to my high school history teacher for the gift. ↩︎
heading: Conclusion
title: Self-questioning: Econ-Learning mentality within the hierarchy of disdain

content: This post documents the process of drawing GIS choropleth maps in Stata. All the data mentioned in this post can be downloaded from the repository.
title: Drawing GIS Choropleth Maps with Stata

content: Getting Map FilesESRI Shapefile files are spatial geographic data developed by the Environmental Systems Research Institute. They store both spatial locations and attribute data. The basic files are mainly: Main file (.shp): stores the spatial information of geometric features, i.e., XY coordinates. The map outline information of a GIS image is stored in this file. Table file (.dbf): a dBase table that stores the attribute information of the geographic data. Index file (.shx): stores index information about how the .shp data is stored — where the XY coordinate input points are, how many XY coordinate pairs there are, and so on. Here are some data sources I found: Dabing’s blog National Catalogue Service for Geographic Information GADM data: comprehensive international maps. China map data found on GitHub Rstata materials: provincial divisions of the China map. Domestic courses are world-class; personally I think the best Stata-focused content comes from “Lianxianghui” and “Rstata”. Even though I’m a firm freeloading open-source advocate, I often read their popular-science articles to learn Stata. Here a kind soul has uploaded the database related to Rstata. Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, CAS: perhaps China’s semi-official source? Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, CASIf you still can’t find what you want, you can use the Alibaba Cloud map to generate map files. Go to Alibaba Cloud DataV, click to download the file (I recommend the “other download” option, which gives you a .json file). After downloading, go to the converter to convert it. Click Select, upload the .json file, then click export to export the converted file. It seems that because of data encoding or encryption, files converted from the Alibaba Cloud map sometimes can’t be read by Stata. In that case, use spshape2dta to convert them.
heading: Getting Map Files
title: Drawing GIS Choropleth Maps with Stata

content: Basic StataGis Operations
heading: Basic StataGis Operations
title: Drawing GIS Choropleth Maps with Stata

content: Installing the Required CommandsYou just need the main file (.shp) and the table file (.dbf). Install the relevant commands in Stata beforehand. ssc install shp2dta, replace //file conversion command ssc install mif2dta, replace //file conversion command ssc install spmap, replace //GIS plotting command
heading: Installing the Required Commands
title: Drawing GIS Choropleth Maps with Stata

content: Converting and Fixing Encoding IssuesUsing a GIS map file made by a Bilibili user: 2019 China Map - Map Approval No. GS(2019)1822 The example data I use here is: PKU Digital Financial Inclusion Index 2011_2020 There are two files to convert here: the China map file 市 (cities) and the nine-dash line file 九段线 (nine-dash line). clear cd F:\桌面\GIS_sum\2019中国地图审图号\例子 //set the working folder, since some gis command options work better with relative paths import excel "F:\桌面\GIS_sum\2019中国地图审图号\例子\北大数字普惠金融指数2011_2020.xlsx", sheet("Sheet1") firstrow keep if year == 2020 rename pref_name_year18 ct_name save d2020data ,replace //load the data spshape2dta 市 spshape2dta 九段线 //here I use spshape2dta because shp2dta cannot convert these clear cd F:\桌面\GIS_sum\2019中国地图审图号\例子 unicode encoding set gb18030 unicode analyze 市.dta unicode translate 市.dta, invalid //recompile to fix some garbled Chinese characters //one-time command; to reuse it you need to delete the generated encoding file bak.stunicode in the directoryIf a file can’t be converted — for example, the Alibaba Cloud map — it seems maps made in GIS also can’t be converted by shp2dta. That’s why spshape2dta is used here. Apart from this, the two commands don’t differ much. The downside of spshape2dta is that you can’t customize the name; you just follow it directly with the filename, and it automatically generates the two files you need. The label file is .dta, and the outline file is _shp.dta.

content: Parameter ExplanationsThe parameter explanations below were generated by GPT 3.5, with some additions by me. grmap type: specifies the graph type as a map. using chinaprov40_coord.dta: specifies the map data file, which contains the coordinate information of the provincial administrative divisions. id(ID): specifies the unique identifier variable in the map data. It links the map coordinates to the labels and data. osize(vvthin ...) and ocolor(white ...): set the thickness and color of the map boundary lines. vvthin is a predefined line style in Stata; it means a very thin line. When drawing maps, you can use different line thicknesses to distinguish different geographic features or boundaries. From thin to thick: vvthin, vthin, thin, medium, thick, vthick, vvthick. clmethod(custom) and clbreaks(0 1 2 3 4 5): custom classification method and classification intervals. Here they correspond to the provincial categories: municipalities directly under the central government, provinces, special administrative regions, and so on. fcolor(...): specifies the fill colors for different categories. The example uses RGB color definitions; you can check the color codes in PowerPoint’s custom color picker. RGB color definitionleg(...): sets the order and labels of the legend. graphr(margin(medium)): sets the graph margins. line(data(chinaprov40_line_coord.dta) by(group) ...): draws the map boundary lines, specifying the boundary line data file and attributes such as color. Here the nine-dash line file is used. polygon(data(polygon) fcolor(black) ...): draws map polygons, specifying fill color, line thickness, and other attributes. Here it’s the legend and the compass. label(data(chinaprov40_label) ...): labels the map, specifying the label data file and label text. label(ename) is English, label(cnname) is Chinese. ti("一级标题: 2019 年中国省级行政区划"): sets the main title. subti("二级标题"): sets the subtitle. caption("使用 Stata 绘制中国省级地图", size(*0.8)): sets the graph caption.

content: PlottingBasic CommandThe advantage of this command is that you can layer maps with simple parentheses. geoplot (area regions fortell, label("@lb-@ub (N=@n)")) (line regions)area means drawing an area map here, using the map outline of the regions macro; the plotting variable is fortell. label: on the map, these variables are replaced with their actual values. For example, if a region’s lower bound is 20, its upper bound is 50, and it contains 100 cells, the final label will read "20-50 (N=100)". @lb: the lower bound of each region. @ub: the upper bound of each region. @n: the number of each region. line means calling the line plot of regions. Bubble Chartgeoplot /// (area regions) /// (point capitals i.size [w=pop98], color(Set1, opacity(50)) mlcolor(%0)) /// (label capitals city if pop98>250000, color(black)) /// , legend compass sbar(length(300) units(km))Bubble chart(area regions): draws the map area, representing the boundaries or extent of the geographic region. (point capitals i.size [w=pop98], color(Set1, opacity(50)) mlcolor(%0)): draws a scatter plot of cities, where city size is determined by i.size, colors use the Set1 palette, opacity is 50%, and the city label color is %0, i.e., black. City size is based on the pop98 variable, which represents the city’s population. (label capitals city if pop98>250000, color(black)): labels city names, but only for cities with population above 250,000, with black label color. , legend compass sbar(length(300) units(km)): adds a legend, compass, and scale bar. The scale bar length is 300 units, in kilometers. Zoomed-In Mapgeoplot (area regions) /// (area regions if id==1, fc(Coral*.5) lc(gray)) /// (label regions region if id==1, color(black)) /// (area regions if id==1, fc(Coral) lc(gray) /* */ box(circle pad(5) fc(gs14))) /// (pie regions relig1 relig2 relig3 if id==1, lab(, reverse)) /// , legend(pos(se) rowgap(1)) zoom(4/5: 6 90 210)(area regions): draws the map area, representing the boundaries or extent of the geographic region. (area regions if id==1, fc(Coral*.5) lc(gray)): draws the map area of a specific region where id==1, with fill color Coral*.5 and gray boundary line color. (label regions region if id==1, color(black)): labels the name of the specific region, but only where id==1, with black label color. (area regions if id==1, fc(Coral) lc(gray) /* ... */ box(circle pad(5) fc(gs14))): draws the map area of a specific region where id==1, and adds a box around it with fill color Coral and gray boundary line color. (pie regions relig1 relig2 relig3 if id==1, lab(, reverse)): draws a pie chart in the specific region, but only where id==1. The pie chart includes the relig1, relig2, and relig3 variables, with labels reversed. , legend(pos(se) rowgap(1)): sets the legend position to the southeast, with row gap 1. zoom(4/5: 6 90 210): sets the map zoom ratio to 4/5 and specifies the displayed range. content: Map Usage StandardsNotice of the Ministry of Natural Resources on Issuing the “Specifications for the Representation of Public Map Content” Use Maps Correctly — Not a Single Mistake Allowed TL;DR: using a single-province map or a street/township map is fine; using the full map of China is more troublesome. When using the full map of China, the scale and framing requirements are strict. Boundary lines: some national borders are temporarily undetermined or change slightly every year. Territory issues: Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan, the islands of Hainan, the Diaoyu Islands, and so on. The nine-dash line must never be missing! Annotations of confidential data such as military-related information must not appear. It’s best to include a legend and compass, and keep them consistent with the official versions. For journals, it’s best to refer to: Standard Drawing of Map Illustrations in Scientific Journals and Common Problems For the most official maps, see: Standard Map Service. After drawing your own map, you can also submit it here for review. The official source does not provide shp files, only eps and jpg files. The “official” shp files circulating on the market are all made by individuals, so you need to check them carefully.
heading: Map Usage Standards
title: Drawing GIS Choropleth Maps with Stata

content: Problem 1Environment: Hugo extended version + the LoveIt theme series Hugo generates a table of contents for every blog post, and the TOC headings should support click-to-jump. A few days ago I noticed that on my blog, the Chinese pages couldn’t jump to headings, while the English ones still could. Hugo TOC generation
heading: Problem 1
title: Table of Contents Navigation Fails on the Chinese Blog

content: The causeAfter asking the doit theme maintainer, I got the cause of the error: I’d added a BGM to the page (as below) — this feature uses APIayer, and APIayer in turn calls smoothScroll. smoothScroll’s default settings use English parameters; after introducing APIayer to play music, the TOC jump return value becomes null. if (location.hash !== this.hash) window.history.pushState(null, null, this.hash) // using the history api to solve issue #1 - back doesn't work // most browser don't update :target when the history api is used: // THIS IS A BUG FROM THE BROWSERS. // change the scrolling duration in this call var node = document.getElementById(this.hash.substring(1)) if (!node) return; // Do not scroll to non-existing node
heading: The cause
title: Table of Contents Navigation Fails on the Chinese Blog

content: The solutionIn the end I found a solution in the blog post APlayer causing blog TOC navigation to fail. Modify APlayer.min.js in the <personal website>\assets\lib\aplayer directory. The blogger 鱼の乐 has provided his modified APlayer.min.js. If the blogger’s domain hasn’t been renewed, you can refer to the file I copied: APlayer.min.js Just replace the whole file. These problems have been exposed since 2018, and it looks like there won’t be any maintenance going forward, so I suggest fixing it yourself.
heading: The solution
title: Table of Contents Navigation Fails on the Chinese Blog

content: Problem 2When I added the giscus comment section, this problem appeared again? The previous solution also stopped working. Huge thanks here to @yllhwa for the help😍👍. Copy themes\LoveIt\assets\data\cdn\jsdelivr.yml to <your website>\assets\data\cdn\jsdelivr.yml. Then comment out aplayerJS: aplayer@1.10.1/dist/APlayer.min.js. It seems it still comes down to a call problem
heading: Problem 2
title: Table of Contents Navigation Fails on the Chinese Blog

content: When writing economic empirical papers, it is common to output a large number of tables (mainly descriptive statistics and regression results). Mastering instant table output techniques is like casting spells without incantations! When discussing variable selection with others, responding instantly feels just like this!Currently, Stata has a plethora of corresponding commands—asdoc, outreg2, logout, estout. Here’s a brief summary of where each command is commonly used and its characteristics.
title: Stata Export Word Tables

content: Estout: Versatile, LaTeX Outputestout is written by Professor Ben Jann from the University of Bern, Institute of Sociology. (The CODE_PLACEHOLDER_1 command was also developed by this expert). It excels in customization, making it a mainstream command for result outputs. Its most powerful feature is support for LaTeX export.
heading: Estout: Versatile, LaTeX Output
title: Stata Export Word Tables

content: Asdoc: Descriptive StatisticsAdd asdoc to your operations to save the corresponding file. The downside is that regression table customization is poor and does not meet the general journal requirements. It is generally used only to display descriptive statistics. tabout supports powerful descriptive statistics custom tables. For the latest installation, see: [https://tabout.net.au/docs/home.php^1] ssc install asdoc, replace //Download command sysuse "auto.dta", clear //Use Stata’s built-in sample data asdoc sum price mpg rep78 trunk weight, dec(4) save(Table1_Descriptive_Statistics1.doc) title("Table 1 Descriptive Statistics 1") asdoc reg price mpg rep78 trunk weight, robust, save(Table2_Basic_Regression.doc) title("Table 2 Basic Regression")asdoc descriptive statisticsasdoc regression statistics
heading: Asdoc: Descriptive Statistics
title: Stata Export Word Tables

content: Logout: Mean Difference and Correlation Coefficient Testslogout stands out by being able to output mean difference tests and correlation coefficient tests in addition to descriptive statistics and regression results1. ssc install logout //Download command ************Descriptive Statistics***************** sysuse "auto.dta", clear //Use Stata’s built-in sample data //Output to Word (RTF format) logout, save(Filename) word replace: /// tabstat price wei len mpg rep78, /// stats(mean sd min p50 max) c(s) f(%6.2f) //Output to Excel (XML format) logout, save(Filename) excel replace: /// tabstat price wei len mpg rep78, /// ************Mean Difference Tests***************** ssc install ttable2 //Mean t-tests by Professors Li Chuntao and Zhang Xuan from Zhongnan University of Economics and Law logout, save(Filename) word excel replace: /// ttable2 price mpg trunk trunk weight length turn headroom, /// by(foreign) f(%12.3f) ************Correlation Coefficient Tests***************** logout, save(Correlation_File_Name) word excel replace: /// pwcorr_a rep78 headroom trunk weight length, /// star1(0.01) star5(0.05) star10(0.1) //Add * annotationslogout correlation coefficient output
heading: Logout: Mean Difference and Correlation Coefficient Tests
title: Stata Export Word Tables

content: Outreg2: Regression OutputFor table outputs, I choose outreg2! Tables are aesthetically pleasing, support Word, and are convenient to export. The command ssc hot, n(10) will show the top 10 most popular Stata commands. outreg ranks first! Stata external command rankingsssc install outreg2 //Download command webuse grunfeld,clear //Use default data xtset company year //Define panel data ************Descriptive Statistics***************** outreg2 using Filename.doc, replace sum(log) keep(company year invest mvalue kstock time) eqkeep(N min mix) title(Descriptive statistics) ************Regression Results Output***************** //Perform random effects, fixed effects, and mixed effects regression, then merge //Starting a new table or merging corresponds to replace and append xtreg invest mvalue kstock, re outreg2 using Filename.doc, replace tstat bdec(4) tdec(4) rdec(4) ctitle(RE) keep(mvalue kstock) e(r2_a,F) addstat(F test, e(p)) addtext(Company FE, NO, Year FE, NO) xtreg invest mvalue kstock i.year, fe outreg2 using Filename.doc, append tstat bdec(4) tdec(4) rdec(4) ctitle(FE) keep(mvalue kstock) e(r2_a,F) addstat(F test, e(p)) addtext(Company FE, YES, Year FE, YES) reg invest mvalue outreg2 using Filename.doc, append tstat bdec(4) tdec(4) rdec(4) ctitle(OLS) keep(mvalue) e(r2_a,F) addstat(F test, e(p)) addtext(Company FE, YES, Year NO, NO) //bdec(4) tdec(4) rdec(4) represent decimal places for coefficients, t-tests, and R^2 respectively //addstat and addtext correspond to adding statistics and table content //keep(var1 var2 var3) selects the output coefficients to keepoutreg2 regression output
heading: Outreg2: Regression Output
title: Stata Export Word Tables

content: Putdocx Series: Unified SolutionThe docx series commands are developed by Crawler Club. Most of the above commands (not including asdoc) mean that a table output takes up a separate Word file. The docx series allows reusing a single file. ssc install sum2docx, replace ssc install corr2docx, replace ssc install t2docx, replace ssc install reg2docx, replaceThe following example code is from “Jun Sheng Wo Wei Sheng! Stata Output: One-Click Paper Tables - reg2docx-corr2docx.” clear all set more off putdocx begin //Create a new Word document putdocx paragraph, halign(center) //Center the paragraph *-Define font, size, and basic settings putdocx text ("Attachment: Tables to be inserted in the article"), /// font("Huawei Kaiti", 16, black) bold linebreak *-Save the Word document as My_Table.docx putdocx save "My_Table.docx", replace *-Load data sysuse "auto.dta", clear *-----Table 1----- sum2docx price-length using "My_Table.docx", append /// obs mean(%9.2f) sd min(%9.0g) median(%9.0g) max(%9.0g) /// title("Table 1: Descriptive Statistics") *-Note: The append option adds this new table to the end of "My_Table.docx". *-----Table 2----- putdocx begin putdocx pagebreak putdocx save "My_Table.docx", append corr2docx price-length using "My_Table.docx", append /// star(* 0.05) fmt(%4.2f) /// title("Table 2: Correlation Matrix") *-----Table 3----- putdocx begin putdocx pagebreak putdocx save "My_Table.docx", append t2docx price-length using "My_Table.docx", append /// by(foreign) title("Table 3: Between-Group Mean Difference t-Test") *-----Table 4----- putdocx begin putdocx pagebreak putdocx save "My_Table.docx", append reg price mpg weight length est store m1 reg price mpg weight length foreign est store m2 probit foreign price weight length est store m3 reg2docx m1 m2 m3 using "My_Table.docx", append /// r2(%9.3f) ar2(%9.2f) b(%9.3f) t(%7.2f) /// title("Table 4: Regression Results") shellout "My_Table.docx" //Done! Open the generated Word document
heading: Putdocx Series: Unified Solution
title: Stata Export Word Tables

content: Etable: Supports ChineseThe output command built into Stata 17 is not very user-friendly but seems to be the only one2 that supports Chinese encoding. clear input str6 Gender Income Expenditure Others "Male" 8 1 90 "Female" 9 2 21 "Female" 10 3 22 "Male" 11 4 31 "Male" 1 6 49 "Female" 2 7 95 "Female" 3 8 86 "Male" 4 9 17 end reg Expenditure Income Others if Gender == "Male", robust est store Male_Regression reg Expenditure Income Others if Gender == "Female", robust est store Female_Regression reg Expenditure Income Others, robust est store Overall_Regression etable, estimates(Male_Regression Female_Regression Overall_Regression) column(estimates) keep(Income Others) /// cstat(_r_b, nformat(%9.3f)) /// cstat(_r_se, nformat(%9.3f)) /// mstat(N, nformat(%9.0f)) /// mstat(r2, nformat(%9.3g)) /// stars(0.10 "*" .05 "**" .01 "***", attach(_r_b)) /// showstars showstarsnote /// title("Table 1: Etable Regression Results") /// note("Data source: custom") /// export("Filename.docx")etable regression command
heading: Etable: Supports Chinese
title: Stata Export Word Tables

content: Today, when I ran Anaconda, it suddenly could not open the startup interface, but I could directly open and run Jupyter and Notebook. The error situation is shown in the picture below. I can’t understand this eitherThe commonly used solutions online did not work, but I will still list them here. Upgrade the installation packages, conda update navigator conda update anaconda-navigator conda update conda conda update --allDelete files Delete the .condarc file (usually found in C drive, Users, Current User). There was no similar situation online, and in the end, I opened the Anaconda Powershell Prompt and saw the specific issue, which was a problem with path recognition. I can’t understand this eitherThe reason was a conflict in Windows environment variables: my user variable path and system variable path settings conflicted and were inconsistent. This caused Anaconda in the user variable to be recognized as the Java environment in the system variable. Solution: unify user variables and system variables, or delete Java pathSolution: unify user variables and system variables, or delete the Java path. Personally, it was because an invalid path blocked the way. I deleted the incorrect Java path: %Java_Home%\bin;%Java_Home%\jre\bin. After that, I checked that the Java environment was not affected, and the Anaconda environment was restored.
title: [Anaconda Error Solution] Anaconda bytes object has no attribute get

content: Time: March 2024. I landed in Wuhan at 11:00 and my next flight was at 17:10, which gave me 6 hours and 50 minutes for the layover. Wuhan is one of the main transfer airports for northbound flights in China, and plenty of routes come with a long layover here. Yellow Crane Tower is famous, and the airport connects directly to it by metro, so if you have the time, it’s worth doing a quick run.
title: Tianhe Airport Layover Guide: A Quick Trip to Yellow Crane Tower (6 h)

content: I. Airport prepFollow the WeChat account “Transfer Passenger Service”. The transfer service gives out free meal vouchers and luggage storage, and you can also book through-check baggage in advance. Through-checked baggage: This needs to be booked ahead of time and lets your checked luggage transfer seamlessly to the next flight. Transit meal: Tap to get the QR code. It can be used at the restaurant at the end of Corridor A in the departure hall outside security. You can redeem either a 30-yuan meal voucher or a small gift. I picked the 30-yuan chicken set at “食尚坊,” which also came with an egg and soy milk. My companion ordered a 26-yuan plate of hot dry noodles instead. Compared with the chicken set, that felt like a terrible deal. The 30-yuan chicken set at “食尚坊”: chicken stewed with mushrooms, steamed egg, rice, plus the extra egg and soy milkLuggage storage: Tap to get the QR code. The storage point is at the JD Express counter at the end of Corridor F in the departure hall outside security. Requirements: registration with your ID card, just like airport security. Items that cannot be checked, such as power banks, are not accepted for storage. Please forgive the overexposure on my phone cameraI did not use through-checked baggage on this quick trip. I landed at 11:00, picked up my luggage, stored it, had lunch, and by then it was exactly 12:00.
heading: I. Airport prep
title: Tianhe Airport Layover Guide: A Quick Trip to Yellow Crane Tower (6 h)

content: II. Metro rideMetro route: Line 2 $ \rightarrow$ Jiyuqiao $\rightarrow$ Pengliuyang Metro Station $ \xrightarrow {步行} $ Yellow Crane Tower Pengliuyang Metro Station: both Exit A and Exit C work if you want to get out and spot Yellow Crane Tower right away, but I recommend Exit C because that is where the internet-famous wall is. I got on the airport metro at 12:00 sharp and reached the entrance to the Yellow Crane Tower scenic area at 13:10. The internet-famous wall. I blurred the photo a bit for portrait privacy.
heading: II. Metro ride
title: Tianhe Airport Layover Guide: A Quick Trip to Yellow Crane Tower (6 h)

content: III. The towerYou can buy tickets through a WeChat mini-program. Student tickets are half price at 35 yuan. If you do not have your student ID with you, you can verify your status through Xuexin (also via WeChat mini-program). Special thanks to @leland for being my guide. There is one main route up the tower. On each floor, you circle around once before reaching the staircase to the next level. The way down is a different corridor, and it leads straight down continuously. Honestly, there is not that much to do insideFrom the higher levels of Yellow Crane Tower, you can look out over both the newer red bridge and the older white bridge spanning the Yangtze. (I forgot to take a photo.) After finishing the visit, I walked back to the metro station. The whole visit took no more than 40 minutes, and the time was 13:50. I then spent about an hour on the metro back and got to the airport around 15:00. That still left an hour to retrieve my stored luggage, clear security, and get ready to board. By 16:00, the quick run was complete.
heading: III. The tower
title: Tianhe Airport Layover Guide: A Quick Trip to Yellow Crane Tower (6 h)

content: IV. In shortAfter arriving at the airport, Spend one hour storing your luggage and eating lunch. Spend one hour taking the metro and walking to Yellow Crane Tower. Forty minutes is enough to see Yellow Crane Tower. Spend one hour heading back from Yellow Crane Tower. Spend one hour at the airport handling the return procedures.
heading: IV. In short
title: Tianhe Airport Layover Guide: A Quick Trip to Yellow Crane Tower (6 h)

content: Xiangzi went to his death convinced that he simply had not tried hard enough. Of course, Xiangzi kept his eyes fixed on the outside world. He thought he saw society clearly, yet missed one thing: when you only look outward, you can take in every corner of the world outside you, but you still cannot see yourself. And if you cannot see yourself, you cannot begin to talk about yourself in relation to your time. As protagonists, we are always looking outward. Only as readers can we watch “the world and me,” and then turn back to examine ourselves. That is why Lu Zhishen could say, “Only today do I finally know who I am.” I think that is exactly the point. Good television often has this kind of turn, like a beautiful painting: bright surface color alone can move the viewer, but if the hidden structure and ideas underneath move you further, then it becomes art. For me, the 2023 conversation around fate falls into two camps: the chroniclers and the absurdists.
title: 2024 viewing roundup: a few ways of living with fate

content: Blossoms Shanghai and The Long SeasonBlossoms Shanghai and The Long Season belong to the chronicler camp. People always seem at a loss when history starts moving under their feet. The Long Season asks why Wang Xiang, a model worker, could still be laid off; why his son became a murderer; why nobody around him ever quite figured out how to live. One snowfall lasts twenty years. He never gets over that ridge, and keeps trying to dig old ghosts out of the world. Shen Mo asks Wang Yang, “Do you believe in fate?” Wang Xiang and Biaozi can no longer make sense of life either, so they too begin to call it “fate.” In Blossoms Shanghai, Wong Kar-wai stages a whole chain of missed connections1. A Bao and four women—Xuezhi, Lingzi, Miss Wang, and Li Li—keep missing one another. Wealth, place, status, and experience never quite line up, so feelings have to twist and double back. The show says, “From Zhenyuan Garden on, every ending had already been decided,” and “Everything is inevitable fate.” The novel ends with a line like this: walking through the whirlpool of fate, people eventually drift apart, until only you are left.
title: 2024 viewing roundup: a few ways of living with fate

content: Only the River Flows and Journey to the WestOnly the River Flows and Journey to the West belong to the absurdist camp. When too many low-probability events pile up together, they leave people bewildered. In Only the River Flows, Ma Zhe refuses to accept that a madman could be the killer, and drifts farther and farther from the truth. The film quotes Camus: “Human beings cannot understand fate, so I disguised myself as fate. I put on God’s stupid and incomprehensible face.” In Journey to the West, Tang Zhijun believes fate is guiding him toward extraterrestrials. Every coincidence is inevitable. When we stay only inside the protagonist’s point of view, we always look outward, free to mock Kong Yiji. But as readers, we can feel that each of them is taking a different stance toward fate.
title: 2024 viewing roundup: a few ways of living with fate

content: The Long Season is reconciliationOne snowfall lasts twenty years. That is long enough, just as a truth can wait twenty years before finally coming to light. Wang Yang’s poemSnap your fingers, he said let’s snap together in resonance distant things will be shaken to pieces the people in front of us still do not know it yet Blow a whistle, I said, blow a slanting whistle like a piece of iron, then a needle, the arc of magnetic poles brushing past green glass Drink a glass of water, and watch the river when it is calm, calm, when it is not calm, we miss one layer of steps a small tear falls on stone and will not dry for a long time the whole season turns it into amber, flowing in a solid stream, the particular light behind it comes from distant things Wang Xiang answers to that finger snap: one case keeps him from getting over it for twenty years. At first, he believes that as long as he works hard and earns merit, he can avoid being laid off. Then the reversal arrives, at the workers’ assembly, when the truth comes out: the factory owner can fire whoever he wants and keep whoever he wants. It was the plant director who organized the stripping of assets. Wang Xiang’s lifelong pride in Northeast industry finally shatters. Beneath the murder mystery, what is really rotting is the Northeast itself. An individual cannot withstand the upheavals of an era. At best, he can do what One Sentence Is Worth Ten Thousand Sentences suggests: hold on to the answer he needs and keep looking ahead. Fate cannot be resisted. People eventually have to learn to move forward. So the train begins to sound again, rolling slowly along the tracks through the cornfields.

content: Blossoms Shanghai is also reconciliationA Bao can walk in and become Bao Zong, then walk out willing to be A Bao again, calm and unhurried2, still holding on to The Count of Monte Cristo’s motto: In the face of fate, there are only two words: wait and hope.

content: Only the River Flows is just plain madnessThe absurdist camp only raises the predicament; it never answers it. People cannot fight the era. That is where it stops. Once you understand that, you understand Cthulhu: there is no solution, and because people still want one, they go mad. Absurd events naturally have no answer, because we cannot understand them. Reality simply keeps flowing without pity—Only The River Flows…
title: 2024 viewing roundup: a few ways of living with fate

content: Journey to the West is waking upLike the party in Journey to the West, the main group maps onto Tang, Sun, Sha, and Zhu as they head west. Tang Zhijun wants to find his own true scripture—an alien. On the surface, they are looking for extraterrestrials. In truth, they are looking for an answer. An unhappy marriage, a bruising working life, the meaning of human existence—if human beings cannot solve these things, then could aliens? It looks like an obsession with science fiction, but underneath it is still a life cast adrift. The ending wants to turn back inward: searching for aliens is an outward move, and maybe it is unnecessary. Human beings are already a miracle, so at last one lets go. But the film does not unfold that process very smoothly.
title: 2024 viewing roundup: a few ways of living with fate

content: Living with fateWhen human smallness runs into an era the people inside it cannot understand, we use “fate” as a convenient blur. Those who come later, and those watching from outside, usually see more clearly. But when it lands on your own head, you still get dizzy. That is the scale of fate. Most people question fate, and the answers are always some version of this: “There is only relative fairness, never absolute fairness”; “Heroism is seeing the world clearly and still loving it”; “The world has kissed me with pain, and I answer with song.” At that point, truth is not the important thing. What matters is holding on to a philosophy of survival. Right or wrong, anything that helps us keep the will to go on living has some value. But when someone really wants to understand the relationship between a person and the tide of history, these answers are not enough3. Either you fall into madness, or you learn to compromise—accept everything, live for tomorrow, keep looking ahead. That is survival philosophy. Some things have already been proven impossible, and still your hands itch to go after them. That is fate and human beings. Giving up on thinking is one answer. Thinking until you collapse is another. Thinking until you compromise is another. Those, I suppose, are a few ways of getting along with fate. Honestly, online marketing is terrifying. See You Tomorrow has already been quietly forgotten in the corner and somehow rehabilitated. ↩︎ Keynesians object to the idea that the market is always right. ↩︎ Because this question usually appears in moments of historical tragedy, we tend to assume that individuals cannot resist their era, and “fate” becomes a gray, heavy word. ↩︎

content: IntroductionWhat is a web crawler? It’s scraping that follows “what you see is what you get”. Every website has source code, and that source code naturally contains the information the website displays. When you grab the source code, data and code are mixed together; we then clean it up to get clean data. The Stata code is attached at the end. Crawler code isn’t very reusable; this post mainly documents my web scraping learning process. Crawler workflowFor the whole crawling process, getting the website’s source code is the most critical step. For heavily encrypted websites (like “China Judgments Online”), you’d also need to spoof IPs, switch between multiple accounts, and break through text encryption — unfortunately Stata can’t do any of that. What Stata is good at is crawling defenseless websites and then quickly cleaning and processing the data. Although the part Stata is good at — “splitting code and data” — is just a matter of practice, using Stata for a first taste of web scraping is still pretty friendly for an individual.

content: Each Hugo theme handles custom fonts a little differently, and there are not many clear guides online on how to change them. Here, we’ll introduce how to change fonts in the LoveIt theme.
title: The Custom Font in Hugo

content: Two Methods of ModificationAccording to the LoveIt documentation, customizing fonts requires the extended version of Hugo, and there are two methods: In assets/css/_custom.scss, you can add CSS style code to customize the style. In assets/css/_override.scss, you can override variables in themes/LoveIt/assets/css/_variables.scss to customize the style. The first approach, writing the CSS yourself, is not especially beginner-friendly. The second approach relies on overriding font variables. Here, we’ll focus on the second method, which involves using the Google Fonts API to import fonts.
heading: Two Methods of Modification
title: The Custom Font in Hugo

content: Set Font VariablesOpen the _override.scss file located in the <YourWebsite>/assets/css directory. Here, you can override the font variable settings of the theme. If you don’t have an _override.scss file, you can create one yourself. Alternatively, you can copy the css folder from themes\LoveIt\assets to the <YourWebsite>\assets directory. Once you have it open, you’ll find two key files — _variables.scss and _override.scss. _variables.scss: This file is used to define font variables. For example, the website title font is a variable area; the directory font is another variable area. You can change the font for each area by modifying the corresponding variables in this file. For example, if the default title font is set to a sans-serif font, and you want to make it more decorative, you can modify the corresponding variable in the _variables.scss file to specify a different font family or style. HeiTiIn <YourWebsite>\assets\css\override.scss, input the following code: @import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Ma+Shan+Zheng&family=Madimi+One&family=Merriweather:ital,wght@0,300;0,400;0,700;0,900;1,300;1,400;1,700;1,900&family=Noto+Serif+SC&display=swap'); $header-title-font-family:Ma Shan Zheng, Madimi One; $header-title-font-size: 35px; $header-title-font-height: 2rem;Ma Shan Zheng@import url: The API for a specific font. $header-title-font-family: The name of the font. $header-title-font-size: The font size. $header-title-font-height: The line height.
