content: Archiving material I think is good, including advice on literary aesthetics and economic research. Under the advance of economic imperialism, no one knows where economics is heading. Some say economics is a skill for slaying dragons, but this world has no dragons to slay; some say economics is over-mathematized and has long drifted from the reality of the world; some say economists only use assumptions to solve problems… Positivism, post-positivism, constructivism — research paradigms crisscross without a single certain answer. Today, economics increasingly resembles the fable genre of constructivism, using data and examples to tell well a fable we need. From this angle, economics and literature have quite a few similarities, so here I collect and arrange articles I like, as reference.
title: Repost: Writing Advice

content: Literature
heading: Literature
title: Repost: Writing Advice

content: Maugham’s “Writing Advice”You must become bored before your audience does. The writer’s motto must be: cut what can be cut, cut again, straight to the peak of the audience’s attention. What we writers must study is still the ordinary person. Ordinary people are the writer’s more fertile soil. He preferred strong, forceful words to pleasant-sounding ones. Only years later did I understand that writing is a delicate art, acquired only through hard work. It is useless to strive at something for which one has no talent. Surprised at the poverty of my vocabulary, I took paper and pen to the British Museum, wrote down the names of curios, the Byzantine colors of old enamel, the feel of fabrics against the body, and then carefully devised sentences to put all of it into. Fortunately, I found no occasion to use this material; it still lies in that old notebook, ready for anyone who wants to write nonsense. I wanted to cast aside ornate phrasing and write as plainly and unaffectedly as I could. I discovered my own limits, and the only sensible thing for me was to set my goal at the best I could achieve within those limits. I knew I had no gift for lyricism. I thought to myself that I should aim at clarity, simplicity, and euphony. In a writer’s work one can find two kinds of obscurity, one arising from carelessness, the other deliberate. People write obscurely often because they have not taken the trouble to learn how to write clearly. Another cause of obscurity is that the author is not quite certain of his own meaning. Many writers do not think before writing but only as they write — the pen itself gives birth to the thought. This is indeed a danger the writer must constantly guard against. It is easy to persuade oneself that a word one does not quite understand contains far more meaning than one realizes. To achieve clarity requires strict training. Simplicity and naturalness are the truest marks of excellence. Euphony is the last of the three qualities I mentioned, and a good many readers, as well as many respected writers, lack it. Words have weight, sound, and appearance; only by taking these into account can you write sentences that are graceful and pleasing. I do not write as I wish; I write as I am able. A far-fetched, worn-out, even affected word is not unsuitable in my eyes as long as it sounds better than a plain, clear one, or gives a sentence better balance. Though you may yield to pleasing sound without hesitation, you should never give way to a word that blurs the meaning. I think the author had best have a stronger faculty of boredom than the reader, so that he senses boredom before the reader does. Once people labor to form a style, they can rarely afterwards write with complete freedom. If you can write clearly, simply, euphoniously, and vividly, you will write perfectly; you will write like Voltaire. Good style shows no trace of effort; what you write should look as though it came to you by a happy accident. If in the end I achieved an effect of ease, it was only through hard effort. People should write in the manner of their own time. Language is living and changing; striving to write like authors of the distant past can only lead to unnaturalness. I would rather a writer be worldly than affected; for life is worldly, and what the writer pursues is life. In my view, many writers do not observe life at all but merely create their characters, as they already are, out of the many figures of their imagination. They are like draftsmen who draw patterns from memory of antiques and never try to draw a living model. At best they can only give their inner fantasies a plausible shape. The stupid prejudice of the intellectual lies in thinking that only their knowledge matters. content: Camus’s 1957 Nobel Speech, “The Artist and His Time”Your Majesties, Your Royal Highnesses, ladies and gentlemen: Your Academy, in the spirit of freedom, has generously bestowed this honor on me, and since I feel my achievements fall far short of its weight, I am all the more sincerely grateful. Everyone longs for recognition, and the artist more than anyone. I am no different. Only after comparing the effect of your decision with my real self did I truly understand why you made such a decision. A still-young man who has nothing but doubts, whose work is not yet formed, who is used to living alone in his work and shrinking from every friendly advance — for such a recluse, suddenly seized and thrown into this dazzling spotlight, how could he not feel a kind of panic? When the other writers of Europe, even some of the greatest among them, are forced into silence, when his homeland is suffering endless affliction, with what feelings is he to accept this honor? I experienced just such inner dread and unease. To regain calm, I could only accept this generous gift of fate. Since my achievements cannot match this award, I can only lean on the conviction that has sustained my life and that I have never abandoned even in the hardest circumstances: my view of my art and of the writer’s role. Allow me, with gratitude and friendship, to express this thought to you as briefly as I can. For me, without art I could not survive. But I have never placed this art above everything else; on the contrary, it is indispensable to me precisely because it is closely bound to everyone and allows someone like me to live as everyone does. Art, in my view, is not a solitary celebration. Art is a means that, in its own way, presents the common suffering and joy of humanity and thereby moves the majority of people. So it forces the artist not to isolate himself and makes him submit to the simplest and most universal truth. And usually, the person who chooses an artistic career thinking himself different soon finds that only by acknowledging what he shares with all beings can his art and his distinctive talent draw nourishment. It is in this constant coming and going between himself and others, in his dealings with the beauty he cannot set aside and the community from which he cannot be detached, that the artist tempers himself. That is why true artists despise nothing; they demand of themselves that they understand everything, not judge everything. If they must choose a side in this world, they can perhaps belong only to the kind of society built in Nietzsche’s great words: a society ruled by creators rather than judges, whether those creators are laborers or intellectuals. Likewise, the writer’s role is burdened with a difficult duty. As a writer, in times like ours, he should not serve those who make history; he should serve those who endure it. Otherwise he will be isolated and will also lose his art. A writer who keeps company with a tyrant cannot escape that loneliness even if the tyrant marches with a host of thousands. But at the other end of the world, a nameless prisoner abandoned to humiliation — his silence is enough, again and again, to rescue the writer from this lonely exile, as long as, while enjoying the rights of freedom, he never forgets that silence and, through the means of art, makes it resound. None of us is great enough to take up this mission. But in all the circumstances of his life, whether neglected or celebrated for a time, whether crushed under the yoke of tyranny or enjoying a momentary freedom of speech, only by serving truth and freedom loyally and to the best of his ability can the writer’s profession become great and can he win from the people a vindication that comes from the heart. content: Chuck Palahniuk’s (author of Fight Club) Writing GuideIn six seconds, you’ll hate me. But in six months, you’ll be a better writer. From now on — for at least the next six months — you may not use “thought” verbs. These include: think, know, understand, realize, believe, want, remember, imagine, desire, and the hundred others you love to use. The list also includes: love and hate. It also includes: be and have, but let’s get to those two in a moment. Until around Christmas, you can’t write: Kenny thought Monica probably didn’t like him going out at night… Instead, you have to unpack that sentence into: “Some mornings Kenny stayed out late, missed the last bus, until he had to hitchhike or pay for a cab, and came home to find Monica pretending to be asleep, because she never slept that quietly; those mornings she would only put her own cup of coffee in the microwave. Never his.” Instead of writing what your character knows, you must now provide details that let the reader know those things. Instead of writing that a character wants something, you must now describe that thing so the reader wants it too. Instead of saying: “Adam knew Gwen liked him.” you have to say: “Between classes, when he went to open his locker, Gwen was always leaning against it. She’d roll her eyes, push herself off with one foot, leaving a black heel print on the painted metal, but she also left her perfume. On the combination lock there was still the warmth of her hip. Next period, Gwen would be leaning there again.” Simply put, there are no shortcuts anymore. Only concrete sensory details: action, smell, taste, sound, and feeling. Typically, authors use these “thought” verbs at the start of a paragraph (you can call them “thesis sentences” here; I’ll complain about that in a bit). In a sense, they point out the whole paragraph’s intent. What follows explains those intents in detail. For example: “Brenda knew she couldn’t make the deadline. She was coming from the bridge, past eight or nine exits. Her phone was dead. At home, the dog needed to be walked or it would make a mess to clean up. Plus she’d promised to water the neighbor’s flowers…” Do you see how that opening thesis sentence steals the thunder from the paragraph that follows? Don’t do that. At the very least, cut the opening line and put it after all the other sentences. Better yet, move it somewhere else and change it to: Brenda couldn’t make the deadline. Thinking is abstract. Knowing and believing are invisible. If you show only physical actions and the details of the character, and let your reader do the thinking and knowing, as well as the loving and hating, your story will always be stronger. Don’t tell your reader “Lisa hated Tom.” Instead, argue your case like a courtroom lawyer, speak through details, and present every piece of evidence. For example: “At roll call, in the breath after the teacher called Tom’s name, in the instant before he answered, right then, Lisa would whisper ‘jerk.’ Just as Tom said ‘here.’” One of the most common mistakes of beginning authors is leaving their characters alone. When you write, you can be alone. When they read, your readers can be alone. But your characters should very, very rarely be alone. Because a lonely character will start thinking, worrying, or wondering. For example: “While waiting for the bus, Mark started to worry about how long the trip would take…” A better way to show it: “The schedule said the bus would arrive at noon, but Mark’s watch showed it was already 11:57. You could see to the end of the road, all the way to the mall — not a single bus. No doubt the driver had stopped at the transfer station, at the far end of the route, and was dozing. content: Samuelson | Why Am I the One Who Wrote Economics?Source: Tales of the Economics World This article was written by Samuelson for the fiftieth anniversary of the publication of Economics, from Scientific Papers of Paul Samuelson No. 587. Translator: Lü Ji’er, forwarded by teacher Lai Jiancheng. Wang Laohu revised parts of the text, hoping not to have run counter to the translator’s original meaning. It is shared here because I like the article; the original-protection mark is added to protect teacher Lü’s rights as translator. Teacher Lü invites friends to offer corrections so the translation can be improved. For your corrections, the translator expresses heartfelt thanks! Translator’s email: zjjier@163.com Economics Turns FiftyEconomics has reached its fiftieth birthday, and over this half century it has witnessed the considerable development of economics. Economics has come a long way, yet to this day it has no right to boast of having reached the state of an exact science — as is probably true of any social science. Economics is forever a discipline that merges science and art, and there is a world of difference between a vigorous economics and a pedantic, outdated one. Today, the things economists can do are increasing day by day, whether in government, the private sector, or academia. Compared with the late 1940s, the volume of data in statistical databases has grown explosively. Now computers can obtain and process statistical information and all kinds of knowledge at the speed of light, and we can obtain information quickly. Whether theoretical or applied economics, research in political economy has benefited enormously from advances in computer hardware and software — more, perhaps, than any other field. Even so, the foundational areas of economics have barely moved forward. The world has learned some economic principles from history (at least from economic history) and has studied and tested them diligently. Economists treat fickle economic slumps and the inflation that produces false prosperity as laboratory mice, conducting controlled experiments like chemists in a lab. (The translator omits one sentence here.) At the same time, the perfectly competitive free market has failed to bring humanity equality of opportunity and equality of income. The fact that “poverty is always with us” forces democracies around the world to evolve into a “mixed economy” — neither a laissez-faire market nor a Robin Hood utopia. Only after studying the basic principles of economics can the public understand and be convinced of how to strike the right middle course between self-interested individual initiative on the one hand and government regulation, the maintenance of stability, and redistribution on the other. Willingly or not, a mixed economy must be a “limited mixed economy.” Looking BackA fiftieth birthday is an excellent occasion for looking back. What story can we see in the popularity of this best-selling textbook, which has led the field? How was this textbook born? We have to pull our gaze back to 1945. The Second World War ended with the defeat of Germany and Japan, and the people returning home filled American universities to overflowing. At that time, economics happened to be entering a golden age. The Great Depression of 1929 to 1935 turned economics around, casting aside the old ideas that had once held orthodoxy and replacing them with ambitious plans, with strong monetary and fiscal policies. Britain and the United States adopted new ways of mobilizing their economies for war, something Hitler, Mussolini, and Hirohito could never have dreamed of. At the time, we could not yet know of the later Marshall Plan and the American occupation of Japan, but they were about to set the stage for decades of postwar economic growth. content: Lu Ming: Experience and Advice for Scholars Doing Empirical ResearchSource: Econometrics Circle “Carrying Empirical Research Through to the End” is an article I wrote back in 2004, published in The Economist’s Teahouse. It drew a certain response, beyond my expectations, which also shows that empirical research is receiving more and more attention in China. At such a time, we do need some articles like this to help everyone clarify some understandings about econometrics. Today I especially want to help everyone clear up several misunderstandings — misunderstandings that happen to be ones I heard from students myself in the course of working with them, so they are not something I invented. The first misunderstanding is that empirical research is applied, and applied work is not academic enough and has little value, as if it only answers a question in reality and the conclusions found seem to be things we already knew. The second is a phrase everyone often says: empirical research is easy to do, easier than theoretical research, and when you can’t continue with theory you switch to empirical research. Speaking of which, this winter vacation I was just reunited with one of my former students, now a PhD student at KU Leuven in Belgium. Her recent work is related to social economics, and she does theory. When we met over the winter break and talked, I asked her, why don’t you do empirical work on this topic? She said empirical work is too hard. So I think that on some questions, it is not as everyone imagines — that when you can’t do theory you do empirics; it may well be the reverse: when you can’t do empirics you do theory. I’ll talk about the relationship between empirics and theory later, and I’ll tell everyone that both theory and empirics are very important and complementary. Third, students often think empirical research is very simple: just put the data into the computer, the results come out, and you can write a paper. Once, a colleague said, with some self-deprecation: he felt very uneasy, because the data wasn’t collected by himself — much of the large-sample data we use was collected by others — and the idea wasn’t very new, not his own; then the programs were ready-made, Stata already coded. After that, we put data we didn’t collect and an idea that wasn’t too new into Stata, the results came out, and we felt very uneasy. And our students think that a master of economic research should be full of mathematical symbols plus programs they wrote themselves, and then draw very fancy figures — that’s what counts as high level. The fourth misunderstanding is that many students think that when we now study China’s problems, we should do theory, because theory is in line with international standards. Especially for beginners: when taking the master’s and doctoral entrance exams in economics, you are tested on micro and macro, and in your first year you take a great deal of micro and macro theory, so you feel that is the mainstream of economics and only that is prestigious; even when doing research on China, you should write China’s problems as mathematics, or simply not do research related to China at all. Is that really so? Should Chinese economics research really do theory first? The questions I’m going to talk about next are an attempt to clear away the misunderstandings in everyone’s minds. Today I will cover these questions: first, why do we do empirical research? Second, what is the relationship between empirics and theory, including ideas? Third, what is the relationship between empirical research and the development of Chinese economics? Fourth, how do you complete a piece of empirical research? 1. Why Do Empirical Research?I think the functions of empirical research in the process of modern economic research and development are as follows: First, empirical research is used to test theory. content: It was only after a long, long time that I began to understand—in the sorrow of the last emperor, “the last” far outweighs “the emperor.” When the whip of history drives forward, it does not stop lashing because of the traveler’s identity; it simply, monotonously repeats the actions of closing and opening doors, always ready to close the next one. History has no emotions; the suffering and happiness of life merely push people forward, adding fuel to an indifferent flame. This carriage does not care who is outside, brushing off the rising dust, even though those lingering outside were once the masters of the carriage. This “door” is the spokesperson of history in the film, embodying the dual meanings of “connection and separation.” It is majestic, for we cannot see the other side of the era; It is stern, capable of isolating a person at the end of an era; It is merciful, allowing everyone to sense the possibility of crossing over. The Last Emperor—the noblest person, the one who cannot catch up, the door that cannot be opened; Suzume—the distance between death and everyday life is just a door; The Whale—does the self-saver have the courage to cross the threshold of sorrow? It’s just that during this period, I abruptly watched a series of movies, all of which involved doors, so much so that when I began to look back, a tall door always appeared before my eyes. And the reality of the siege, the surge of artificial intelligence, feels like another opening and closing of a door, leaving people from two eras staring at each other. If the wise have already sensed the existence of the door, what would they say about their own powerlessness? Perhaps only when a person passes through doors of various shapes and sizes can they get closer to the door of history, but they will also be blocked by the next door they cannot pass through. Just a sigh: In the vastness of life, we are but fleeting travelers. ———————— By the way: They say this AI is the next industrial revolution. Although I use GPT very happily, I still have doubts. Because an industrial revolution requires an energy revolution as its foundation, and currently, GPT Plus is constantly shrinking and halting sales due to reaching a bottleneck in computing power. 5G is strong, but the cost of materials greatly limits its spread. Without an energy revolution, AI’s computing power is insufficient, which greatly restricts its potential. Also, everything about AI is currently in the experimental stage, like Go. AI has not brought much displacement; the industries it has spawned are mostly tools. Recently, the most popular thing is that a simple bug can defeat KATAgo by exploiting a small weakness, showing that once a bug in AI is found, it can paralyze everything. Therefore, AI can only be a tool. For example, no matter how much autonomous vehicle technology develops, as long as the road shape remains unchanged, it will never pass review. Language models are only a part of intelligence, and it is hard to say directly that they can surpass humans.

title: A Quick Guide to Cleaning Economic Microdata

content: 1. Popular domestic databases:Most microdata database files are mainly in DTA, SAS, and EXCEL formats. They’re split by subject (community questionnaire, household questionnaire, social files) and by theme (background info, health, economy…). Each year’s cross-section data is also separate, so you need to process it into panel data yourself. Apply on the official site with a student email. Application experience: CFPS\CHARLS\CHIP\CGSS have a very good application experience. It’s just that the site occasionally crashes and won’t open, so once your application is approved, I suggest downloading all the data right away.
heading: 1. Popular domestic databases:
title: A Quick Guide to Cleaning Economic Microdata

content: Large, comprehensive databasesCFPS: www.isss.pku.edu.cn/cfps/ China Education Panel Survey: CFPS is implemented by the Institute of Social Science Survey (ISSS) at Peking University. It tracks data at three levels — individual, household, and community — reflecting changes in Chinese society, economy, population, education, and health, and provides a data foundation for academic research and public policy analysis. CMDS: Data application (chinaldrk.org.cn) China Migrants Dynamic Survey: A large-scale annual national sampling survey of the migrant population conducted by the National Health Commission since 2009. Its content covers basic information about the migrant population and their family members, migration range and trends, employment and social security, income and expenditure and housing, basic public health services, marriage/childbearing and family planning service management, children’s migration and education, psychological culture, and more. CMDS has stopped updatingCHARLS: China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (pku.edu.cn) China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study: China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. A large interdisciplinary survey project hosted by the National School of Development at Peking University and executed by the Institute of Social Science Survey, representing high-quality microdata on households and individuals aged 45 and above in China. CSS: Chinese Social Survey (http://css.cssn.cn/css_sy/) Chinese Social Survey: A nationwide large-scale continuous sampling survey project initiated by the Institute of Sociology at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences in 2005. Its purpose is to obtain data on social change in China during the transitional period through long-term longitudinal surveys of the public’s employment, family and social life, social attitudes, and more, thereby providing detailed and scientific basic information for social science research and government decision-making. Currently, eight waves of CSS data — 2006, 2008, 2022, 2013, 2015, 2017, 2019, and 2021 — have been made open to the public. CHIP: China Household Income Project (http://www.ciidbnu.org/) China Household Income Project: Launched by the Income Distribution Research Institute at Beijing Normal University1. The project aims to collect household survey data for potentially useful empirical analysis of trends in China after reform and opening up, such as income, inequality, and poverty. CGSS: China Household Income Survey (http://www.cnsda.org/) Chinese General Social Survey (CGSS) is China’s first nationwide, comprehensive, and continuous large-scale social survey project. Its purpose is to periodically and systematically collect data on all aspects of Chinese people and Chinese society, summarize the long-term trends of social change, explore social issues of major theoretical and practical significance, promote the openness and sharing of domestic social science research, and provide data for government decision-making and international comparative research. China Statistical Yearbook: city data, regional data… The panel data organized from this is all over the internet. Others: for example, there’s also the China Household Finance Survey CHFS (https://chfser.swufe.edu.cn/datasso/Home/Login?4813085540248732983). We can also use some small specialized databases to supplement the main databases for analysis. For example, the Peking University Digital Inclusive Finance Index: Peking University Digital Inclusive Finance Index, the Innovation and Entrepreneurship Index, the Government Governance Index… For example, when it comes to measuring urban digital economy nowadays, most people use Zhao Tao’s (2020)2 method, taking the urban statistical yearbook + inclusive finance data as indicators. With the “digital economy” craze, who knows how many people’s first econometrics paper started with digital economy, urban resilience,,,,,, There are

content: 2. Cleaning approach and its purposeWhat exactly does cleaning data involve? Basically these tasks. Table matching: match and merge different database tables, aiming to integrate and screen indicators, divided into horizontal and vertical matching. Removing bad data: remove bad data. For example, blank data, extreme data, unneeded data… Filling in blank data: fill in data. For panel data and time series, we often use linear interpolation to fill in missing values in the middle or at the edges. Data aggregation: build indicators through specific methods, like principal components, entropy weighting, analytic hierarchy process… The most important thing is to master the W!O!R!K!F!L!O!W! When running regressions, “not enough variables”, “lost variables” and other disasters usually happen; we may need to go back at any time to update variables and check where mistakes happened, so keeping a complete workflow folder is very necessary. WorkflowRule of thumb!!!!! Keep one folder for raw data, one folder for after table matching, and one more folder for the cleaning process! Writing code so that it runs smoothly from data cleaning all the way to outputting results in one breath — that’s the highest level of a pipeline! First, it lets us present each work step for easy checking; second, it makes it convenient to “redo” from any intermediate step.

content: 2. Matching databasesIt basically revolves around integrating around the sample’s ID, yearID, and year. imgStata matching code — only brief explanations below //master_data.dta is the base database, using_data.dta is the database we want to match onto it //m:n id means m ids in the first data can correspond to n sample ids in the second database //In short, m:n is many-to-one, n:n is 1-to-1, m:m is many-to-many // So we can also add multiple matching conditions, e.g. merge 1:1 id year treat ...... ************horizontal match 1************************** use "master_data.dta" merge m:n id using "using_data.dta" drop _merge save "new_data.dta" ************horizontal match 2************************** use "master_data.dta" joinby id using "using_data.dta" ************vertical match************************** use "data1.dta" append using "data2.dta" save "new_data.dta"About horizontal matchingmerge is suitable when the identifier of the matching side or the matched side is unique. For one-to-many matching, e.g. when the master data’s identifier is unique but the matched data repeats, with each repeated identifier row missing different variables, you can use merge’s append-match subcommand to only update the missing part each time. use "master_data.dta" merge 1:m id using "using_data.dta", update nogen forceFor many-to-many matching, you need to use joinby. For details, see: Many-to-many merge - merge - joinby

content: 3. Quickly selecting variablesShortcuts like Shift\ctrl are basically universal in software design; once you use them a lot, you can apply them to other software too. There’s a variable window in the top-right of Stata. Right-click to get select-all and other options; it can also serve as a search box. Simultaneous selection is ctrl+multiple clicks. If you need to select a dozen scattered variables at once, use it actively. To select a middle range, click one variable, then shift+click another variable, and it selects the middle range. For example, you can first right-click, select all, then ctrl+click to remove the variables you don’t want; For example, to check the completeness of specific data, name them “x_i” first during processing, then filter for those named x and select all. Before python has this kind of window, I won’t consider running regressions superior to stata

content: 4. InterpolationLinear interpolation, panel data. As usual for panel data, first mark the individual id and year id, xtset id year by id: ipolate YY year,gen(YYY) //interpolation, middle missing values, named as new variable YYY after filling by id: ipolate XX year,gen(XXX) epolate //extrapolation, edge missing values, named as new variable XXX after fillingMy suggestion is, use forvalues whenever you can5, and make good use of variable macros. Once you know the basic loop commands + variable nesting + conditional filter commands, writing code becomes free-flowing. For example, the following batch interpolation loop: $var_i \stackrel{interpolate}{\longrightarrow}varx_i\stackrel{extrapolate}{\longrightarrow}varn_i\stackrel{replace}{\longrightarrow}var_i\stackrel{delete}{\longrightarrow}varx_i $ global var var0 var1 var2 var3 genshin *pack up all the variables to be interpolated foreach i in $var { by id: ipolate `i' year,gen(varx`i') by id: ipolate varx`i' year,gen(varn`i') epolate replace `i' = varn`i' drop varx`i' varn`i' } Similarly, cleaning bad data in questionnaire data is the same loop global var var0 var1 var2 var3 genshin *pack up all the variables to be interpolated foreach i in $var { drop if `i' == -88 drop if `i' == -99 drop if `i' ==. drop if `i' <=0 } The internet also circulates a “one-click significance” cleaning. The idea is to brute-force permute the control variables, and later even start screening samples. My view: you can look at the control-variable-selection code, but don’t casually touch the samples. A core soul of econometrics is the “randomized experiment”; interfering with sample selection easily breaks data randomness, which is basically fabrication. (Though purely in terms of code thinking, this does show that once you’ve mastered the filtering, judging, and looping commands, there’s already a lot you can do. The same cleaning task — how you combine the algorithms is what tests the person.)

content: 6. Date transcoding6Sometimes the date codes we download can’t be recognized by stata, in which case we need the date function. For example, in a class assignment, I wanted to show China’s confidence! Give the teacher a little Chinese shock. (This is China.jpg) I used iiMedia’s Huawei and Apple laptop Taobao data. ps: at the time I also found export trade data for China, Japan, Russia, and the US; data source World Bank. But awkwardly, the date format loaded from Excel was Y-M-D, which stata can’t directly recognize. 2 is Huawei, 1 is Apple; sales is number, date is the year columnUsing the code (I found it on the Jinggu forum): clear import excel "E:\桌面\笔记本.xlsx", sheet("Sheet1") firstrow generate date=date(year,"YMD") //recognize the date format date %td //further conversionGreen is Apple, gold is Huawei. You can see that after processing, date becomes a special date form, and it can be directly used to draw scatter plots in stata. The original plot is gone, so I just redrew it simply; please ignore this garish color schemeGreen is Apple, gold is Huawei. You can see that after processing, date becomes a special date form, and it can be directly used to draw scatter plots in stata. The original plot is gone, so I just redrew it simply; please ignore this garish color scheme. Another example, a dataset about air pollution. In Excel, the date column is in “short date format” imgImport into stata, use the date function to plot generate year=date(date, "YMD") //recognize the date format year %td //further conversionFrom this plot it’s easy to see seasonalityFrom descriptive statistics plotting, we can see air pollution has seasonality. So we want to slice out the month separately for season numbering. generate month = month(year) //slice the month from the already-processed year date //for a more detailed explanation, see: https://stata-club.github.io/stata_article/2017-10-29.html gen spring = 1 if month == 3 |month == 4 | month == 5 replace spring = 0 if spring != 1 gen summer = 1 if month == 6 |month == 7 | month == 8 replace summer = 0 if summer != 1 gen fall = 1 if month == 9 |month == 10 | month == 11 replace fall = 0 if fall != 1 gen winter = 1 if month == 12 |month == 1 | month == 2 replace winter = 0 if winter != 1Fitting by season classification shows the linear trend is more obvious. We find temperature and pollution are correlated, which is why the previous plot shows periodicity; we can also hypothesize that the lower the temperature, the more heating, heated beds, and coal use, leading to more air pollution

content: 7. Deletion and conditional statementsStata’s command to delete specific columns is the drop command. I suggest directly typing “h drop” to view the help. Making good use of if conditions and forvalues loops is when algorithmic ability is tested! What kind of data do you need to process, and what is your goal? How can the goal be decomposed, into what flow, which if conditions filter faster, and which forvalues loops can simplify your cleaning steps as quickly as possible? Make good use of stata’s do files and consider code reusability, so that after writing code, it can be reused in loops later, e.g. by only changing variable names.

content: 1. The VLOOKUP functionAfter using it a lot, I feel stata is much faster than Excel. For example, I did a task on descriptive statistics of rural revitalization levels, where I needed to show the number of villages above the mean for each indicator. In Excel this is fairly troublesome, involving judgment (if you haven’t mastered VBA); stata handles it much faster. global $xlist x1 x2 x3 x4 x5 foreach i in $xlist { egen b = mean(`i') gen a = 1*(b < `i')+0*(b>= `i') egen sum_`i' = sum(a) drop a drop b }The easiest data to find and analyze in economics is definitely urban panel data, and city code matching is unavoidable Please refer to: link, which thoughtfully includes the city codes; many thanks! When using the vlookup function, you may also encounter a situation; excel’s format settings are truly bizarre!

Excel’s current feature is quite smart, mainly very handy for cleaning panel data that needs accumulation. Note: the pivot table’s “sum function” requires the excel format to be “number”, while the “count function” has no format restriction. Sometimes data imported from excel imghas a format defaulting to “text”, and needs adjustment (at least first set it to “general” format).

content: 3. Splitting textAs far as econometrics goes, the current top-tier approach is DID. If your school has a student econometrics paper competition, it’s very likely pure “difference-in-differences” hand-to-hand combat (dog head) When doing DID, we need to manually record the policy variables. For example, smart cities and innovation cities piloted in three batches over several years. At this point we can’t foolishly copy-paste one by one; please use Excel’s text splitting. For example, splitting the set of pilot cities “Beijing, Chongqing, Tianjin, Shanghai”, you can select that cell, $Data\Rightarrow Text to Columns$, In the “Text to Columns Wizard” dialog, choose “Delimited”, click “Next”, and check “,” in “Delimiters”. At this point the rows are split. Then combine with the VLOOKUP function to match.

The pits of data cleaning are hard to guard against Some Excel files have cityid as 1100, some as 110000 Some say Chengdu, some say Chengdu with the word “City” tacked on! Excel remove-character operation: A2=LEFT(A1,LEN(A1)-1) Excel add-character operation: A2=A1&“市”

content: “The Calling of Spirits”: Prosperity’s zenith, sorcery’s sway,Where power’s mirage, in twilight, may play. During the boring time of the Chinese New Year holidays, I finally finished reading “The Calling of Spirits.” In 1768, a panic of sorcery called “The Calling of Spirits” swept across the land of the Qing Empire. Surprisingly, the terms “prosperous era” and “sorcery” became parallel concepts. Kong Feili followed the thread of the “sorcery/hair-cutting case” and dissected the entire class structure of the Qing Dynasty—faced with the unheard-of sorcery of hair-cutting, each class had its own interpretation. In summary, the “Calling of Spirits” case involves three main threads: The panic and public dissemination of sorcery among common people. The political concerns and exploitation of the “Calling of Spirits” by the emperor. The bureaucratic dilemma of officials fearing pressure from above and below.
heading: “The Calling of Spirits”: Prosperity’s zenith, sorcery’s sway,
title: The Calling of Spirits

content: First, public opinion: folk legends and population mobility.The “Calling of Spirits” case involved an unheard-of form of sorcery where one’s money could be stolen simply by cutting off their braid. For the common people, who believed in the existence of the soul, “calling of spirits” was a widely circulated folk custom, providing a foundation for belief in sorcery. China’s deep-rooted local sentiment made it easier for people to demonize outsiders. At this time, Chinese construction workers and the monk class, due to the transient nature of their professions, were particularly susceptible to suspicion. The expansion of the “Calling of Spirits” incidents originated from these transient populations.
heading: First, public opinion: folk legends and population mobility.
title: The Calling of Spirits

content: Second, cultural contradictions: Manchu rule over the Han.Faced with sorcery, the Qing Dynasty faced inherent cultural contradictions. Despite Emperor Qianlong’s early attempts to distance the “hair-cutting case” from political dissent, the braided queue remained a symbol of Manchu identity. As rulers of the Qing Dynasty, their attitude reflected not only fear of rebellion but also dissatisfaction with the Sinicization of the Manchus. The inherent weakness of feudal dynasties was evident in the legal ambiguity regarding “sorcery.” While the emperor and the state used the concept of “divine right” to bolster their legitimacy, sorcery was seen as both a miracle and a threat. This led to vague laws regarding sorcery in the Qing Dynasty, which had to be established nonetheless.
heading: Second, cultural contradictions: Manchu rule over the Han.
title: The Calling of Spirits

content: Third, bureaucratic politics: examination and clubs.The bureaucratic system of the Qing Dynasty was rife with inequality.The core of Kong Lifai’s research lies in the impact of this system on information dissemination and policy implementation. The emperor regarded bureaucrats as tools, establishing various channels. Although the ceremonial language was cumbersome, it served both as a means of communication and a way to delineate status. Without the ceremonial aspects, the emperor would struggle to bear the burden of pushing through tasks, yet reverting to formality also led to inefficiency. In the “hair-cutting case,” the most prominent aspect was the prevalence of officials’ evaluations filled with flattery and mutual protection. Under the system of mutual recommendation for official selection, actions at all levels were aligned along an axis of interests. Bureaucratic evaluations manifested as a strip, with flattery revolving around imperial power. Qing officials’ evaluations were brief and crude, with achievements attributed to “events.” What’s terrifying is that officials had the ability to control these events, and the moral risk of self-directed deception occurred easily under the desire for positive imperial evaluations and mutual concealment among peers. From this moment on, imperial evaluations had never had such power to influence the course of events, yet Qianlong’s decisions remained loyal to his position as a Manchu emperor. Was this management by an ethnic minority a political distortion? Regardless, as the “calling souls” case shattered, the actors on the stage retreated one by one.
heading: Third, bureaucratic politics: examination and clubs.
title: The Calling of Spirits

content: Fourth, Political Crimes: The Accessible Power and FearHow was the “Haircut Case” classified? This is a “political crime” similar to a “literary inquisition,” where anyone can be charged with an unfounded accusation of political crime. For most people, this means - everyone has never had such an opportunity to get close to “power” and “fear.” For the masses, it is fear as well as a weapon. For bureaucrats, it is an event. For the emperor, it is a threat and a tool. For some people, it’s just fun. At this point, the “Haircut Case” / “Sorcery” / “Haircut,” mixed with various classes, has exploded into a chemical reaction.
heading: Fourth, Political Crimes: The Accessible Power and Fear
title: The Calling of Spirits

content: Conclusion: The “Soul Calling” of Cyberpunk“The Soul Calling” achieves a remarkable balance between academic rigor, detailed and vast content, and a compelling narrative. Faced with the same “soul calling” and hair-cutting incidents, the experiences of different social classes are completely different. Kong Feili has conducted a perfect “heterogeneity” analysis and class analysis of society. It is worth noting that this result is a structured classification rather than a combination of multiple quantities. Therefore, I believe that the discussion of “The Soul Calling” should be separated from “The Crowd: A Study of the Popular Mind”. The “Soul Calling” case has many similarities with the characteristics of the Qing Dynasty. This is an explanation of the decline and turning point under the prosperous age, and it is also the inevitable result of the historical operation of the feudal dynasty. Although the case seems to revolve around the emperor’s attitude, the emperor remains faithful to his class. However, China at this time had not yet achieved harmonious integration of its diverse cultural groups, leading to distortions in the operation of power. How could absurd sorcery emerge in a “prosperous age”? Perhaps coincidence is just a turning point in history. The big fish lurking beneath the surface of the water has never stopped swimming, just casting fleeting shadows in the rise and fall of governance. But we must be vigilant, for history occasionally drops insane fuses. Once the elements are in place—there is nothing to stand in the way of this madness.
heading: Conclusion: The “Soul Calling” of Cyberpunk
title: The Calling of Spirits

content: Some Simple ReflectionsAs for why the “Call Soul Case” had such far-reaching consequences in the Qing Dynasty, I couldn’t help but think of cyberpunk. At a time of prosperity in the Qing Dynasty, why did superstition prevail? Certainly, the feudal cultural characteristics of the Qing Dynasty and its simplistic evaluation system played a role. But the tragic events of political crimes have recurred throughout history. The “Call Soul Case” created a collective “illusion of power” for people of all classes, with political crimes becoming the fear and weapon of everyone. In modern society, educated individuals are unlikely to be superstitious about “souls,” but in contemporary society (for example, online discourse), everyone seems to crave power more than ever: Educating others, a wield of power, Judging others, a wield of power, Assessing others, a wield of power. The discussion of three views is gradually becoming a weapon, Like blocking and reporting, once tools for maintaining discussion environment, Now wielded as weapons to attack dissenters. Misalignment of ideologies leads to explosions, Each fighting for their beliefs, But are we battling for truth itself, Or falling into the illusion of power? Israel’s deadly attacks on the West Bank of the Jordan River are still ongoing.Israel deadly assault on the west bank of the Jordan River continues
title: The Calling of Spirits

content: Image reference insertionThe process is: first use tikzit to save multiple groups of vector diagrams you’ve drawn, number them, then insert them into the tex file. (Refer to the similar insertion approach for LaTeX bibliography and image insertion.) The specific process, Create a folder named tikzpaper. Put tikzit.sty inside it. Inside the tikzpaper folder, create a folder called figures, and save all the diagrams tikzit has saved into it. Create paper.tex in the tikzpaper folder. The paper.tex environment is as follows: Here \tikzfig{ddd} and \ctikzfig{ddd} are the two ways to reference images; the content inside the curly braces {} is the image filename saved in the figures folder. % paper.tex \documentclass{article} \usepackage{tikzit} %\input{sample.tikzstyles} \begin{document} A tikz picture as an equation: \begin{equation} \tikzfig{ddd} \end{equation} A centered tikz picture: \ctikzfig{ddd} \end{document}The result

content: Other toolsOpen-source software is small and elegant, and much of it works straight out of the box. mathcha (web, paid) tikzcd-editor (many answers mention this site, but the trouble is it doesn’t tell you which package you need; though now that we have GPT, it hardly matters) \usepackage{tikz} \usetikzlibrary{cd} \\tikz sub-package for calling the tikzcd command environment of relationship diagramsinkscape (you can treat it as an open-source PS) ipe (free and open-source, but there’s no Chinese localization yet, though the page is mostly graphics) When downloading ipe, don’t have Chinese characters in the install path, or it will error when opening. (For ipe, I suggest pairing it with a teaching video on Bilibili: Bilibili tutorial) latexdraw (free and open-source) LaTeXdrawTikzEdit (free, open-source, English, but easy to understand tikzeditTikzedit is like a just-in-time compiling tex; the page is also exactly the same as tex. I’ve tried both TikzEdit and latexdraw. latexdraw’s visual editing is better — text position and color can also be adjusted visually. TikzEdit is more about visual moving-editing of points and lines. But neither can visually edit arrow styles. For someone with some background, TikzEdit is more convenient. The dark-art method: use flashy tools (like PPT, processon (an online web page)) to draw, save as PDF, then crop and insert it into latex as a PDF file (this also reduces the typesetting and code-running pressure on latex). This is a diagram I casually drew using the processon web version, though the latex formulas inside lose fidelity when saved as PDF; other Chinese formats won’t.Here is the local environment for inserting a cropped PDF: \begin{figure} \centering \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=0.5\textwidth]{实践时间是.pdf} \\the square brackets control the PDF's size (width and height); the curly braces hold the PDF's name \caption{Title} \end{figure} By the way, here's the complete environment for inserting a whole-page PDF file: \documentclass[a4paper]{article} \usepackage{pdfpages} \begin{document} \includepdf[pages={1,2,4,7}]{PDF的名字.pdf} \\the content inside the square brackets is the page numbers of the original PDF \end{document}

content: What is LaTeX?LaTeX (/ˈlɑːtɛx/, often pronounced /ˈlɑːtɛk/ or /ˈleɪtɛk/) is a high-quality typesetting system based on TeX, developed in the early 1980s by the American computer scientist Leslie Lamport. It is very suitable for producing high-print-quality scientific, mathematical, and physics documents, and is especially good at typesetting complex tables and math formulas. LaTeX is the de facto standard for scientific literature exchange and publication. (Wikipedia) Word: what you see is what you get LaTeX: the typesetting format and the text content are separate (The typesetting is adjusted through code, and the best part is the various packages — you call them to do all sorts of things, like inserting a few emoji into your article~) Inserting emoji, something Word can’t do this naturally~For me, LaTeX’s typesetting is genuinely beautiful, and getting a comfortable layout just right is very satisfying. If your article contains a lot of math formulas, figures, and tables, then LaTeX is definitely the better choice~ Word typesettingLaTeX typesettingOur team describing a queueing model in a math modeling competition, typeset in LaTeX

content: During the holiday, I accompanied my teachers to conduct research at several county-level poverty alleviation and relocation sites in Zhaotong, Yunnan. Zhaotong is a city located at the junction of Sichuan and Yunnan provinces, famous for its Zhaotong apples. In the past, Zhaotong was renowned for its bold and vigorous people, but now, with a strong emphasis on education, the situation has improved significantly. The rural revitalization efforts here focus on supporting the special industry of Gastrodia elata.
title: Research Note 1: Zhaotong, Yunnan

heading: County Town Scenic Spot
title: Research Note 1: Zhaotong, Yunnan

content: YanjinYanjin in Yunnan is known as a “front-line city,” with its main body built along the river. The roads are narrow, leaving only a single main road passing through the city. To accommodate this barely passable dual-carriageway, residents have had to extend their houses and plots along the riverbank slopes, resulting in houses predominantly made of reinforced concrete. The entire old town area is like LEGO blocks inserted between the two sides of the river. Often, just one family will occupy an entire building. Due to this terrain, the river here is swift-flowing, leading to relatively frequent flooding each year. A “first-tier” city built along rivers and canyonsThe mountainous terrain in Yunnan is diverse, and there are many types of mushrooms, most of which are poisonous. Therefore, the community places particular emphasis on safety education to prevent both water disasters and food poisoning. As a precautionary measure, the community has even signed agreements with residents regarding food poisoning caused by mushrooms, stipulating that individuals bear responsibility for the consequences. local square at night
heading: Yanjin
title: Research Note 1: Zhaotong, Yunnan

content: Tea Horse Ancient RoadThe Tea Horse Ancient Road is home to the famous “Dousha Pass” and the cliff burials of the “Bo People Hanging Coffins”. During the Tang Dynasty, emissaries were sent to administer Yunnan, and the cliff carvings here serve as important evidence. Thanks to its strategic location as a transportation hub for the province, despite having the narrowest roads in some areas, it was the first to connect to the Southwest Silk Road, subway, train, and expressway. The scenic spot here is known as “One View and Five Roads”. Waterways, Roads, Plank Roads, Railways, SubwaysThe word “僰” in Chinese carries the ideographic meaning of people pulling a vine strip to swing.
heading: Tea Horse Ancient Road
title: Research Note 1: Zhaotong, Yunnan

content: Other County TownsOther county towns have relatively fewer attractions, so I won’t mention them in detail. Yunnan’s terrain is mainly mountainous and hilly, which makes road construction more costly and tolls on expressways higher. Due to the limited availability of land caused by the terrain, urban planning in Yunnan faces many constraints, and construction costs are also higher. Take Ludian County as an example, where most residents live in the mountains. In the evening, walking up the road along the mountain, you can see scattered lights in the distance on the mountain, like stars in the night sky. Therefore, the local area also calls the relocation operation as a “picking star action.”

content: Research SummaryThe relocation targets residents in remote mountainous areas, affected by environmental and economic factors, and generally suffering from chronic diseases. What needs to change is not just their physical living environment, but also their consciousness. The key to relocation is how to help relocated households adapt to the transformation of identity and consciousness from rural to urban towns. In rural areas, they were self-sufficient, without water and electricity bills, growing their own vegetables. Now, they face property management fees, water and electricity bills, which they may not fully understand. Therefore, the community has adopted a transitional plan: water and electricity are free for the first three years, with gradually increasing payment proportions thereafter. To adapt to rural culture, the community also provides services for both happy and sad occasions. All can be handled within the community. Implementing grid management (a classic special term 🙃), establishing files, and finely managing in batches. Classify those with disabilities, those without disabilities, those with major illnesses, and elderly families… Regular training is needed to help residents adapt to the internet, at least to learn to read WeChat notifications. Multi-dimensional poverty alleviation employment, preventing relapse into poverty. Employment subsidies for working outside, poverty alleviation employment workshops within the community, local industry poverty alleviation employment, and entrepreneurial subsidies (opening a stall, buying snacks is also considered entrepreneurship). Leveraging comparative advantages. Yunnan’s advantage in developing industries is green food—such as Gastrodia elata, bamboo shoots, oranges, and others. Its weaknesses lie in transportation, and processing and manufacturing capabilities. The local area lacks money, really lacks money! There are many arrears in project payments.
heading: Research Summary
title: Research Note 1: Zhaotong, Yunnan

content: Research BanquetsDuring county-level research, it’s inevitable to interface with local leaders, and these interactions often involve banquets where baijiu (a strong Chinese liquor) is typically served. Excessive drinking is always harmful to health. Here are some personal insights based on my experiences. The banquets I encountered in several counties generally followed four stages: Stage One: Personal introductions, after which individuals start drinking voluntarily. Stage Two: Mutual exchanges and inviting others to drink, one-on-one. Stage Three: Speech by leaders, giving collective advice, followed by a group toast where everyone stands and toasts around the table. Stage Four: As the banquet wraps up, exchanging WeChat contacts. Strategies for drinking should be flexible and adapted according to each stage. Spell casting preparation: Emphasize repeatedly that you don’t drink, haven’t drunk before, to reduce the difficulty level as much as possible. Stage One: Usually, when standing up to introduce yourself, you can start pouring a bit of the drink from the small or medium-sized glass. Alternatively, you can discreetly pour it out under the table beforehand. When raising the glass, use your hand to cover the side of the glass (fully covering the glass would look too fake!), so that others can’t see the level of the drink, thinking it’s in the pouring state. Stage Two: Because it’s a university student survey, you can eat and drink casually without knowing the rules. Pay attention to see if there’s milk or tea cups on the table. Drink water to one-third full, hold the wine in your mouth after the toast (be careful not to puff your mouth up! Tongue might be quite rough), pretend to drink the beverage, and spill the wine into the beverage. If no beverage is available, the filled bowl of rice or soup is the best hiding tool When others interject to add to the conversation, it’s also a good opportunity for a small move. Typically, at a drinking session, everyone usually watches the person speaking. Stage three: Here, the meal is almost over and most people are at least tipsy, so they can rest assured. When toasting, cover the sides of the glass with your hands. Join the toasting group and pretend to be drinking, but no wine enters your mouth. Move around a lot. At this time, everyone is usually trying to please others and will usually not notice small movements. It is recommended to use the teachings in Liu Qian’s magic class - big movements cover up small movements to mislead the other party’s attention. For example, one hand makes movements to attract attention, and the other hand gently pours wine on the ground.
heading: Research Banquets
title: Research Note 1: Zhaotong, Yunnan

content: The Mogao Grottoes aspire to be more than mere tourist attractionsIn practice, it has yet to be rated because it is considered an endeavor in scientific education, falling under the purview of the Cultural Relics Bureau rather than the Tourism Bureau. The Tourism Bureau has granted the Forbidden City the highest rating and naturally desires to do the same for Dunhuang. However, the Mogao Grottoes have not acquiesced. In former days, the Taoist king had already cast out all the gold, and the resplendent treasures rode makeshift cattle carts, wandering into foreign lands. The sedimented history pays no heed to transient hustle and bustle, while the British Museum, destined for daily foot traffic, bustles incessantly. History chuckles. Faced with vast, magnificent toys, infants find themselves bewildered. Yet, the entirety of culpability does not solely rest upon the Taoist king—Dunhuang was not unearthed in an auspicious era, and even today, I cannot easily sketch the contours of ancients. Thus, here, cultural heritage preservation and dissemination intertwine. To behold Dunhuang is to encounter Dunhuang yet not entirely Dunhuang. This journey has also lifted the veil of mystery in my mind. The image of Dunhuang, akin to the temples of the Maya, has dissolved. The Mogao Grottoes are neither a testament to the grandeur of a mysterious dynasty nor a site of blessings for unknown merchants. The “donors” are part of the Mogao Grottoes culture. In other words—who carved which caves. Everything is recorded plainly! After all, without leaving names, how would the deities receive their “payments”? Dunhuang lacks the unsolved mysteries of the Maya, but conversely, beneath the Maya civilization, there is no deeply sedimented loess land. The establishment of the grottoes spans from the Southern and Northern Dynasties to the Yuan Dynasty, and the marginal expansion of its scale reflects the prosperity and decline of the Silk Road. From the Li family of the Tang Dynasty to nameless merchants, if you dare to dig, you can dig. There are thousands of caves, each unique. Setting aside wealth, these grottoes embrace the “donors” who come and go, regardless of status, place of origin, or time. Relying solely on “flying apsaras” cannot uphold the phrase “Chinese treasure.” The most precious aspect of Dunhuang lies in the flowing years and its unique cultural temperament. History flows over these precipitous cliffs, time flips upside down, and finally condenses at the depths of the caves. From the tiles of the Southern and Northern Dynasties to the Yuan Dynasty, patterns evolve from simple geometric shapes to rounded lotuses. Whether angry or smiling, sharp or gentle, the myriad heavenly deities and Buddhas respond to the times. The multitude of cave entrances symbolizes the interaction of communities. In the long river of history filled with wars, there indeed exists such a solid port of ethnic integration. Inside the caves, there is no strong light; instead, the mineral pigments from the Tang Dynasty cover every surface, creating a faint fluorescent effect. Most of the sculptures I observed were of figures like Shakyamuni Buddha and Guanyin. Simply speaking of the sculptures, I did not perceive any advanced craftsmanship or exquisite expressions. According to the introduction, the internal craftsmanship mainly involves unique filling methods, often utilizing local materials, with a deeper cultural significance such as the reclining Buddha in Nirvana. Observing the seated Buddha indoors is quite marvelous. Unlike viewing the Leshan Giant Buddha under the bright sunlight, leaving nothing unseen, looking up at the seated Buddha inside the cave is different. The shadows above exude a profound sense of emptiness, making the Buddha statue appear enigmatic and compelling one to kneel in reverence. The murals of Dunhuang, illuminated by the dim light within the caves, leave one spellbound. The a
heading: The Mogao Grottoes aspire to be more than mere tourist attractions
title: The Mogao Grottoes aspire to be more than mere tourist attractions

content: The Hexi Corridor, truly formidable, unfolds its rugged terrain. The Qilian Mountains, with their majestic peaks and ridges, reveal the lean loess skin weathered over ages, adorned with streaks of black and red hues. The mountain summits swell like vertebrae, encircling the narrow passage with a slow, imposing embrace. Today, it serves as a natural pastureland, but yesterday, it was a treacherous gorge. Traveling along the main road, the distant mountains loom, pressed into ink wash, with shades of ochre and cyan dominating the scene. Once vegetation is lost and the mountains no longer provide cover, the vast sky and embracing Gobi become desolate. In this land of beacon fires and billowing smoke, tufts of grass resemble slender arrows, rudely piercing the desert’s skin at inopportune moments. In the valleys adorned with shrubs, occasional glimpses of the gentle ruins of the Great Wall emerge, nearly worn away by wind and sand, resembling mere road markers. Occasionally, a herd of horses, a group of cattle, or a few windmills appear, only to vanish behind the car window in the blink of an eye. If Don Quixote were to behold the slender white windmill blades at the foot of the mountain, he might indeed be astonished to encounter such elegantly slender giants, wouldn’t he? Yet, who created these giants? Who nurtured the creatures in the desert? The sands of history have never ceased to erode and bury, yet some have ventured far from the encroaching desert. There are always camel bells ringing in the dryness, and the aging loess also boasts the merit of blocking the billowing smoke. Initially, no one paid attention to the flowers aging beneath the cliffs, until the monuments of history stood tall above the sands of time. The distant sands carry no echoes, but who traversed the Hexi Corridor? The Hexi Corridor
title: The Hexi Corridor

content: Archiving past reflections. During a high school reading class, I casually picked up Yan Lianke’s literary essays. His advocacy for Divine Realism lingers with me to this day. While working through advanced mathematics, I suddenly grasped the shared essence of “Divine Realism” and “Magical Realism.” They both take “conveyance” as their mission, much like the rhetoric of ancient Greece, creating a reality of their own. Yet, the crux lies in the scene the novelist chooses to craft—that is where true artistry resides. Confucius said: “Let words convey meaning, and no more.” A critique of the futility in ornate expression, this statement forms the foundation of Divine Realism. These writers forgo flowery language or dazzling rhetoric. Instead, they emphasize the construction of a scene, delivering a visceral experience often laden with lingering aftertaste. The aroma of horses’ hooves, a monk balancing water—is this not such art? Such techniques cannot be summarized as “indirect or metaphorical”; they transcend simplistic categorizations. They emerge from meticulous contemplation of life’s interwoven relations, threading subtle details into profound undertones, capturing the nexus of things with precision. Yan Lianke’s example, recalled now, feels remarkably fitting: imagine the Titanic sinking beneath the waves. How might this be conveyed in a novel? Perhaps a seagull soars by, its body adorned with a small compass, quivering as it passes above the sea, sensing the ship’s magnetic pull. This construct rests firmly upon reality while radiating an uncanny tension. Truly, it embodies the ideal of “The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons”: an antelope hanging its horns on a tree, leaving no trace to follow. Consider the horns of a sheep. Perhaps we know a sheep by its horns because they are familiar to us, but the essence of a sheep is not bound to its horns. Many sheep lack them entirely. If we seize upon the horns as the cornerstone of a sheep’s image, our perspective gains a unique angle. Should this image then shift towards demonic figures or other forms, it ascends to the realm of extraordinary creation. Here lies the ethereal beauty of writing—a spiritual elegance, indeed. The balance between illusion and reality is delicate, like the elusive harmony of “unexpected yet reasonable.” Science rarely speaks in human terms, but pondering such constructs, one realizes that no matter how illusory they appear, their foundation is life’s meticulous observation: feel first, discern connections, then create. Material dictates consciousness—a truth that resonates deeply within me. img
title: Divine Realism

content: Striving to emulate the writing style of Walden. The beauty of its prose varies greatly between versions. Though I have yet to finish it, each reopening yields fresh insights. I have never been fond of winter’s blazing sun—the crimson orb that casts its light upon an indifferent air. The scant warmth teases the faces of passersby, much like a damp and probing tongue. By mere touch, I feel the burn upon my skin—a harsh caress of light peeling back layers like a blade, as if Siegfried himself wielded his gleaming sword, leaving one’s cheeks tingling, itching, raw. Perhaps it is the rush of blood within, but walking in such weather brings alternating waves of warmth and chill. The body becomes a vessel of fleeting seasons, encased momentarily in ice, then swiftly embraced by sunlight’s fervent touch, only to await the next frost. This interplay of sensation often unfolds on the school’s winter grounds. Uncomfortable though it may be, the symphony of voices brings solace, like the lilting melody of “Ballade pour Adeline,” leaving one entranced. The rhythmic tapping of footsteps and the lively echoes of play compose a sonorous celebration of life. What could rival this healthful and jubilant cadence of existence? The bounce of a basketball on the court sings a hymn of exuberance, its fervor untamed. The friction of a soccer ball against the turf whispers secrets, the soft rustle akin to a golden monkey slipping through the forest’s embrace. Beneath the throbbing drumbeat and the delicate chime of silver bells, the feathery stroke of a badminton bird weaves its airy tapestry—like the frantic flutter of startled pheasants alighting from treetops. Wood, rubber, and plastic collaborate in a playful harmony: the sturdy “thunk” of a paddle meeting ball, the hushed “swoosh” of air past a balloon, the frenetic “hiss” of a rapid volley. Thus, the wise cynic of the West reclines in a shattered barrel, bidding Alexander not to obscure his sun; Zhuangzi likens himself to a mud-bathing turtle, blissfully wagging its tail. Even now, humans find delight in a few planks and a ball—as do I, sharing in their joy. Such simple pleasures cost so little. Adults swing tirelessly at golf, elevating the game to a mark of elegance, their engagements a ceaseless negotiation of self-image. Children, meanwhile, find endless mirth in the toss of a stick. Yet adults, constrained by societal constructs, cannot stop at sticks, striving instead for gilded wheels of industry. Gold outshines the stars, black oil surpasses sweet springs. Two grown men building sandcastles might seem foolish and pitiable; yet, to me, they embody the true essence of life. For life, in its unadorned purity, is nature itself. The earth offers us a tranquil haven, yet humanity, in its pride, constructs fortresses of wealth and power, losing itself in self-made illusions. Only those willing to descend from their towers can truly reclaim themselves, returning to the soil from which they arose. Some may question my seeming indolence. To them, I ask only that they peer deep into Walden’s crystalline depths. A simple life soothes the weary soul; indeed, simplicity is the sole truth of existence.
title: Reflections on Walden
